greek: Θεὸς γὰρ ὢν ὁμοῦ τε καὶ ἄνθρωπος τέλειος ὁ αὐτὸς τὰς δύο αὐτοῦ οὐσίας ἐπιστώσατο ἡμῖν, τὴν μὲν θεότητα αὐτοῦ διὰ τῶν σημείων ἐν τῇ τριετίᾳ τῇ μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, τὴν δὲ ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς τριάκοντα χρόνοις τοῖς πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, ἐν οἷς διὰ τὸ ἀτελὲς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα ἀπέκρυβε τὰ σημεῖα τῆς αὐτοῦ θεότητος, καίπερ θεὸς ἀληθὴς προαιώνιος ὑπάρχων.

citation: Gregory Thaumaturgus — Declaration of Faith (Son clause)
author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
english: There is one Lord, only of the Only, God of God, stamp and image of the Godhead, the active Word, Wisdom that holds together the constitution of all things, and Power that makes the whole creation; true Son of the true Father, Invisible of Invisible, Incorruptible of Incorruptible, Immortal of Immortal, Eternal of Eternal.
translator_notes: Greek from Schaff, Creeds of Christendom II (Hahn text). Remapped away from ANF paraphrase that added “and through him we are saved,” which is not in this clause.
notes: Edition: Schaff/Hahn Greek of the ἔκθεσις πίστεως. Print-check against Hahn/Mansi still advised before sellable GTG.
greek: Εἷς κύριος μόνος ἐκ μόνου, θεὸς ἐκ θεοῦ, χαρακτὴρ καὶ εἰκὼν τῆς θεότητος, λόγος ἐνεργός, σοφία τῆς τῶν ὅλων συστάσεως περιεκτικὴ καὶ δύναμις τῆς ὅλης κτίσεως ποιητική, υἱὸς ἀληθινὸς ἀληθινοῦ πατρός, ἀόρατος ἀοράτου καὶ ἄφθαρτος ἀφθάρτου καὶ ἀθάνατος ἀθανάτου καὶ ἀΐδιος ἀϊδίου.

citation: Dionysius of Alexandria — On Nature (via Eusebius PE 14.23–24)
author: Dionysius of Alexandria
english: Some give the name “atoms” to certain imperishable and most minute bodies, infinite in number, and they put forward a void of unbounded extent. These atoms, they say, are borne about at random in the void, collide of themselves through an irregular rush, and tangle because they are many-shaped and catch hold of one another — and so produce the world and what is in it, or rather worlds without number. Epicurus and Democritus held this view.

How are we to bear with them when they say that the wise and therefore beautiful works of creation are chance coincidences? Works of which each, as it came into being by itself, and likewise all of them together, were seen to be good by the One who commanded them to be made. For Scripture says: “And God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good.”

They are not even instructed by the small, familiar examples at their feet, from which they could learn that no useful work made for benefit is finished without design or by mere accident, but is crafted by hand for its fitting service — and only when it falls into uselessness is it dissolved and scattered at random, because the wisdom that cared for its standing no longer manages or orders it.
translator_notes: Greek locked from local First1K Eusebius PE TEI (Dindorf) at the Dionysius anti-Epicurus block (vign ~773–774), despite mislabeled book heads. Rematched away from the earlier unverified “evil is not a substance / free creature” English.
notes: PE TEI book n=14 is mis-headed in file; locus verified by Greek content + closing attribution to Dionysius the bishop against Epicurus.
translation_mode=abridged: Abridges Democritus/Epicurus disagreement detail and Eusebius narrative bridge. Omissions marked with […] where mid-span cuts remain.
greek: οἶ μὲν γὰρ ἀτόμους προσειπόντες ἄφθαρτά τινα καὶ σμικρότατα σώματα πλῆθος ἀνάριθμα, καί τι χωρίον κενὸν μέγεθος ἀπεριόριστον προβαλόμενοι, ταύτας δή φασι τὰς ἀτόμους ὡς ἔτυχεν ἐν τῷ κενῷ φερομένας αὐτομάτως τε συμπιπτούσας ἀλλήλαις διὰ ῥύμην ἄτακτον καὶ συμπλεκομένας διὰ τὸ πολυσχήμονας οὔσας ἀλλήλων ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι, καὶ οὕτω τόν τε κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ κόσμους ἀπείρους ἀποτελεῖν. ταύτης δὲ τῆς δόξης ’Επίκουρος γεγόνασι καὶ Δημόκριτος· τοσοῦτον δὲ δὲ διεφώνησαν ὅσον ὁ μὲν ἐλαχίστας πάσας καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀνεπαισθήτους, ὁ δὲ καὶ μεγίστας εἶναί τινας ἀτόμους ὁ Δημόκριτος ὑπέλαβεν. ἀτόμους δὲ εἶναί φασιν ἀμφότεροι καὶ λέγεσθαι διὰ τὴν ἄλυτον στερρότητα. οἶ δὲ τὰς ἀτόμους μετονομάσαντες ἀμερῆ φασιν εἶναι σώματα, τοῦ παντὸς μέρη, ἐξ ὧν ἀδιαιρέτων ὄντων συντίθεται τὰ πάντα καὶ εἰς ἃ διαλύεται. καὶ τούτων φασὶ τῶν ἀμερῶν ὀνοματοποιὸν Διόδωρον γεγονέναι· ὄνομα δὲ, φασὶν, αὐτοῖς ἄλλο Ἡρακλείδης θέμενος ἐκάλεσεν ὄγκους, παρ’ οὗ καὶ Ἀσκληπιάδης ὁ ἰατρὸς ἐκληρονόμησε τὸ ὄνομα.” Ταῦτ’ εἰπὼν ἐξῆς ἀνασκευάζει τὸ δόγμα διὰ πολλῶν, ἀτὰρ καὶ διὰ τούτων ‟Πῶς αὐτῶν ἀνασχώμεθα τυχηρὰ λεγόντων εἶναι συμπτώματα τὰ σοφὰ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὰ καλὰ δημιουργήματα; ὣν ἕκαστόν τε καθ’ ἑαυτὸ γενόμενον ὤφθη τῷ προστάξαντι γενέσθαι καλὸν καὶ συλλήβδην ὁμοίως ἅπαντα. καὶ εἶδε γὰρ, φησὶν, ὁ θεὸς τὰ πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησε, καὶ ἰδοὺ καλὰ λίαν. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἀπὸ τῶν μικρῶν τῶν συνήθων καὶ παρὰ πόδας νουθετοῦνται παραδειγμάτων, ἐξ ὧν δύνανται μανθάνειν ὅτι χρειῶδες μὲν καὶ πρὸς ὠφέλειαν ἔργον οὐδὲν ἀνεπιτηδεύτως οὐδὲ συμβατικῶς ἀπεργάζεται, ἀλλὰ χειρουργούμενον εἰς τὴν πρέπουσαν ὑπηρεσίαν καταρτίζεται· ὅταν δὲ εἰς ἄχρηστον μεταπίπτῃ καὶ ἀνωφελὲς, τότε διαλυόμενον ἀορίστως καὶ ὡς ἂν τύχῃ διασκίδναται, ἅτε μηκέτι μεταχειριζομένης μηδὲ διαταττούσης αὐτὸ τῆς σοφίας, ᾗ τοῦ συνεστάναι τοῦτο ἔμελεν.

author: Tatian
english: But we ourselves stand above fate. Instead of wandering demons we have learned one Master who does not wander, and since we are not driven by fate we have refused the ones who wrote its laws.
greek: Ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ εἱμαρμένης ἐσμὲν ἀνώτεροι, καὶ ἀντὶ πλανητῶν δαιμόνων ἕνα τὸν ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην μεμαθήκαμεν, καὶ οὐ καθ’ εἱμαρμένην ἀγόμενοι τοὺς ταύτης νομοθέτας παρῃτήμεθα.
translator_notes: New English from locked Greek. εἱμαρμένη = fate; ἀπλανῆ δεσπότην puns against planetary (πλανῆται) demons.
notes: fate-foreknowledge-mine 2026-09-12

citation: Victorinus of Pettau — On the Creation of the World (sixth day)
author: Victorinus of Pettau
work: On the Creation of the World
english: On the fifth day land and water brought forth their young. On the sixth day the things still lacking were created; and so God formed the human being from the soil as lord of all he had made on land and water. Yet he created angels and archangels before he fashioned the human, putting spiritual things before earthly ones. For light was before heaven and earth. This sixth day is called parasceve — preparation of the kingdom. He completed Adam after his image and likeness. For that reason he finished his works before he created the angels and fashioned the human, lest they falsely claim they had been his helpers.
translator_notes: Latin locked to printed Migne PL 5 / Routh Reliquiae Sacrae III continuous sixth-day column (local PL PDF Vision OCR + Wikisource/Routh cross-check).
Restored omitted “Prius enim lux, quam coelum et terram.” Walker conjectures (terra / delete quem / asseverarent) recorded as variants only.
Dropped earlier ANF-mediated gloss that smuggled in “capacity to know and to choose.”
notes: Promoted 2026-09-10 after second-model hold-unlock PASS.
Printed Migne/Routh continuous Latin; Walker conjectures in apparatus only.
latin: Die quinto terra et aqua foetus suos ediderunt. Die sexto creata sunt, quae deerant; ac sic Deus hominem de humo instruxit, dominum omnium rerum, quae super terram et super aquam creavit. Prius tamen angelos atque archangelos creavit, quam hominem finxit, spiritalia terrenis anteponens. Prius enim lux, quam coelum et terram. Hic dies sextus parasceve appellatur, praeparatio scilicet regni; Adam enim quem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam consummavit. Idcirco autem prius opera sua consummavit, quam angelos creavit, et hominem fabricavit, ne forte adjutores se fuisse falsa dictione asseverant.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: This is the one after the image and likeness: the true knower, who imitates God as far as he can, leaving out nothing that belongs to that possible likeness — self-controlled, enduring, living justly, ruling his passions, sharing what he has as he is able, and doing good in word and deed. He is greatest in the kingdom, Scripture says, who both does and teaches, imitating God by giving gifts of the same kind. For God’s gifts are for the common good.
greek: Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ κατ’ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν, ὁ γνωστικός, ὁ μιμούμενος τὸν θεὸν καθ’ ὅσον οἷόν τε, μηδὲν παραλιπὼν τῶν εἰς τὴν ἐνδεχομένην ὁμοίωσιν, ἐγκρατευόμενος, ὑπομένων, δικαίως βιούς, βασιλεύων τῶν παθῶν, μεταδιδοὺς ὧν ἔχει, ὡς οἷός τέ ἐστιν, εὐεργετῶν καὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ. οὗτος μέγιστος, φησίν, ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ὃς ἂν ποιῇ καὶ διδάσκῃ μιμούμενος τὸν θεὸν τῷ παραπλήσια χαρίζεσθαι· κοινωφελεῖς γὰρ αἱ τοῦ θεοῦ δωρεαί.
translator_notes: New English from locked Greek. ὁ γνωστικός = Clement’s Christian knower, not a heretical sectarian.
κατ’ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν = image and likeness; likeness as moral imitation of God.
notes: image-likeness-mine 2026-09-12: image/likeness as lived imitation, not destroyed nature.

author: Irenaeus
english: God gave the good, as the apostle also testifies in the same letter. Those who work it will receive glory and honor, because they worked the good when they were also able not to work it.

Those who do not work it will receive God’s just judgment, because they did not work the good when they were able to work it. The showing is not that some are good by nature and others evil, but that the good lies in human choice.
translator_notes: Locked to continuous Harvey Latin for AH 4.37.4 only; no counsel/necessity sentence from the next section.
notes: Re-audit follow-up 2026-09-10: continuous Harvey Latin extracted from vol.2 free-will block (Dedit ergo Deus bonum… electione sit bonum). Counsel paragraph moved out — it belongs to 4.37.5.
Harvey OCR cleaned; print-check still advised before sellable.
latin:
Dedit ergo Deus bonum, quemadmodum et Apostolus testificatur in eadem epistola, et qui operantur quidem illud, gloriam et honorem percipient, quoniam operati sunt bonum cum possint non operari illud; hi autem qui illud non operantur, judicium justum excipient Dei, quoniam non sunt operati bonum cum possint operari illud.

Ostensio quod non natura quidam boni sint, quidam vero mali, sed quod in hominis electione sit bonum.

author: Justin Martyr
english: We do not say that what happens to people is done or suffered by fate. Each person succeeds or sins by deliberate choice (προαίρεσις), and wicked demons also work against the serious — as they did against Socrates and his like — while a Sardanapalus or an Epicurus seems to prosper.

The Stoics missed this and declared that everything happens by fate’s necessity. But God made both the race of angels and of human beings self-determining (αὐτεξούσιον) from the beginning; therefore they justly receive punishment in eternal fire for whatever they do wrong.
It is the nature of everything that has come to be to be capable of vice and virtue. Nothing of theirs would be praiseworthy if it did not also have the power to turn either way.
translator_notes: Compressed; expand on full Greek/ANF pass for Second Apology fate discussion.
notes: Legacy id justin_2apol_7 retained; canonical locus is ch.6 (εἱμαρμένη / προαίρεσις). Stale anf_mediated note removed after Greek rematch.
translation_mode=abridged: Selected continuous span within ch.6; not the whole chapter. Omissions marked with […] where mid-span cuts remain.

author: Tatian
english: How then am I to accept a birth under fate, when I see such “managers” of it? I do not want to be king. I do not want to be rich. I have refused generalship. I have hated fornication. I do not sail for greed. I do not compete for crowns. I am free of glory-madness. I despise death. I rise above every kind of sickness. Grief does not consume my soul.

If I am a slave, I endure slavery; if I am free, I do not boast of noble birth. I see one sun for all, and one death for all through pleasure and lack. We were not made in order to die — we die through ourselves. Self-determining power (τὸ αὐτεξούσιον) ruined us; we who were free became slaves; we were sold through sin. God made nothing base; we displayed the wickedness — and those who displayed it are also able to refuse it again.

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: The tree of knowledge was not evil as a tree; disobedience was evil. Knowledge itself is good when used rightly. Adam was still a child; he could not yet receive knowledge as he should.
That is why God forbade him to take from the tree for a time — not from jealousy, but so that he might grow first. Disobedience finally brought death.
translator_notes: Removed earlier “obedience would have brought life” clause — that parallel sits in Ad Autolycum 2.27, not in the locked 2.25 Greek block.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: I know many who continually attack us and say that what does not hinder is a cause. They say the one who did not guard, or did not prevent, is cause of a theft — as the one who did not put out a fire at the start is cause of the blaze, and the pilot who did not furl the sail is cause of shipwreck. The law even punishes such “causes.”

We answer that a cause is understood in doing and acting and effecting, while what does not hinder is, as such, inactive. The cause stands with the activity — as the shipbuilder with the ship’s coming to be.
translator_notes: Stromata 1.17 is providence/causation (μὴ κωλῦον ≠ αἴτιον), not the ANF “drag by the hair” locus.
notes: Rewritten from Greek; prior hair/persuade English discarded as wrong citation.

author: Origen
english: This also is defined in the church’s proclamation: that every rational soul is of free choice and will; and that it has a struggle against the devil and his angels and opposing powers — because they strive to weigh it down with sins, while we, if we live rightly and wisely, try to throw off that kind of burden.
translator_notes: Locked from Rufinus Latin preface. Glossary: free choice / will (arbitrium), not later system slogan “free will.”
notes: OCR noisy at margins; human clear against print still needed.

author: Lactantius
english: This is why someone who would rather go without or die than harm another or snatch something seems foolish — people think a human being is destroyed by death. From that persuasion come the errors of the crowd and of the philosophers.

If after death we are nothing, it is most foolish not to manage this life so that it lasts long and is full of every advantage — and whoever does that must leave the rule of justice. But if a better and longer life remains for a human being — which we learn from great philosophers’ arguments, oracles of seers, and divine voices of prophets — then it is the wise person’s part to despise the present with its goods, since every loss is weighed against immortality.
notes: Previous ANF-sense English (“God wants us good / does not force”) did not match CSEL Inst 5.18; rewritten from locked Latin.

citation: Methodius — Concerning Free Will (On God and Matter 11)
author: Methodius of Olympus
english: How then do you say he left the qualities of the worthless as they were? Was he able to remove them too, but unwilling — or did he lack the power?

If you say he was able but unwilling, you must call him their cause: able to make them not be bad, he allowed them to remain as they were — especially when he began to craft the matter. If he had no care for matter at all, he would not be cause of what he let remain; but since he crafts one part and leaves another as it is, though able to turn that too toward the better, he seems to me to incur blame for leaving a wicked part of matter to the ruin of what he crafted.
translator_notes: Remapped: ANF “eye watches the runner” not in First1K tlg002; locked from ch.11 Greek on ἀνάγκη / divine blame if evil left by choice.
notes: Foreknowledge illustration retired; this locus is necessity/blame vs coeternal matter.

author: Hermas
english: “Do you see this shepherd?” “I see him, Lord.” “This,” he said, “is the angel of luxury and deceit. He wears down the souls of God’s servants and turns them from the truth, deceiving them with the wicked desires in which they perish.
They forget the commandments of the living God and walk in deceits and empty luxuries, and they are ruined by this angel — some unto death, some unto corruption.”
translator_notes: Compressed from longer similitude; expand on next fidelity pass.
notes: translation_mode=abridged: Selected span within Sim. 6. Omissions marked with […] where mid-span cuts remain.

author: Mathetes (Epistle to Diognetus)
english: Christians are not distinguished from the rest of people by land, language, or customs. They live in Greek and barbarian cities as each one’s lot falls; they follow local customs in dress and food and the rest of life.

Yet they show a striking and admittedly paradoxical citizenship of their own. They live in their own countries — but as sojourners. They share all things as citizens, and endure all things as foreigners. Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland a foreign land.
translator_notes: Lived obedience as public apologetic — keep the poised paradoxes.

author: Irenaeus
english: and his coming from the heavens in the Father’s glory to sum up all things again, and to raise all flesh of all humankind,

so that before Christ Jesus your Lord — and God, and Savior, and King — by the good pleasure of the invisible Father, every knee of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth may bend, and every tongue may confess him.
translator_notes: ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι kept as ‘sum up again’ (recapitulate), not ‘restore’ alone.
Greek locked from sources/greek/irenaeus_ah.xml (Massuet I.x.1 / Harvey I.ii). Witness reads Κυρίῳ ὑμῶν.
notes: Unused locus for atonement-recapitulation (prior mines: 5.1.2, 5.21.1, Melito incarnation fr.).
greek: καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ Πατρὸς παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα, καὶ ἀναστῆσαι πᾶσαν σάρκα πάσης ἀνθρωπότητος, ἵνα Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ὑμῶν, καὶ Θεῷ, καὶ Σωτῆρι, καὶ Βασιλεῖ, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ Πατρὸς τοῦ ἀοράτου, πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ καταχθονίων, καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται αὐτῷ

author: Anonymous (Diognetus)
english: For God loved human beings. For their sake he made the world. To them he subjected everything on the earth. He gave them reason and mind. To them alone he allowed an upward look toward himself. He formed them from his own image. To them he sent his only-begotten Son. To them he promised the kingdom in heaven — and he will give it to those who have loved him.
translator_notes: ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας εἰκόνος ἔπλασε: ‘formed from his own image’ (Gen 1:26–27 echo).
δι᾽ οὕς taken as ‘for whose sake’.
Pass A ≠ Pass B. Distinct from diognetus_10_2_universal_call (same chapter, different clause).
greek: ὁ γὰρ θεὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἠγάπησε, δι᾽ οὓς ἐποίησε τὸν κόσμον, οἷς ὑπέταξε πάντα τὰ ἐν τῇ γῇ, οἷς λόγον ἔδωκεν, οἷς νοῦν, οἷς μόνοις ἄνω πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁρᾶν ἐπέτρεψεν, οὓς ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας εἰκόνος ἔπλασε, πρὸς οὓς ἀπέστειλε τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ, οἷς τὴν ἐν οὐρανῷ βασιλείαν ἐπηγγείλατο, καὶ δώσει τοῖς ἀγαπήσασιν αὐτόν.

author: Anonymous (Didache)
english: About baptism, baptize this way. After you have said all these things beforehand, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, in living water.
If you do not have living water, baptize in other water; if you cannot use cold, use warm.
If you have neither, pour water on the head three times in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Before the baptism let the baptizer and the one being baptized fast, and any others who can. You are to tell the one being baptized to fast for one or two days beforehand.
translator_notes: ὕδωρ ζῶν kept as ‘living water’ (running water), not ‘fresh’ alone.
Instructional second person retained in Pass B.
greek: Περὶ δὲ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, οὕτω βαπτίσατε· ταῦτα πάντα προειπόντες, βαπτίσατε εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἐν ὕδατι ζῶντι. ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἔχῃς ὕδωρ ζῶν, εἰς ἄλλο ὕδωρ βάπτισον· εἰ δ᾽ οὐ δύνασαι ἐν ψυχρῷ, ἐν θερμῷ. ἐὰν δὲ ἀμφότερα μὴ ἔχῃς, ἔκχεον εἰς τὴν κεφαλὴν τρὶς ὕδωρ εἰς ὄνομα πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος. πρὸ δὲ τοῦ βαπτίσματος προνηστευσάτω ὁ βαπτίζων καὶ ὁ βαπτιζόμενος καὶ εἴ τινες ἄλλοι δύνανται· κελεύεις δὲ νηστεῦσαι τὸν βαπτιζόμενον πρὸ μιᾶς ἢ δύο.

author: Justin Martyr
english: and that he would be believed by people from every race,
and that God calls him Son and has promised to put all enemies under him,
and how the demons, as far as they can, try to flee both the authority of God the Father of all and Master and the authority of Christ himself,
and how God calls everyone to repentance before the day of judgment comes.
translator_notes: Lock from sources/greek/justin_1apology.xml; αἰτοῖς/αἰτοῦ normalized to αὐτοῖς/αὐτοῦ (lookalike OCR).
εἰς μετάνοιαν καλεῖ πάντας: ‘calls everyone to repentance.’
greek: καὶ ὅτι πιστεύεσθαι ἔμελλεν ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκ παντὸς γένους ἀνθρώπων, καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸν υἱὸν καλεῖ ὁ θεὸς καὶ ὑποτάσσειν αὐτῷ πάντας ἐχθροὺς ἐπήγγελται, καὶ πῶς οἱ δαίμονες, ὅσον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς, τήν τε τοῦ πατρὸς πάντων καὶ δεσπότου θεοῦ καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐξουσίαν φυγεῖν πειρῶνται, καὶ ὡς εἰς μετάνοιαν καλεῖ πάντας ὁ θεὸς πρὶν ἐλθεῖν τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς κρίσεως.

author: Barnabas
english: When he renewed us in the forgiveness of sins, he made us another kind of thing, so that we have a child’s soul, as if he were forming us again.

For the Scripture speaks about us when he says to the Son: “Let us make the human according to our image and according to our likeness, and let them rule the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven and the fish of the sea.”
And the Lord said, seeing our good formation: “Grow and multiply and fill the earth.”
He said these things to the Son. I will show you again how he speaks to us: he made a second formation in the last times.
And the Lord says: “See, I make the last things like the first.”
translator_notes: ἀναπλάσσοντος: ‘forming us again’ (second creation after forgiveness).
κατ᾽ εἰκόνα καὶ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν: Gen 1:26 lock.
greek: ἀνακαινίσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἀφέσει τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς ἄλλον τύπον, ὡς παιδίων ἔχειν τὴν ψυχήν, ὡς ἂν δὴ ἀναπλάσσοντος αὐτοῦ ἡμᾶς. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ περὶ ἡμῶν, ὡς λέγει τῷ υἱῷ· Ποιήσωμεν κατ᾽ εἰκόνα καὶ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμῶν τὸν ἄνθρωπον, καὶ ἀρχέτωσαν τῶν θηρίων τῆς γῆς καὶ τῶν πετεινῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ τῶν ἰχθύων τῆς θαλάσσης. καὶ εἶπεν κύριος, ἰδὼν τὸ καλὸν πλάσμα ἡμῶν· Αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε καὶ πληρώσατε τὴν γῆν. ταῦτα πρὸς τὸν υἱόν. πάλιν σοι ἐπιδείξω, πῶς πρὸς ἡμᾶς λέγει δευτέραν πλάσιν ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτων ἐποίησεν. λέγει δὲ κύριος· Ἰδού, ποιῶ τὰ ἔσχατα ὡς τὰ πρῶτα.

author: Anonymous (Didache)
english: Then the human race will come into the fire of testing. Many will stumble and be ruined, but those who hold out in their faith will be saved by the Curse-bearer himself.

And then the signs of the truth will appear: first a sign of opening in heaven, then a sign of a trumpet blast, and third the rising of the dead — not of all, but as it was said: “The Lord will come, and all the holy ones with him.”
Then the world will see the Lord coming on the clouds of heaven.
translator_notes: καταθέματος: ‘Curse-bearer’ (Christ who became a curse), not ‘deposit’.
greek: τότε ἥξει ἡ κτίσις τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰς τὴν πύρωσιν τῆς δοκιμασίας, καὶ σκανδαλισθήσονται πολλοὶ καὶ ἀπολοῦνται, οἱ δὲ ὑπομείναντες ἐν τῇ πίστει αὐτῶν σωθήσονται ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ καταθέματος. καὶ τότε φανήσεται τὰ σημεῖα τῆς ἀληθείας· πρῶτον σημεῖον ἐκπετάσεως ἐν οὐρανῷ, εἶτα σημεῖον φωνῆς σάλπιγγος, καὶ τὸ τρίτον ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν· οὐ πάντων δέ, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐρρέθη· Ἥξει ὁ κύριος καὶ πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ. τότε ὄψεται ὁ κόσμος τὸν κύριον ἐρχόμενον ἐπάνω τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ.

author: Hermas
english: “Hear now,” he said, “about faith. There are two angels with a human being: one of righteousness and one of wickedness.”
“How then, Lord,” I said, “will I know their workings, since both angels live with me?”

“Hear,” he said, “and you will understand them. The angel of righteousness is tender, shamefast, gentle, and quiet. When he rises in your heart, he at once speaks with you about righteousness, purity, dignity, contentment, every righteous work, and every holy virtue. Those are the works of the angel of righteousness. Trust him and his works.

Look also at the works of the angel of wickedness. First of all he is quick-tempered, bitter, and senseless, and his works are wicked, overthrowing the servants of God. When he rises in your heart, know him from his works.”
translator_notes: Two angels with the person = two moral ways.
greek: Ἄκουε νῦν, φησί, περὶ τῆς πίστεως. δύο εἰσὶν ἄγγελοι μετὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, εἷς τῆς δικαιοσύνης καὶ εἷς τῆς πονηρίας. Πῶς οὖν, φημί, κύριε, γνώσομαι τὰς αὐτῶν ἐνεργείας, ὅτι ἀμφότεροι ἄγγελοι μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ κατοικοῦσιν; Ἄκουε, φησί, καὶ συνήσεις αὐτάς. ὁ μὲν τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἄγγελος τρυφερός ἐστι καὶ αἰσχυντηρὸς καὶ πραῢς καὶ ἡσύχιος· ὅταν οὖν οὗτος ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου ἀναβῇ, εὐθέως λαλεῖ μετὰ σοῦ περὶ δικαιοσύνης, περὶ ἁγνείας, περὶ σεμνότητος, περὶ αὐταρκείας, καὶ περὶ παντὸς ἔργου δικαίου καὶ περὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς ἁγίας. ταῦτα οὖν ἐστι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ ἀγγέλου τῆς δικαιοσύνης. τούτῳ οὖν πίστευε καὶ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ. ὅρα οὖν καὶ τοῦ ἀγγέλου τῆς πονηρίας τὰ ἔργα. πρῶτον πάντων ὀξύχολός ἐστι καὶ πικρὸς καὶ ἄφρων, καὶ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ πονηρά, καταστρέφοντα τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ· ὅταν οὖν οὗτος ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου ἀναβῇ, γνῶθι αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ.

author: Barnabas
english: And he himself endured — so that he might abolish death and show the rising from the dead — because he had to be made visible in flesh, so that he might pay the promise to the fathers, and so that, preparing a new people for himself while he was on the earth, he might show that he himself, having made the resurrection, will judge.
translator_notes: καταργήσῃ τὸν θάνατον: abolish death (2 Tim 1:10 echo).
greek: αὐτὸς δέ, ἵνα καταργήσῃ τὸν θάνατον καὶ τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν δείξῃ, ὅτι ἐν σαρκὶ ἔδει αὐτὸν φανερωθῆναι, ὑπέμεινεν, ἵνα τοῖς πατράσιν τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν ἀποδῷ, καὶ αὐτὸς ἑαυτῷ τὸν λαὸν τὸν καινὸν ἑτοιμάζων ἐπιδείξῃ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ὤν, ὅτι τὴν ἀνάστασιν αὐτὸς ποιήσας κρινεῖ.

author: Hermas
english: For before a person bears the name of the Son of God, he says, that person is dead; but when he receives the seal, he puts away the deadness and takes up life.
The seal, then, is the water: into the water the dead go down, and they come up living. So this seal was also preached to them, and they used it, so that they might enter the kingdom of God.
translator_notes: σφραγὶς = baptismal seal identified with water.
greek: πρὶν γάρ, φησί, φορέσαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, νεκρός ἐστιν· ὅταν δὲ λάβῃ τὴν σφραγῖδα, ἀποτίθεται τὴν νέκρωσιν καὶ ἀναλαμβάνει τὴν ζωήν. ἡ σφραγὶς οὖν τὸ ὕδωρ ἐστίν· εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ οὖν καταβαίνουσι νεκροὶ καὶ ἀναβαίνουσι ζῶντες. κἀκείνοις οὖν ἐκηρύχθη ἡ σφραγὶς αὕτη καὶ ἐχρήσαντο αὐτῇ, ἵνα εἰσέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.

author: Tatian
english: And the power of the Word, having in itself foreknowledge of what will turn out, was not predicting outcomes according to fate, but according to the judgment of free choosers.
By prohibitions it became a restrainer of wickedness, and a praiser of the goods that remain.
translator_notes: οὐ καθ᾽ εἱμαρμένην vs αὐτεξουσίων γνώμῃ kept sharp.
greek: Ἡ δὲ τοῦ λόγου δύναμις ἔχουσα παρ᾿ ἑαυτῇ προγνωστικὸν τὸ μέλλον ἀποβαίνειν, οὐ καθ᾿ εἱμαρμένην, τῇ δὲ τῶν αἱρουμένων αὐτεξουσίων γνώμῃ, τῶν μελλόντων προὔλεγε τὰς ἀποβάσεις· καὶ τῆς μὲν πονηρίας κωλυτὴς ἐγίνετο δι᾿ ἀπαγορεύσεων, τῶν δὲ μενόντων ἀγαθῶν ἐγκωμιαστής.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: For the teaching of godliness is a gift, and faith itself is grace. By doing the will of God we come to know the will.
translator_notes: χάρις δὲ ἡ πίστις: faith named as grace, not mere unaided assent.

added_allusions.reason: open gates of righteousness nearby in Strom context.

greek: δωρεὰ γὰρ ἡ διδασκαλία τῆς θεοσεβείας, χάρις δὲ ἡ πίστις. ποιοῦντες γὰρ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ θέλημα γινώσκομεν.

author: Tatian
english: For the heavenly Word, who became Spirit from the Father and Word from the rational power, made the human being an image of immortality after the pattern of the Father who begot him, so that, just as incorruption is with God, a human who shares in a portion of God may also have immortality.
translator_notes: εἰκόνα τῆς ἀθανασίας locked as ‘image of immortality’.
greek: Λόγος γὰρ ὁ ἐπουράνιος, πνεῦμα γεγονὼς ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ λόγος ἐκ τῆς λογικῆς δυνάμεως, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ γεννήσαντος αὐτὸν πατρὸς μίμησιν εἰκόνα τῆς ἀθανασίας τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐποίησεν, ἵνα, ὥσπερ ἡ ἀφθαρσία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον θεοῦ μοῖραν ἄνθρωπος μεταλαβὼν ἔχῃ καὶ τὸ ἀθάνατον.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: For the Word, like the herald’s call at Olympia, calls whoever is willing, and crowns whoever is able.
translator_notes: καλεῖ μὲν τὸν βουλόμενον: open call without compulsion.
greek: ὁ γάρ τοι λόγος καθάπερ τὸ κήρυγμα τὸ Ὀλυμπίασι καλεῖ μὲν τὸν βουλόμενον, στεφανοῖ δὲ τὸν δυνάμενον.

author: Ignatius of Antioch
english: There is one physician, both fleshly and spiritual, begotten and unbegotten, God in a human, true life in death, both from Mary and from God, first passible and then impassible — Jesus Christ our Lord.
translator_notes: εἷς ἰατρός kept as ‘one physician’ (healing Savior).
ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ Θεός: God in a human — not abstract ‘God in man’ only.
greek: εἷς ἰατρός ἐστιν, σαρκικός τε καὶ πνευματικός, γεννητὸς καὶ ἀγέννητος, ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ Θεός, ἐν θανάτῳ ζωὴ ἀληθινή, καὶ ἐκ Μαρίας καὶ ἐκ Θεοῦ, πρῶτον παθητὸς καὶ τότε ἀπαθής, Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν.

citation: Methodius of Olympus — Symposium 8 (Word incarnate; dragon)
author: Methodius of Olympus
english: And as arch-shepherd and arch-prophet, the Word also became arch-virgin for the church by becoming human. John, taken by Christ, shows this to us in the book of Revelation when he says: “I looked, and behold, the Lamb standing on Mount Zion.”

Christ, long since conceived, was not snatched away to God’s throne the moment he was born out of fear that the serpent might harm him. Rather, for this he was born and himself came down from the Father’s thrones: to master the dragon while remaining as the dragon rushed against the flesh.
translator_notes: χειρώσηται: master/subdue the dragon — soteriological conquest in the flesh.
OCR παοστρέχοντα normalized to προστρέχοντα from sense of Bonwetsch apparatus.

added_allusions.reason: dragon vs male child / church birth.

greek: ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἀρχιπάρθενος, ὃν τρόπον καὶ ἀρχιποιμὴν καὶ ἀρχιπροφήτης, γέγονεν ὁ λόγος ἐνανθρωπήσας τῆς ἐκκλησίας· καὶ ὁ χριστόληπτος ἡμῖν παρίστησιν ἐν βίβλῳ τῆς Ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰωάννης λέγων· καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἰδοὺ τὸ ἀρνίον ἑστὼς ἐπὶ τὸ ὄρος Σιών. ὁ δὲ Χριστὸς πάλαι κυηθεὶς οὐχ ἡρπάσθη ὁπότε ἐτέχθη πρὸς τὸν θρόνον τοῦ θεοῦ, φόβῳ τοῦ μὴ λυμήνασθαι αὐτὸν τὸν ὄφιν· ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο ἐγεννήθη καὶ κατῆλθεν αὐτὸς ἀπὸ τῶν θρόνων τοῦ πατρός, ἵνα τὸν δράκοντα χειρώσηται, μείνας προστρέχοντα τῇ σαρκί.

author: Athenagoras
english: Would we, then, cleanse ourselves like this if we did not think God stands over the human race? It is impossible to say so.

But since we are persuaded that we will render an account of this whole life here to the God who made both us and the world, we choose a measured, humane, and easily scorned life, thinking we will suffer no such great evil here — even if some take our soul — compared with what we will receive there from the great Judge for a gentle, humane, and equitable life.
Plato said Minos and Rhadamanthys would judge and punish the wicked; but we say that even if it were Minos or Rhadamanthys or their father, not even he would escape the judgment of God.
translator_notes: ὑφέξειν λόγον: render an account — courtroom sense.

added_allusions.reason: each will give account to God.

greek: Ἆρα τοίνυν, εἰ μὴ ἐφεστηκέναι θεὸν τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει ἐνομίζομεν, οὕτως ἂν ἑαυτοὺς ἐξεκαθαίρομεν; Οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐπεὶ πεπείσμεθα ὑφέξειν παντὸς τοῦ ἐνταῦθα βίου λόγον τῷ πεποιηκότι καὶ ἡμᾶς καὶ τὸν κόσμον θεῷ, τὸν μέτριον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον βίον αἱρούμεθα, οὐδὲν τηλικοῦτον πείσεσθαι κακὸν ἐνταῦθα νομίζοντες, κἂν τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμᾶς ἀφαιρῶνταί τινες, ὧν ἐκεῖ κομιούμεθα τοῦ πράου καὶ φιλανθρώπου καὶ ἐπιεικοῦς βίου παρὰ τοῦ μεγάλου δικαστοῦ. Πλάτων μὲν οὖν Μίνω καὶ Ῥαδάμανθυν δικάσειν καὶ κολάσειν τοὺς πονηροὺς ἔφη, ἡμεῖς δέ, κἂν Μίνως τις κἂν Ῥαδάμανθυς ᾖ κἂν ὁ τούτων πατήρ, οὐδὲ τοῦτόν φαμεν διαφεύξεσθαι τὴν κρίσιν τοῦ θεοῦ.

citation: Methodius of Olympus — On Things Created (De Creatis / Photius) §2
author: Methodius of Olympus
english: Either these things were set before all the Greeks and the other unbelievers by Christ’s disciples and were proclaimed, and turned them from impiety to faith in Christ — just as we who believe confess — and then “do not throw your pearls before pigs” can no longer be read as it was said;

or, if that saying is taken as it was said, we are forced to claim that faith in Christ and freedom from impiety never came to any of the unbelievers we were comparing — from the apostolic teachings that light the soul like pearls. And that is blasphemous.
translator_notes: New treatise for Methodius lane (not Symposium / De libero arbitrio).
ἐλευθερία = freedom from impiety, not free-will slogan.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Greek locked from methodius_tlg005.xml.

added_allusions.reason: pearls before pigs — the verse under reductio.

greek: ἢ οὖν πᾶσι τοῖς Ἕλλησι καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀπίστοις ταῦτα παρεβλήθη παρὰ τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ μαθητῶν καὶ ἐκηρύχθη, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀσεβείας μετέβαλεν αὐτοὺς εἰς τὴν εἰς Χριστὸν πίστιν ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ πιστεύοντες ὁμολογοῦμεν, καὶ οὐκέτι δύναται νοεῖσθαι τό »μὴ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων«, ὡς ἐρρήθη· ἢ τούτου ὡς ἐλέχθη νοουμένου, ἀνάγκη ἡμᾶς λέγειν ὡς οὐδενὶ τῶν ἀπίστων, οὓς ἀπεικάζομεν, ἐκ τῶν ἀποστολικῶν διδαγμάτων, μαργαριτῶν δίκην τὰς ψυχὰς καταυγαζόντων, ἡ εἰς Χριστὸν πίστις καὶ ἡ τῆς ἀσεβείας ἐλευθερία γεγένηται. βλάσφημον δὲ τοῦτο.

author: Hippolytus
english: Taught who the true God is, you will escape these things. You will have an immortal body, incorruptible together with the soul, and you will receive the kingdom of the heavens — you who lived on earth and came to know the heavenly King. You will be a companion of God and co-heir with Christ, no longer enslaved to desires or passions and diseases.

For you have become god: whatever sufferings you endured as a human, he was giving (because he is one human); and whatever belongs to God, God has promised to provide, because you were deified, begotten immortal. That is what “Know yourself” means: recognizing the God who made you. For to know yourself turns out to be to be known by the one who calls you.

So do not be enemies to yourselves, humans, and do not hesitate to turn back. For Christ is the God over all, who ordered sin to be washed away from humans, making the old human new, having called him image from the beginning and showing through that type his affection for you. Obeying his solemn commands and becoming a good imitator of the Good, you will be like him, honored by him. For God is not impoverished when he also makes you god for his glory.
translator_notes: Underfilled author; new locus beyond 10.33 αὐτεξούσιον slice.
Christ as God over all who washes sin and makes the old human new; co-heir promise.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Greek locked from First1K Refutatio.

added_allusions.reason: put off old human / put on new.
partakers of divine nature / deification horizon.

greek: Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐκφεύξῃ θεὸν τὸν ὄντα διδαχθείς, ἕξεις δὲ ἀθάνατον τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἄφθαρτον ἅμα ψυχῇ, [καὶ] βασιλείαν οὐρανῶν ἀπολήψῃ, ὁ ἐν γῇ βιοὺς καὶ ἐπουράνιον βασιλέα ἐπιγνούς, ἔσῃ δὲ ὁμιλητὴς θεοῦ καὶ συγκληρονόμος Χριστοῦ, οὐκ ἐπιθυμίαις ἢ πάθεσι καὶ νόσοις δουλούμενος. Γέγονας γὰρ θεός· ὅσα γὰρ ὑπέμεινας πάθη ἄνθρωπος ὤν, ταῦτα ἐδίδου, ὅτι ἄνθρωπος εἷς, ὅσα δὲ παρακολουθεῖ θεῷ, ταῦτα παρέχειν ἐπήγγελται θεός, ὅτι ἐθεοποιήθης, ἀθάνατος γεννηθείς. Τουτέστι τὸ Γνῶθι σεαυτόν, ἐπιγνοὺς τὸν πεποιηκότα θεόν. Τὸ γὰρ ἐπιγνῶναι ἑαυτὸν ἐπιγνωσθῆναι συμβέβηκε τῷ καλουμένῳ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ. Μὴ φιλεχθρήσητε τοίνυν ἑαυτοῖς, ἄνθρωποι, μηδὲ τὸ παλινδρομεῖν διστάσητε· Χριστὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ κατὰ πάντων θεός, ὃς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀποπλύνειν προσέταξε, νέον τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀποτελῶν, εἰκόνα τοῦτον καλέσας ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, διὰ τύπου τὴν εἰς σὲ ἐπιδεικνύμενος στοργήν, οὗ προστάγμασιν ὑπακούσας σεμνοῖς, καὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἀγαθὸς γενόμενος μιμητής, ἔσῃ ὅμοιος ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τιμηθείς. Οὐ γὰρ πτωχεύει θεὸς καὶ σὲ θεὸν ποιήσας εἰς δόξαν αὐτοῦ.

author: Novatian
english: Who then would doubt — when at the end it is said, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” — that Christ, whose birth it is, is human because he became flesh, and is God because he is the Word of God, and would not hesitate to say so, especially when he notices that the evangelical Scripture has bound both those substances into one concord of Christ’s nativity?

For this is the one who “goes out from his chamber like a bridegroom; he exulted like a giant to run the course; his going out is from the highest heaven and his return is to the highest,” since no one has gone up to the highest into heaven except the one who came down from heaven — the Son of Man who is in the heavens.
translator_notes: Underfilled Latin author; new locus beyond novatian_trinity_1 regula.
John 1:14: Word is human as flesh and God as Word; both substances in one nativity.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Latin locked from restored Latin Library De Trinitate.

added_allusions.reason: Verbum caro factum est et habitavit in nobis.
no one ascended except who descended; Son of Man in heaven.

latin: Quis igitur dubitet, cum in extrema parte dicitur: Verbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis, Christum, cuius est natiuitas, et quia caro factus est, esse hominem, et quia uerbum Dei, Deum incunctanter edicere esse, praesertim cum animaduertat scripturam euangelicam utramque istam substantiam in unam natiuitatis Christi foederasse concordiam? 4. Hic est enim qui sicut sponsus egreditur de thalamo suo, exultauit ut gigas ad currendam uiam; a summo caelo egressio eius et usque ad summum regressio eius, quoniam usque ad summum nec quisquam in caelum ascendit, nisi qui de caelo descendit; Filius hominis qui est in caelis.

author: Commodian
locus: 26 STULTE NON PERMORERIS DEO; 27 Trade te Christo
english: Instruction 26 — Fool, you do not perish utterly before God. Fool, you will not die through and through, nor as a dead man escape your deeds — even if you arrange to feel nothing once you have died. You are beaten, senseless one: the God who founded the world lives, whose lawful claims cry out that they still hold for the dead. While you rush to live without God, you judge a person extinguished in the fates, or you believe it is fate. The eternal God did not arrange it as you think — that the dead are forgetful of what they did before. He has now made for us the holding-places of death for the unskilled; but after our ashes we will see those things. Tear yourself free, fool, who think that after the funeral you are not. You have made out that your Ruler and Lord can do nothing. But death is not into a void, if you turn it over in the heart. Know what should be hoped for — for late you will feel him.

You were ruler of the flesh; certainly the flesh was not ruling you. Freed from it, that flesh of yours is stored away. Rightly is a mortal human separated from flesh. Therefore mortal eyes will not be able to match this — so deep is our abyss concerning God’s secrets. So now, while you are fragile and dying, give honor to God, and believe that Christ makes you alive again from the dead. You ought to return praises to the Almighty in the church.
Instruction 27 (close): Hand yourself over to Christ already, so that good deeds may follow you.
translator_notes: Cyprian beyond Unity unavailable this pass (404/Unity-only).
Underfilled Commodian; new locus beyond preface instr_1.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Latin locked from Latin Library Instructiones.

added_allusions.reason: Son makes alive whom he wills.
I am the resurrection and the life.
present yourselves to God as alive from the dead.

latin: 26 STULTE NON PERMORERIS DEO. Stulte, non permoreris nec mortuus effugis actus, Tu licet disponas nihil te sentire defuncto. Uinceris, insipiens: uiuit Deus conditor orbis, Legitima cuius clamat ualere defuncto. Tu autem dum praeceps sine Deo uiuere quaeris, Extinctum in fatis iudicas aut fatale credis. Non ita disposuit, ut tu putas, Deus aeternus, Obliuitos esse mortuos de gesto priore. Nunc nobis imperita fecit receptacula mortis, Post cineres autem nostros uidebimus illa. Erue te, stulte, qui putas, post funera non sis. Rectorem dominumque tuum nihil posse fecisti. Mors autem in uacuum non est, si corde retractes. Optandum noscas, nam sero senties illum. Rector eras carnis, non te certe caro regebat; Exemptus ab illa reconditur illa tuorum. Recte mortalis homo separatur a carne. Idcirco nec poterint oculi mortales aequare, Sic habet abyssus noster de Dei secreta. Da nunc ergo Deo, fragilis dum moreris, honorem, Et crede, quod Christus uiuum te de mortuo reddit. Omnipotenti laudes in ecclesia reddere debes. [27] Trade te iam Christo, ut te benefacta sequantur.

author: Lactantius
english: Let people learn and understand why the highest God, when he was sending his legate and messenger to instruct mortality with the precepts of justice, willed him to be clothed with flesh and afflicted with torment and punished by death. For since there was no justice on earth, he sent a teacher as a living law, to found a new name and temple, to sow true and pious worship through the whole earth by words and by example.

Yet so that it would be certain he was sent by God, he did not need to be born as a human is born, compounded from both mortal parents; but so that it would appear that even in the human he was heavenly, he was created without a father’s agency. For he had God as the spiritual father — and as the father of his spirit is God without a mother, so the mother of his body is a virgin without a father.

He was therefore both God and human, set as middle between God and human — which is why the Greeks call him mediator — so that he might be able to lead the human to God, that is, to immortality. Because if he had been God only, as said above, he could not offer humans examples of virtue; if human only, he could not compel humans toward justice unless authority and power greater than a human were added.
translator_notes: Underfilled Lactantius beyond Inst. 2.17 / 5.18: God and man mediator.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Latin locked from CSEL TEI Divinae Institutiones IV.25.

added_allusions.reason: one mediator between God and humans.
Word became flesh; heavenly in the human.

latin: Discant igitur homines et intellegant quare deus summus cum legatum ac nuntium suum mitteret ad erudiendam praeceptis iustitiae mortalitatem, uoluerit eum carne indui et cruciatu adfici et morte multari. nam cum iustitia nulla esset in terra, doctorem misit quasi uiuam legem, ut nomen ac templum nouum conderet, ut uerum ac pium cultum per omnem terram et uerbis et exemplo seminaret. sed tamen ut certum esset a deo missum, non ita illum nasci oportuit, sicut homo nascitur ex mortali utroque concretus, sed ut appareret etiam in homine illum esse caelestem, creatus est sine opera genitoris. habebat enim spiritalem patrem deum et sicut pater spiritus eius deus sine matre, ita mater corporis eius uirgo sine patre. fuit igitur et deus et homo, inter deum atque hominem medius constitutus, unde illum Graeci μεσίτην uocant, ut hominem perducere ad deum posset id est ad inmortalitatem: quia si deus tantum fuisset, ut supra dictum est, exempla uirtutis homini praebere non posset, si homo tantum, non posset homines ad iustitiam cogere, nisi auctoritas ac uirtus homine maior accederet.

citation: Victorinus of Pettau — On the Creation of the World (Christ–Adam day typology)
author: Victorinus of Pettau
work: On the Creation of the World
english: So now you may see the unerring glory of God in providence being recalled; yet, as far as a small mind can, I will try to show it. That he might remake that Adam through the week, and bring help to his whole creation, was accomplished by the birth of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.

Who, then, taught in God’s law, who filled with the Holy Spirit, would not see in the heart that on the day the dragon seduced Eve, the angel Gabriel brought good news to the Virgin Mary; that on the day he made light, the Holy Spirit flooded the Virgin Mary; that on the day he made earth and water, he was turned into flesh; that on the day he made the stars, he was turned to milk; that on the day earth and water brought forth their young, he was in blood; that on the day he built the human from soil, he was turned into flesh; that on the day he fashioned the human, Christ was born; that on the day Adam fell, he suffered; that on the day he made light, he rose from the dead.
translator_notes: Beyond victorinus_creation sixth-day image: Christ remakes Adam by week / shared days.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Latin locked from Migne PL5 / Wikisource; OCR corroborates.

added_allusions.reason: dragon / Eve seduction day paired with Annunciation.
Gabriel to Mary; Spirit floods virgin.
Adam / second man typology in same treatise context.

latin: Nunc igitur de inerrabili gloria Dei in providentia videas memorari; tamen, ut mens parva poterit, conabor ostendere. Ut Adam illum per septimanam reformaverit, atque universae suae creaturae subveniret, nativitate filii sui Jesu Christi Domini nostri factum est. Quis itaque lege Dei doctus, quis plenus Spiritu sancto, non respiciat corde, ea die Gabriel angelum Mariae virgini evangelizasse, qua die draco Evam seduxit; ea die Spiritum sanctum Mariam virginem inundasse, qua lucem fecit; ea die in carne esse conversum, qua terram et aquam fecit; ea die in lacte esse conversum, qua stellas fecit; ea die in sanguine, qua terra et aqua foetus suos ediderunt; ea die in carne esse conversum, qua die hominem de humo instruxit; ea die natum esse Christum, qua hominem finxit; eadem die esse passum, quo Adam cecidit; ea die resurrexit a mortuis, qua lucem fecit.

author: Lactantius
english: I have spoken about humility and frailty and suffering — why God preferred to undergo these. Now the reason of the cross itself must be given and its force told. What the highest Father disposed from the beginning, and how he ordered all things that were done, is taught not only by the prophets’ foretelling, which truly went ahead into Christ, but also by the reason of the passion itself. For whatever he suffered was not empty, but had a great figure and meaning — just as those divine works he did also did: their force and power were effective for the present, yet they also declared something for the future.

He was — that is, innocent and just and holy — who, sacrificed by those same Jews, is for salvation to all who have written on their own forehead the sign of the blood, that is, of the cross by which he poured out blood. For the forehead is the human’s highest threshold, and wood smeared with blood is a signification of the cross. Finally the immolation of the animal by those who keep the Passover is named from “to suffer,” because it is a figure of the passion, which God, foreknowing things to come, handed over through Moses for his people to celebrate. But then the figure prevailed in the present toward driving away danger, so that it might appear how much the truth itself would prevail toward protecting God’s people in the extreme necessity of the whole world.
translator_notes: Cyprian beyond Unity still unavailable (Latin Library 465).
Underfilled Lactantius beyond Inst. 2.17 / 5.18 / 4.25: cross-reason and Passover figure.
Pass A ≠ Pass B; Latin locked from CSEL TEI Divinae Institutiones IV.26.
latin: Dixi de humilitate et fragilitate et passione, cur haec deus subire maluerit: nunc ipsius crucis ratio reddenda est et uis enarranda. quid summus pater a principio disposuerit et quemadmodum cuncta quae gesta sunt ordinarit, non tantum diuinatio prophetarum, quae in Christum uera praecessit, sed etiam ratio ipsius passionis docet. quaecumque enim passus est, non fuerunt inania, sed habuerunt figuram et significantiam magnam sicut etiam diuina illa opera quae fecit: quorum uis et potentia ualebat quidem in praesens, sed declarabat aliquid in futurum. fuit, id est innocens et iustus et sanctus, qui ab isdem Iudaeis immolatus saluti est omnibus, qui signum sanguinis, id est crucis qua sanguinem fudit, in sua fronte conscripserint. frons enim summum limen est hominis et lignum sanguine delibutum crucis significatio est. denique immolatio pecudis ab iis ipsis qui faciunt pascha nominatur ἀπὸ τοῦ πάσχειν , quia passionis figura est, quam deus praescius futurorum tradidit per Moysen populo suo celebrandam. sed tum figura ualuit in praesenti ad depellendum periculum, ut appareret quantum ueritas ipsa ualitura sit ad plebem dei protegendam in extrema totius orbis necessitate.

author: Lactantius
english: First, then, people ought to know that the highest God’s plan proceeded from the beginning this way: as the end of the age drew near, it was necessary for God’s Son to descend to earth in order to constitute a temple for God and teach justice — yet not in an angel’s virtue or heavenly power, but in human form and mortal condition; and when he had finished his teaching office, he would be handed over into the hands of the impious and take up death, so that death too, subdued by virtue, might rise again, and so that to the human whom he had put on and was bearing he might both offer hope of conquering death and admit him to the rewards of immortality.

Lest anyone not know this plan, we will teach that all things we see completed in Christ were foretold. Let no one lend faith to our assertion unless I show that the prophets, long beforehand, foretold that God’s Son would someday be born as a human, do wonders, sow the worship of God through the whole earth, and finally be fixed to the gibbet and rise again on the third day. When I have proven all this from the very writings of those who violated their God while he used a mortal body, what else will stand in the way of it being clear that true wisdom dwells in this religion alone?

latin: In primis igitur scire homines oportet sic a principio processisse dispositionem summi dei, ut esset necesse adpropinquante saeculi termino dei filium descendere in terram, ut constitueret deo templum doceretque iustitiam, uerum tamen non in uirtute angeli aut potestate caelesti, sed in figura hominis et condicione mortali, et cum magisterio functus fuisset, traderetur in manus inpiorum mortemque susciperet, ut ea quoque per uirtutem domita resurgeret et homini, quem induerat, quem gerebat, et spem uincendae mortis offerret et ad praemia inmortalitatis admitteret. hanc ergo dispositionem ne quis ignoret, docebimus praedicta esse omnia quae in Christo uidemus esse conpleta. nemo adseuerationi nostrae fidem commodet, nisi ostendero prophetas ante multam temporum seriem praedicasse, fore aliquando ut filius dei nasceretur sicut homo et mirabilia faceret et cultum dei per totam terram seminaret et postremo patibulo figeretur et tertio die resurgeret. quae omnia cum probauero eorum ipsorum litteris qui deum suum mortali corpore utentem uiolauerunt, quid aliut obstabit quominus ueram sapientiam clarum sit in hac sola religione uersari?

author: Lactantius
english: Perhaps someone may ask how, when we say we worship one God, we nevertheless assert that there are two, God the Father and God the Son. This assertion drives many into the greatest error. Though what we say seems probable to them, they think we waver in this one point—that we confess both another God and a mortal God. We have already spoken about mortality; now let us teach about unity. When we say God the Father and God the Son, we do not say something different, nor do we separate the two, because neither can the Father be separated from the Son nor the Son from the Father, if indeed the Father cannot be named without the Son nor can the Son be generated without the Father. When therefore the Father makes a son and the Son a father, there is one mind for both, one spirit, one substance: but the former is like an overflowing fountain, the latter like a stream flowing down from him; the former like the sun, the latter like a ray stretched from the sun. And since he is both faithful and dear to the highest Father, he is not separated, just as neither stream from fountain nor ray from sun, because both the fountain’s water is in the stream and the sun’s light is in the ray; equally neither voice can be severed from the mouth nor virtue or hand torn away from the body.

Wherefore, when the mind and will of the one is in the other—or rather one in both—rightly either is called one God, because whatever is in the Father flows across to the Son and whatever is in the Son descends from the Father. Therefore that highest and singular God cannot be worshiped except through the Son. Whoever thinks he worships the Father alone, just as he does not worship the Son, so he does not even worship the Father. But whoever receives the Son and bears his name—that one truly worships the Father together with the Son, since the Son is legate and messenger and priest of the highest Father. This one is the door of the greatest temple, this the way of light, this the leader of salvation, this the doorway of life.

latin: Fortasse quaerat aliquis quomodo, cum deum nos unum colere dicamus, duos tamen esse adseueremus, deum patrem et deum filium. quae adseueratio plerosque in maximum inpingit errorem. quibus cum probabilia uideantur esse quae dicimus, in hoc uno labare nos arbitrantur, quod et alterum et mortalem deum fateamur. de mortalitate iam diximus: nunc de unitate doceamus. cum dicimus deum patrem et deum filium, non diuersum dicimus nec utrumque secernimus, quia nec pater a filio potest nec filius a patre secerni, siquidem nec pater sine filio nuncupari nec filius potest sine patre generari. cum igitur et pater filium faciat et filius patrem, una utrique mens, unus spiritus, una substantia est: sed ille quasi exuberans fons est, hic tamquam defluens ex eo riuus, ille tamquam sol, hic quasi radius ex sole porrectus. qui quoniam summo patri et fidelis et carus est, non separatur, sicut nec riuus a fonte nec radius a sole, quia et aqua fontis in riuo est et solis lumen in radio; aeque nec uox ab ore seiungi nec uirtus aut manus a corpore diuelli potest. cum igitur a prophetis idem manus dei et uirtus et sermo dicatur, utique nulla discretio est, quia et lingua, sermonis ministra, et manus, in qua est uirtus, indiuiduae sunt corporis portiones. propiore uti exemplo libet. cum quis habet filium quem unice diligat, qui tamen sit in domo et in manu patris, licet ei nomen domini potestatemque concedat, ciuili tamen iure et domus una et unus dominus nominatur. sic hic mundus una dei domus est et filius ac pater, qui unanimes incolunt mundum, deus unus, quia et unus est tamquam duo et duo tamquam unus. neque id mirum, cum et filius sit in patre, quia pater diligit filium, et pater in filio, quia uoluntati patris fideliter paret, nec umquam faciat aut fecerit nisi quod pater aut uoluit aut iussit. denique unum deum esse tam patrem quam filium Esaias in illo exemplo quod superius posuimus ostendit, cum diceret: adorabunt te et in te precabuntur: quoniam in te deus est, et non est deus alius praeter te. sed et alio loco similiter ait: sic dicit deus rex Israhel et qui eruit eum deus aeternus: ego primus et ego nouissimus et praeter me non est deus. cum duas personas proposuisset, dei regis, id est Christi, et dei patris, qui eum post passionem ab inferis excitauit, sicut ostendisse diximus Osee prophetam qui ait: et de manu inferorum eruam eum, tamen ad utramque personam referens intulit: et praeter me non est deus, cum posset dicere \'praeter nos\': sed fas non erat plurali numero separationem tantae necessitudinis fieri. unus est enim, solus, liber, deus summus, carens origine, quia ipse est origo rerum et in eo simul et filius et omnia continentur. quapropter cum mens et uoluntas alterius in altero sit uel potius una in utroque, merito unus deus uterque appellatur, quia quidquid est in patre, ad filium transfluit et quidquid est m filio, a patre descendit. non potest igitur summus ille ac singularis deus nisi per filium coli. qui solum patrem se colere putat, sicut filium non colit ita ne patrem quidem. qui autem filium suscipit et nomen eius gerit, is uero cum filio simul et patrem colit, quoniam legatus et nuntius et sacerdos summi patris est filius. hic templi maximi ianua est, hic lucis uia, hic dux salutis, hic ostium uitae.

author: Lactantius
english: From these things it appears that all the prophets announced concerning Christ that at some time, born bodily from David’s line, he would establish an eternal temple for God—which is called the church—and call all nations together to the true religion of God. This is the faithful house, this the immortal temple, in which if anyone has not sacrificed, he will not have the reward of immortality. And since Christ was the fabricator of a temple both great and eternal, the same one must also have in it an everlasting priesthood, nor can one arrive at the temple and at the sight of God except through him who established it. David teaches that very thing in Psalm 109, saying: “Before the daystar I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest forever.”

And who he would be to whom God was promising an eternal priesthood, Zechariah also taught most openly with the name set down. He, however, exhibited faithfulness to God: for he taught that there is one God and that he alone must be worshiped, and he never said that he himself was God, because he would not have kept faith if, sent to remove gods and assert one, he introduced another besides the one. For this reason—because he stood out so faithful, because he took nothing at all for himself, that he might fulfill the sender’s commands—he received both the dignity of perpetual priest and the honor of highest king and the power of judge and the name of God.

latin: Quibus ex rebus apparet prophetas omnes denuntiasse de Christo, fore aliquando ut ex genere Dauid corporaliter natus constitueret aeternum templum deo, quod appellatur ecclesia, et uniuersas gentes ad religionem ueram dei conuocaret. haec est domus fidelis, hoc inmortale templum, in quo si quis non sacrificauerit, inmortalitatis praemium non habebit. cums templi et magni et aeterni quoniam Christus fabricator fuit, idem necesse est habeat in eo sacerdotium sempiternum, nec potest nisi per eum qui constituit ad templum et ad conspectum dei perueniri. Dauid in psalmo CVIIII id ipsum docet dicens: ante luciferum genui te. iurauit dominus et non paenitebit eum: tu es sacerdos in aeternum. item in Basilion libro primo: et suscitabo mihi sacerdotem fidelem, qui omnia quae sunt in corde meo faciet, et aedificabo ei domum fidelem, et transibit in conspectu meo omnibus diebus. quis autem futurus esset cui deus aeternum sacerdotium pollicebatur, Zacharias etiam nomine posito apertissime docuit. sic enim dixit: et ostendit mihi dominus Iesum sacerdotem magnum stantem ante faciem angeli domini, et diabolus stabat ad dexteram ipsius, ut contradiceret ei. et dixit dominus ad diabolum: imperet dominus in te, qui elegit Hierusalem: et ecce titio eiectus ab igni. et Iesus erat indutus uestimenta sordida, et stabat ante faciem angeli. et respondit et dixit ad circumstantes ante faciem ipsius dicens: auferte uestimenta sordida ab eo et induite eum tunicam talarem et imponite cidarim mundam super caput ipsius. et cooperuerunt eum uestimenta et imposuerunt cidarim super caput eius. et angelus domini stabat et testificabatur ad Iesum dicens: haec dicit dominus omnipotens: si in uiis meis ambulaueris et praecepta mea seruaueris, tu iudicabis domum meam, et dabo tibi qui conuersentur in medio horum circumstantium. audi itaque, Iesu sacerdos magne. quis non igitur captos mentibus tum fuisse Iudaeos arbitretur, qui cum haec et legerent et audirent, nefandas manus deo suo intulerunt? atquin ab eo tempore quo Zacharias fuit usque ad annum quintum decimum imperii Tiberi Caesaris, quo Iesus fixus est, prope quingenti anni numerantur, siquidem Darii et Alexandri adoleuit aetate, qui fuerunt non multo post quam Tarquinius Superbus exactus est. sed illi rursus eodem modo falsi deceptique sunt putantes haec de Iesu esse dicta filio Naue, qui successor Moysi fuit, aut de sacerdote Iesu filio Iosedech: in quos nihil congruit eorum quae propheta narrauit. non enim sorditati umquam illi fuerunt, cum alter eorum potentissimus princeps fuisset, alter sacerdos, aut perpessi sunt aliquid aduersi, ut tamquam titio eiectus ex igni putarentur, aut aliquando in conspectu dei et angelorum steterunt aut propheta de praeteritis loquebatur potius quam futuris. locutus est igitur de Iesu filio dei, ut ostenderet eum primo in humilitate et carne uenturum. haec est enim uestis sordida, ut pararet templum deo et sicut titio igni ambureretur id est ab hominibus cruciamenta perferret et ad ultimum extingueretur. titionem enim uulgus appellat extractum foco torrem semiustum et extinctum. quomodo autem et cum quibus mandatis a deo mitteretur in terram, declarauit spiritus dei per prophetam docens futurum ut cum uoluntatem summi patris fideliter et constanter inplesset, acciperet iudicium atque imperium sempiternum. si in uiis meis inquit ambulaueris et praecepta mea seruaueris, tu iudicabis domum meam. quae fuerint uiae dei et quae praecepta eius, nec ambiguum nec obscurum est. deus enim cum uideret malitiam et falsorum deorum cultus per orbem terrae ita inualuisse, ut iam nomen eius ex hominum memoria fuisset paene sublatum — siquidem Iudaei quoque, quibus solis arcanum dei creditum fuerat, relicto deo uiuo ad colenda figmenta inretiti daemonum fraudibus aberrassent nec increpiti per prophetas reuerti ad deum uellent —, filium suum principem angelorum legauit ad homines, ut eos conuerteret ab inpiis et uanis cultibus ad cognoscendum et colendum deum uerum, item ut eorum mentes a stultitia ad sapientiam, ab iniquitate ad iustitiae opera traduceret. hae sunt uiae dei in quibus eum ambulare praecepit, haec praecepta quae seruanda mandauit. ille uero exhibuit deo fidem: docuit enim quod unus deus sit eumque solum coli oportere, nec umquam se ipse deum dixit, quia non seruasset fidem, si missus ut deos tolleret et unum adsereret, induceret alium praeter unum. hoc erat non de uno deo facere praeconium nec eius qui miserat, sed suum proprium negotium gerere ac se ab eo quem inlustratum uenerat separare. propterea quia tam fidelis extitit, quia sibi nihil prorsus adsumpsit, ut mandata mittentis inpleret, et sacerdotis perpetui dignitatem et regis summi honorem et iudicis potestatem et dei nomen accepit.

author: Lactantius
english: When Christ was fulfilling what God had willed and had foretold through his prophets many ages earlier, those who did not know the divine writings gathered to condemn their God. Knowing this would happen, and saying again and again that he must suffer and be killed for the salvation of many, he withdrew with his disciples—not to escape what he had to endure, but to show that in every persecution one must not seem to have fallen by his own fault—and he announced that he would be betrayed by one of them. They offered him to Pontius Pilate and demanded that he be fixed to a cross, charging him with nothing except that he said he was the Son of God and king of the Jews, and that he had said: “If you destroy this temple, which was built in forty-six years, I will raise it in three days without hands,” signifying his coming passion and that, killed by the Jews, he would rise on the third day. For he himself had been the true temple of God. Pilate found nothing worthy of condemnation in him, yet under the crowd’s shouts and Herod’s pressure he handed him over; they flogged him, mocked him as king with a scarlet robe and thorns, gave him gall and vinegar, spat on him, cast lots for his clothes, and hung him between two robbers—while he uttered no word, as if mute.

What shall we say of the unworthiness of this cross, on which God was hung and fixed by the worshipers of God? The prophets and the Sibylline songs had already announced that these things would happen. Moses said a hanging life would be before their eyes; Zechariah: “They will look upon me whom they pierced”; David in Psalm 21: they dug his hands and feet, numbered his bones, divided his garments and cast lots for his clothing—not of himself as king, but of the one the Spirit spoke of, who would suffer those things ages later. Solomon also prophesied that Jerusalem would perish in vengeance for the holy cross: they abandoned the Lord their God, persecuted their king most beloved to God, and crucified him in great humility—and for this God brought these evils upon them.

latin: Cum igitur ea quae deus fieri uoluit quaeque per prophetas suos multis saeculis ante praedixit, Christus inpleret, ob ea incitati et diuinas litteras nescientes coierunt, ut deum suum condemnarent. quod cum sciret futurum ac subinde diceret oportere se pati atque interfici pro salute multorum, secessit tamen cum discipulis suis, non ut uitaret quod necesse erat perpeti ac sustinere, sed ut ostenderet quod ita fieri oporteat in omni persecutione, ne sua quis culpa incidisse uideatur; ac denuntiauit fore ut ab uno eorum proderetur. itaque ludas praemio inlectus tradidit eum Iudaeis. at illi conprehensum ac Pontio Pilato, qui tum legatus Syriam regebat, oblatum cruci adfigi postulauerunt obicientes ei nihil aliut nisi quod diceret se filium dei esse, regem Iudaeorum; item quia dixerat: si solueritis hoc templum, quod aedificatum est annis XLVI, ego illut in triduo sine manibus resuscitabo, significans futuram breui passionem suam et se a Iudaeis interfectum tertio die resurrecturum. ipse enim fuerat uerum dei templum. has uoces eius tamquam infaustas et inpias insectabantur. quae cum Pilatus audisset et ille in defensionem sui nihil diceret, pronuntiauit nihil in eo damnatione dignum uideri. at illi iniustissimi accusatores cum populo, quem incitauerant, subclamare coeperunt et crucem eius uiolentis uocibus flagitare. tum Pontius et illorum clamoribus et Herodis tetrarchae instigatione metuentis, ne regno pelleretur; uictus est, nec tamen ipse sententiam protulit, sed tradidit eum Iudaeis, ut ipsi de illo secundum legem suam iudicarent. duxerunt igitur eum flagellis uerberatum et priusquam cruci adfigerent, inluserunt: indutum enim coloris punicei ueste ac spinis coronatum quasi regem salutarunt et dederunt ei cibum fellis et miscuerunt ei aceti potionem. post haec conspuerunt faciem eius et palmis ceciderunt. cumque ipsi carnifices de uestimentis eius contenderent, sortiti sunt inter se de tunica et pallio. et cum haec omnia fierent, nullam uocem ex ore suo, tamquam si mutus esset, emisit. tum suspenderunt eum inter duos noxios medium, qui ob latrocinia damnati erant, crucique fixerunt. quid ego hic in tanto facinore deplorem aut quibus uerbis tantum nefas conquerar? non enim Gauianam crucem describimus, quam Marcus Tullius uniuersis eloquentiae suae neruis ac uiribus uelut effusis totius ingenii fontibus prosecutus est, facinus indignum esse proclamans ciuem Romanum contra omnes leges in crucem esse sublatum. qui quamuis innocens fuerit et illo supplicio indignus, mortalis tamen et ab homine scelesto qui iustitiam ignoraret adfectus. quid de huius crucis indignitate dicemus, in qua deus a cultonbus dei suspensus est atque subfixus? quis tam facundus et tanta rerum uerborumque copia instructus existet, quae oratio tantae affluentiae ubertate decurrens, ut illam crucem merito deploret, quam mundus ipse et tota mundi elementa luxerunt? haec autem sic futura esse et prophetarum uocibus et Sibyllinis carminibus denuntiatum est. aput Esaiam ita scriptum inuenitur: non sum contumax neque contradico: dorsum meum posui ad flagella et maxillas meas ad palmas, faciem autem meam non auerti a foeditate sputorum. similiter Dauid in psalmo XXXIIII: congregata sunt in me flagella et ignorauerunt, dissoluti sunt nec conpuncti sunt: temptauerunt me et deriserunt derisum, striderunt super me dentibus suis. Sibylla quoque eadem futura monstrauit: εἰς ἀνόμους χεῖρας καὶ ἀπίστων ὕστερον ἥξει, δώσουσι δὲ θεῷ ῥαπίσματα χερσὶν ἀνάγνοις, καὶ στόμασιν μιαροῖσι ἐμπτύσματα φαρμακόεντα· δώσει δ᾽ εἰς μάστιγας ἁπλῶς ἁγνὸν τότε νῶτον. item de silentio eius, quod usque ad mortem pertinaciter tenuit, Esaias iterum sic locutus est: sicut ouis ad immolandum adductus est et sicut agnus coram tondentibus sine uoce, sic non aperuit os suum. et Sibylla supra dicta: καὶ κολαφιζόμενος σιγήσει, μή τις ἐπιγνῶ τίς λόγος ἢ πόθεν ἦλθεν, ἵνα φθιμένοισι λαλήσει, καὶ στέφανον φορέσει τὴν ἀκάνθινον.

de cibo uero et potu, quem antequam figerent ei obtulerunt, Dauid in psalmo LXVIII sic ait: et dederunt in escam meam fel et in siti mea potum mihi dederunt acetum. idem hoc futurum etiam Sibylla contionata est: εἰς δὲ τὸ βρῶμα χολὴν καὶ εἰς δίψαν ὄξος ἔδωκαν, τῆς ἀφιλοξενίης ταύτην δείξουσι τράπεζαν. Et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat increpat: et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat uersibus: αὐτὴ γὰρ δύσφρων, τὸν σὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἐνόησας παίζοντα θνητοῖσι νοήμασιν, ἀλλὰ ἀπ\' ἀκάνθης ἔστεψας στεφάνῳ φοβερὴν τε χολὴν ἐκέρασσας. fore autem ut Iudaei manus inferrent deo suo eumque interficerent, testimonia prophetarum haec antecesserunt. aput Hesdram ita scriptum est: et dixit Hesdras ad populum: hoc pascha saluator noster est et refugium nostrum. cogitate et ascendat in cor uestrum, quoniam habemus humiliare eum in signo: et post haec sperabimus in eum, ne deseratur hic locus in aeternum tempus, dicit dominus deus uirtutum. si non credideritis ei neque exaudieritis adnuntia tionem eius, eritis derisio in gentibus. unde apparet Iudaeos nullam aliam spem habere nisi se abluerint a sanguine ac sperauerint in eum ipsum quem necauerunt. Esaias quoque facinus eorum designat et dicit: in humilitate iudicium eius sublatam est. natiuitatem eius quis enarrabit? quoniam auferetur a terra uita eius, a facinoribus populi mei abductus est ad mortem. et dabo malos pro sepultura eius et diuites pro morte eius, quia facinus non fecit neque insidias ore suo locutus est. propterea ipse consequetur multos et fortium diuidet spolia, propterea quod traditus est ad mortem et inter facinerosos deputatus est: et ipse peccata multorum pertulit et propter facinora illorum traditus est. Dauid quoque in psalmo XCIII: captabunt in animam iusti et sanguinem innocentem condemnabunt, et factus est mihi dominus in refugium. item Hieremias: domine, significa mihi, et cognoscam. tunc uidi meditationes eorum: ego sicut agnus sine malitia perductus sum ad uictimam: in me cogitauerunt cogitationem dicentes: uenite, mittamus lignum in panem eius et eradamus a terra uitam eius et nomen eius non erit in memoria amplius. lignum autem crucem significat et panem corpus eius, quia ipse est cibus ac uita omnium qui credunt in carnem quam portauit et in crucem qua pependit. de qua tamen apertius ipse Moyses in Deuteronomio ita praedicauit: et erit pendens uita tua ante oculos tuos, et timebis die ac nocte et non credes uitae tuae, idem rursus in Numeris: non quasi homo dominus suspenditur neque quasi filius hominis minas patitur. Zacharias etiam sic tradidit: et intuebuntur in me, quem transfixerunt. item Dauid in psalmo XXI: effoderunt manus meas et pedes meos, di-numerauerunt omnia ossa mea: ipsi autem contemplati sunt et uiderunt me et diuiserunt uestimenta mea sibi et super uestem meam sortem miserunt. quae utique propheta non de se locutus est. fuit enim rex et numquam illa perpessus est, sed spiritus dei per eum loquebatur, qui fuerat illa passurus post annos mille et quinquaginta, tot enim colliguntur anni a regno Dauid usque ad crucem Christi. sed et Solomon filius eius, qui Hierosolymam condidit, eam ipsam perituram esse in ultionem sanctae crucis prophetauit: quodsi auertimini a me, dicit dominus, et non custodieritis ueritatem meam, reiciam Israhel a terra quam dedi illis, et domum hanc quam aedificaui illis in nomine meo, proiciam illam es omnibus, et erit Israhel in perditionem et in inproperium populo, et domus haec erit deserta, et omnis qui transiet per illam admirabitur et dicet: propter quam rem deus fecit terrae huic et huic domui haec mala? et dicent: quia reliquerunt dominum deum suum et persecuti sunt regem suum dilectissimum deo et cruciauerunt illum in humilitate magna: propter hoc inportauit illis deus mala haec.

author: Lactantius
english: When the highest God and Parent of all had willed to transfer his religion, he sent from heaven a teacher of justice, that in him or through him he might give a new law to new worshipers—not as he had done before through a human, yet he still willed him to be born as a human, that through all things he might stand like the highest Father. For God the Father himself, origin and beginning of things, since he has no parents, is most truly named by Trismegistus fatherless and motherless, because he was begotten of no one. For that reason the Son also had to be born twice, that he himself might become fatherless and motherless: in the first, spiritual nativity he was motherless, because without a mother’s office he was generated from God the Father alone; in the second, fleshly nativity he was fatherless, because without a father’s office he was brought forth from a virgin’s womb—so that, bearing a middle substance between God and human, he might be able to lead out this fragile and weak nature of ours as by the hand unto immortality. He was made Son of God through the Spirit and of a human through the flesh, that is both God and human. The power of God in him appeared from the works he did; the frailty of the human from the passion he endured—and why he took that up I will teach a little later.

Meanwhile we learn from the prophets’ oracles that he was both God and human, mixed from both kinds. Isaiah testifies he was God: “Egypt has grown weary… for in you is God, and there is no other god besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel the Savior.” Jeremiah: “This is our God, and another will not be reckoned besides him… After this he was seen on the earth and lived with humans.” David in the psalm: “Your throne, O God, is unto ages of ages… therefore God, your God, has anointed you”—which word also shows the name, since from anointing he is called Christ. And that the same one was human Jeremiah teaches: “And he is a human, and who has known him?” Isaiah: “And the Lord will send them a human who will save them.” Moses in Numbers: “A star will rise from Jacob and a human will arise from Israel.”

Therefore both David and the other prophets announced that Christ would be generated according to the flesh from this very house. In Isaiah: “And there will be in that day the root of Jesse… in him the nations will hope.” And Nathan to David: “I will raise up your seed after you… He will build me a house in my name, and I will raise his throne unto the age, and I will be to him for a father and he will be to me for a son.” The Jews referred this to Solomon, who built a hand-made temple; but Solomon’s rule was not perpetual, he was never called Son of God, and the house he built did not obtain faith as the church does—which is the true temple of God, not in walls but in the heart and faith of humans who believe in him and are called faithful. That Solomonic temple, because it was made by hand, fell by hand.
