Adv. Nat. 2.35: mediae qualitatis; omnipotenti regi; ingenitum.
latin: 35.1. ''Sed si animae, inquiunt, mortales et qualitatis sunt mediae, irmmortales quemadmodum fieri mediis ex qualitatibus possunt?''. - Si nos istud nescire dicamus ac tantummodo auditum ex potentiore credidisse, uhi nostra videbitur credulitas lapsa, si omnipotenti credidimus regi nihil esse difficile, nihil arduum, si quod inpossibile nobis est factu, illi possibile atque ad modum obsecutionis paratum? 2. Est enim quod obstare eius voluntatibus possit, aut quod esse voluerit, non necessario sequitur ut fiat? An numquid nostris ex divisionibus colligemus, quid aut fieri possit aut non possit, nec rationes considerabimus nostras tam esse mortales quam sumus nos ipsi et nullius apud principem nominis?

3. Et tamen, o isti, qui mediae qualitatis animas esse non creditis et in medio limite vitae atque interitus contineri, nonne omnes omnino, quos esse opinatio suspicatur, dii angeli daemones aut nomine quocumque sunt alio, qualitatis et ipsi sunt mediae et in ambiguae sortis condicione nutabiles? [Plat., Tim. 4] 4. Nam si omnes concedimus, unum esse rerum patrem, immortalem atque ingenitum solum, nihilque omnino ante illum quod alicuius vocaminis fuerit invenitur, sequitur ut hi omnes quos opinatio credidit deos esse mortalium aut ab eo sint geniti aut eo iubente prolati. Si sunt prolati et geniti, et ordinis sunt posterioris et temporis; si ordinis posterioris et temporis, ortus necesse est habeant et exordia nativitatis et vitae: quod autem habet introitum et vitae incipientis exordium, necessario sequitur ut habere debeat et occasum.

author: Arnobius
english: Therefore though you be pure and cleansed from every stain of vices, though you have won over and bent those powers so that they do not shut and bar the ways to one returning to heaven, you will be able by no efforts to reach the prize of immortality unless you have received what itself makes immortality, with Christ bestowing it, and have been admitted to true life.

For what you are accustomed to throw at us — that our religion is new and born almost a few days ago, and that we ought not to have left the ancient and ancestral and been led over into barbarian and foreign rites — is urged by no reason. For what if in this way we should wish to blame those earlier and most ancient ages, because when fruits were found they scorned acorns and rejected arbutus berries; because they ceased to be covered and clothed with bark and skins after woven clothing was devised, shorter in use and convenience; or because, when houses were built and richer successes established, they did not love the old huts nor prefer to remain under rocks and caves like beasts?

It is common to all and handed down almost from the cradle itself to prefer goods to evils, to set useful things before useless, and what is agreed to be more precious and gladder, to pursue and seek that and in it to fix the hope of salvation and of saving advantages.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.66: Christo adtribuente; spem salutis.
latin: 66.1. Licet ergo tu purus et ab omni fueris vitiorum contaminatione purgatus, conciliaveris illas atque inflexeris potestates, ad caelum <ne> redeunti vias cludant atque obsaepiant transitum, ad immortalitatis accedere nullis poteris contentionibus praemium, nisi quod ipsam immortalitatem facit Christo adtribuente perceperis et veram fueris admissus ad vitam.

2. Nam quod nobis obiectare consuestis, novellam esse religionem nostram et ante dies natam propemodum paucos neque nos oportuisse antiquam et patriam linquere et in barbaros ritus peregrinosque traduci, ratione istud intenditur nulla. 3. Quid enim, si hoc modo culpam velimus infligere prioribus illis atque antiquissimis saeculis, quod inventis frugibus glandes spreverint et repudiaverint arbuta, quod corticibus contegi et amiciri desierint pellibus, postquam vestis excogitata est textilis usu et commoditate succinctior, aut quod structis domibus et lautioribus successibus institutis non antiquas adamaverint casulas nec sub rupibus et cavernis praeoptaverint ut beluae permanere?

4. Commune est omnibus et ab ipsis paene incunabulis traditum, bona malis anteferre, inutilibus utilia praeponere, et quod esse constiterit pretiosius, laetius, id consectari et petere in eoque defigere spem salutis et salutarium commodorum.

author: Arnobius
english: Therefore, people, stop blocking your hopes with empty questions, and if something stands otherwise than you think, you ought to trust the august reality rather than your opinions.

Times full of dangers press, and deadly punishments hang over us: let us flee to the saving God and not demand a reason for the gift offered. When it is a matter of souls’ salvation and of regard for ourselves, something must be done even without a reason, as Arrian approves Epictetus to have said.

We doubt, we waver, and we suspect that what is said is not full of faith: let us commit ourselves to God, and let our unbelief not weigh more with us than the greatness of his name and power, lest while we hunt arguments by which what we do not want to be may seem false and we strive against the true, the last day steal upon us and we be found in the jaws of hostile death.

Adv. Nat. 2.78: salutarem deum; animarum salus; incredulitas.

added_allusions.reason: must come to God in faith.

latin: 78.1. Quare, homines, abstinete quaestionibus vacuis imspedire spes vestras, nec si aliter quam vos putatis aliquid se habet, vestris potius opinionibus credere quam rei debetis augustae.

2. Urgent tempora periculis plena et exitiabiles imminent poenae: confugiamus ad salutarem deum nec rationem muneris exigamus oblati. Cum de animarum agatur salute ac de respectu nostri, aliquid et sine ratione faciendum est, ut Epictetum dixisse adprobat Arrianus [Arrianus: Epict. fr. Schenkl 7].

3. Dubitamus, ambigimus nec esse quod dicitur plenum fidei suspicamur: committamus nos deo, nec plus apud nos valeat incredulitas nostra quam illius nominis et potentiae magnitudo, ne dum ipsi nobis argumenta conquirimus quibus esse videatur falsum id quod esse nolimus atque adnitimur verum, obrepat dies extremus et inimicae mortis reperiamur in faucibus.

author: Arnobius
english: What do you say, O ignorant ones, even most worthy of tears and pity? Do you so not fear that perhaps these things are true which are contempt to you and furnish matter for laughter? Do you not at least turn over with yourselves under dark thoughts that what today you refuse with stubborn perversity to believe, late time may refute and irrevocable repentance chastise?

Do not even these at least make for you arguments of believing: that already through all lands in so short a span the sacraments of this immense name have been poured out; that there is now no nation of so barbarous custom and ignorant of gentleness that has not, turned by love of it, softened its harshness and migrated into peaceful senses with assumed calm; that orators, grammarians, rhetoricians, jurisconsults and physicians endowed with such great talents, and those probing philosophy’s secrets, seek these teachings, having scorned those they trusted a little before; that slaves prefer to be afflicted by masters with whatever tortures they decree, spouses to be loosed from marriages, children to be disinherited by parents rather than break Christian faith and lay down the sacraments of the saving warfare; that though so many kinds of punishments have been set by you for those following this religion’s laws, the matter grows the more and against all threats and bans of fears the people push more courageously and are spurred to the zeal of believing by the very stimuli of prohibition?

Or do you believe these things happen at random and emptily, that these minds are taken by chance assaults? Is that so not divine and sacred? Or without their God do such conversions of souls happen that, though the butcher’s hooks and other countless tortures, as we said, hang over those about to believe, seized as by a certain sweetness and love of all virtues they accept the known reasons and prefer the friendships of Christ to all the world’s affairs?

Adv. Nat. 2.5: fides Christiana; amicitias Christi; sacramenta.

added_allusions.reason: prefer Christ over family under cost.

latin: 5.1. Quid dicitis, o nescii, etiam fletu et miseratione dignissimi? Ita non extimescitis, ne forte haec vera sint quae sunt despectui vobis et praebent materiam risus? Nec saltem vobiscum sub obscuris cogitationibus volvitis, ne quod hoc die credere obstinata rennuitis perversitate, redarguat serum tempus et inrevocabilis paenitentia castiget?

2. Nonne vel haec saltem fidem vobis faciunt argumenta credendi, quod iam per omnes terras in tam brevi temporis spatio inmensi nominis huius sacramenta diffusa sunt ; 3. quod nulla iam natio est tam barbari moris et mansuetudinem nesciens, quae non eius amore versa molliverit asperitatem suam et in placidos sensus adsumpta tranquillitate migraverit; 4. quod tam magnis ingeniis praediti oratores grammatici rhetores consulti iuris ac medici, philosophiae etiam secreta rimantes magisteria haec expetunt spretis quibus paulo ante fidebant; 5. quod ab dominis se servi cruciatibus adfici quibus statuerint malunt, solvi coniuges matrimoniis, exheredari a parentibus liberi quam fidem rumpere Christianam et salutaris militiae sacramenta deponere; 6. quod cum genera poenarum tanta sint a vobis proposita religionis huius sequentibus leges, augeatur res magis et contra omnes minas atque interdicta formidinum animosius populus obnitatur et ad credendi studium prohibitionis ipsius stimulis excitetur? 7. An numquid haec fieri passim et inaniter creditis, fortuitis incursibus adsumi has mentes? itane istud non divinum et sacrum est?

8. aut sine deo eorum tantas animorum fieri conversiones, ut, cum carnificis unci aliique innumeri cruciatus quemadmodum diximus inpendeant credituris, velut quadam dulcedine atque omnium virtutum amore correpti cognitas accipiant rationes atque mundi omnibus rebus praeponant amicitias Christi?

author: Arnobius
english: You would bring us arguments and the subtleties of suspicions: if Christ himself — with his peace and pardon let me say it — used these in the assemblies of peoples, who would assent, who would hear, who would judge him to promise anything openly, or who, even if foolish and of stupid ease, would follow him tossing empty and bare claims?

Powers set under the eyes and that unheard-of force of things, either which were done by him openly or which were celebrated through the whole world by his heralds — these subjected the flames of desires and made nations and peoples and nations most unlike in customs run together with one mind to the assent of one belief. For those things done in India can be counted and come into the use of reckoning, among the Seres, Persians and Medes, in Arabia, Egypt, in Asia, Syria, among Galatians, Parthians, Phrygians, in Achaia, Macedonia, Epirus, in all islands and provinces which the rising and setting sun traverses, finally at mistress Rome herself, in which though people are occupied with King Numa’s arts and ancient superstitions, they still did not put off leaving ancestral things and coalescing with Christian truth. For they had seen Simon Magus’s chariot and fiery teams blown apart by Peter’s mouth and vanish when Christ was named; they had seen, I say, one trusting false gods and betrayed by the same who feared him cast down by his own weight and lying with broken legs, then afterwards carried to Brundisium, worn by torments and shame, again throw himself from the height of the loftiest peak.

All which things done you neither know nor have wished to know nor ever judged necessary for yourselves, and while you trust your hearts and call pride wisdom, you have given room to deceivers — those noxious ones, I say, whose interest it is that the Christian name grow obsolete — for flooding fogs and obscuring such great things, for snatching faith from you and casting contempt under, so that, because they foresee an end hanging over them for their deserts, they might also cast into you a cause through which you could enter danger and be stripped of divine kindness.

Adv. Nat. 2.12: virtutes; veritati Christianae; nominato Christo.
latin: 12.1. Argumenta vos nobis et suspicionum argutias proferatis: quibus ipse si Christus - cum pace hoc eius et cum venia dixerim - populorum in conventibus uteretur, quis adquiesceret, quis audiret, quis eum promittere aperte aliquid iudicaret, aut quis cassa et nuda iactantem, quamvis esset inprudens et facilitatis stolidae, sequeretur?

2. Virtutes sub oculis positae et inaudita illa vis rerum, vel quae ab ipso fiebant palam vel ab eius praeconibus celebrabantur in orbe toto, ea subdidit adpetitionum flammas et ad unius credulitatis adsensum mente una concurrere gentes et populos fecit et moribus dissimillimas nationes. 3. Enumerari enim possunt atque in usum computationis venire ea quae in India gesta sunt, apud Seras Persas et Medos, in Arabia, Aegypto, in Asia, Syria, apud Galatas Parthos Phrygas, in Achaia Macedonia Epiro, in insulis et provinciis omnibus quas sol oriens atque occidens lustrat, ipsam denique apud dominam Romam, in qua cum homines sint Numae regis artibus atque antiquis superstitionibus occupati, non distulerunt tamen res patrias linquere et veritati coalescere Christianae. 4. Viderant enim currum Simonis magi et quadrigas igneas Petri ore difflatas et nominato Christo evanuisse: viderant, inquam, fidentem dis falsis et ab eisdem metuentibus proditum pondere praecipitatum suo cruribus iacuisse praefractis, post deinde perlatum Brundam cruciatibus et pudore defessum ex altissimi culminis se rursum praecipitasse fastigio.

5. Quae omnia vos gesta neque scitis neque scire voluistis neque umquam vobis necessaria iudicastis, ac dum vestris fiditis cordibus et quod typhus est sapientiam vocatis, dedistis circumscriptoribus locum, illis, inquam, noxiis, quorum nomen interest obsolefieri Christianum, superfundendi caligines atque obscurandi res tantas, eripiendae vobis fidei subiciendique contemptus, ut, quia sibi praesentiunt finem pro meritis imminere, vobis quoque immitterent causam, per quam periculum adire possetis et viduari benignitate divina.

author: Arnobius
english: Nor let that steal upon you or flatter you with airy hope which is said by some sciolists who claim much for themselves: that they are born of God and not subject to fate’s laws if they have lived more strictly, that his hall lies open to them, and after a human’s function, with none forbidding, they are carried back as into the ancestral seat; nor what magi promise, that they have commendatory prayers by which some powers, softened, offer easy ways to those striving to fly up to heaven; nor what Etruria promises in the Acherontic books, that by blood of certain animals given to certain divinities souls become divine and are led out from mortality’s laws.

These are empty blandishments and fomentations of vain vows. Another than almighty God cannot save souls, nor besides is there anyone who can make them long-lived, who can supply the spirit of perpetuity, except he who alone is immortal and perpetual and bounded by no circumscription of time. For since all gods, whether whichever are true or who are said by rumor and opinion to be, are immortal and perpetual by his will and by the gift of his benefit, how can it be that others are able to bestow that which they themselves are, when they have it as another’s and lent by a greater’s power?

Let Etruria slay as many victims as it likes, let the wise deny all human things to themselves, let magi soften and caress all powers: unless from the Lord of things that which reason demands has been given to souls, and that by mandate, it will much afterward repent to have been a mockery, when one begins to come to the sense of perishing.

Adv. Nat. 2.62: deus omnipotens; servare animas; mandatum.
latin: 62.1. Neque illud obrepat aut spe vobis aeria blandiatur, quod ab sciolis nonnullis et plurimum sibi adrogantibus dicitur, deo esse se gnatos nec fati obnoxios legibus, si vitam restrictius egerint, aulam sibi eius patere, ac post hominis functionem prohibente se nullo tamquam in sedem referri patritam; neque quod magi spondent, commendaticias habere se preces quibus emollitae nescio quae potestates vias faciles praebeant ad caelum contendentibus subvolare, neque quod Etruria libris in Acheronticis pollicentur, certorum animalium sanguine numinibus certis dato divinas animas fieri et ab legibus mortalitatis educi.

2. Blandimenta haec cassa sunt et inanium fomenta votorum. Servare animas alius nisi deus omnipotens non potest, nec praeterea quisquam est qui longaevas facere, perpetuitatis possit et spiritum subrogare, nisi qui immortalis et perpetuus solus est et nullius temporis circumscriptione finitus. 3. Cum enim dii omnes, vel quicumque sunt veri vel qui esse rumore atque opinione dicuntur, immortales et perpetui voluntate eius sint et beneficii munere, qui fieri potis est, ut alii praestare id quod ipsi sunt valeant, cum alienum id habeant et maioris potentia commodatum?

4. Caedant licet hostias quantaslibet Etruria, humana sibi omnia sapientes negent, magi cunctas emolliant et commulceant potestates: nisi ab domino rerum datum fuerit animis id quod ratio postulat idque per mandatum, multum postea paenitebit fuisse inrisui, cum ad sensum coeperit interitionis accedi.

author: Arnobius
english: And since you are accustomed to laugh at our faith and to slash at credulity itself with joking strokes, say, O merry ones dyed and filled with wisdom’s neat wine: is there any busy and active kind of work in life that actors take up, seize, and approach without faith going before?

Do you travel and sail without believing you will return home when business is done? Do you split the earth with iron and fill it with variety of seeds without believing you will take fruit in the turns of seasons? Do you join marital partnerships without believing they will be chaste and of dutiful bond toward husbands? Do you take on the offspring of children without believing it will be safe and come through the grades of age to the bounds of old age? Do you commit the body’s illnesses to physicians’ hands without believing diseases can be eased when harshness is softened? Do you wage wars with enemies without believing you will bring back victory by the successions of battles?
Do you reverence and cultivate the gods without believing they exist and turn favorable ears to your prayers?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
latin: 8.1. Et quoniam ridere nostram fidem consuestis atque ipsam credulitatem facctis iocularibus lancinare, dicite, o festivi et meraco sapientiae tincti et saturi potu, estne operis in vita negotiosum aliquod atque actuosum genus, quod non fide praeeunte suscipiant sumant atque adgrediantur actores?

2. Peregrinamini, navigatis non domum vos credentes peractis negotiationibus remeaturos? Terram ferro scinditis atque oppletis seminum variètate non credentes vos frugem percepturos esse vicibus temporariis? 3. Coniugalia copulatis consortia non futura esse credentes casta et officiosi foederis in maritos? Liberorum susceptatis prolem non incolumem credentes fore et per gradus aetatis venturam senectutis ad metas? 4. Aegritudines corporum medicorum committitis manibus non credentes morbos posse mitigata asperitate leniri? Bella cum hostibus geritis non victoriam vos credentes proeliorum successionibus relaturos?
5. Veneramini deos et colitis non credentes illos esse et propitias aures vestris supplicationibus accommodare?

author: Arnobius
english: But let these things hinder nothing and impede nothing, least of all that you ought not to believe and listen to them: and what is it that in this part either you have more or we less?
You believe Plato, Cronius, Numenius, or whom you please: we believe and rest in Christ.

How great is this unfairness, that when we both stand by authors and believing is one and shared for us and you, you want it granted that you may so receive what is said by them, while what is brought forward by Christ you demand we know by syllogisms and like things that they pledge the truth — or are they by that worthy that one must necessarily believe them on the most obscure matters? A contest of persons is not to be weighed by powers of eloquence but by the virtue of deeds done. He is not to be called a good author who put out speech whitely, but who follows up what he promises with a pledge of divine works.

Adv. Nat. 2.11: credimus Christo; divinorum operum.

added_allusions.reason: faith not in eloquence but power.

latin: 11.1. Sed officiant haec <nihil> nihilque impediant, plurimum quominus eis credere atque auscultare debeatis: et quid est, quod in hac parte aut vos plurimum habeatis aut nos minus?
2. Vos Platoni, vos Cronio, vos Numenio vel cui libuerit creditis: nos credimus et adquiescimus Christo.

3. Iniquitas haec quanta est, ut cum utrique auctoribus stemus sit que nobis et vobis unum et socium credere, vobis velitis dari quod ita ab illis dicatur accipere, nos ea quae proferuntur a Christo f. 32b | syllogismi resque aliae similes scire illos veritatem spondent aut ea re digni sunt quibus necessario debeat rebus de obscurissimis credi? Personarum contentio non est eloquentiae viribus set gestorum operum virtute pendenda. Ille <non> est dicendus auctor bonus, qui sermonem candidule prompsit, sed qui quod pollicetur divinorum operum prosequitur sponsione.

author: Arnobius
english: Since these things are so, and since we hold it handed down from the highest author that souls are not set far from death’s openings and jaws, yet can become long-lived by the gift and benefit of the highest prince if only they try and meditate to recognize him — for knowledge of him is a kind of leaven of life and glue of a thing that would otherwise come apart — then, ferocity and inhumanity laid aside, they may take up milder characters so they can be ready for what will be given.

Why are we judged by you as dull and stupid if, because of these fears, we have handed over and bound ourselves to God the liberator? Against harmful strikes and venomous bites of serpents we often seek remedies and protect ourselves with plates, with Psylli and Marsi selling and other peddlers and quacks; and lest colds and fierce suns harm us, we prepare with anxious care of caution the defenses of houses and clothes.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.32: munere; liberatori deo; cognitio.
latin: 32.1. Haec cum ita se habeant et cum ab summo traditum teneamus auctore, non esse animas longe ab hiatibus mortis et faucibus constitutas, posse tamen longaevas summi principis munere ac beneficio fieri, si modo illum temptent ac meditentur adgnoscere - eius enim cognitio fermentum quoddam est vitae ac rei dissociabilis glutinum - tum deinde feritate atque inhumanitate depositis resumant ingenia mitiora, ut ad illud quod dabitur esse possint paratae.

2. Quid est quod a vobis tamquam bruti et stolidi iudicemur, si propter hos metus liberatori dedidimus et mancipavimus nos deo? Adversus ictus noxios et venenatos colubrarum morsus remedia saepe conquirimus et protegimus nos lamminis, Psyllis Marsis vendentibus aliisque institoribus atque planis, ac ne nobis frigora solesque incommodent rapidi, munimenta domorum ac vestium sollicitae praeparamus diligentia cautionis.

author: Arnobius
english: When fear of death is set before us — that is, the destruction of souls — what? Do we not, from the sense of advantage by which we all love ourselves, hold, embrace, and (if only a just exchange stands) prefer before our very souls him who promises he will free us from such danger? You place the salvation of your souls in yourselves and trust you become gods by your own inward effort; but we promise ourselves nothing from our weakness, seeing that our nature is of no strength and is overcome by its own affections in every contest of things.

You think that as soon as you have gone free from the knots of the limbs, wings will be at hand by which you can make for heaven and fly to the stars; we fear such boldness so much and do not reckon it placed in our power to seek the things above, since we hold even this itself uncertain — whether we deserve to receive life and be led away from mortality’s law. You presume you will return of your own accord into the Lord’s hall as into your own seat with none forbidding; but we neither hope that this order of things can happen without the Lord, nor do we judge that so much power and license is granted to any human.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.33: animarum salutem; liberaturum; sine domino.
latin: 33.1. Mortis nobis cum proponatur metus id est animarum interitus, quid? non ex commodi facimus sensu quo amamus nos omnes, quod eum qui nobis spondet tali a periculo liberaturum retinemus amplectimur animisque ipsis nostris, si modo iusta extat vicissitudo, praeponimus? Vos vestrarum animarum salutem in ipsis vobis reponitis fierique vos deos vestro fiditis intestinoque conatu; at vero nos nobis nihil de nostra infirmitate promittimus naturam intuentes nostram virium esse nullarum et ab suis adfectibus in omni rerum contentione superari.

2. Vos cum primum soluti membrorum abieritis e nodis, alas vobis adfuturas putatis quibus ad caelum pergere atque ad sidera volare possitis; nos tantam reformidamus audaciam nec in nostra ducimus esse positum potestate res superas petere, cum et hoc ipsum habeamus incertum, an vitam accipere mereamur et ab lege mortalitatis abduci. Vos in aulam dominicam tamquam in propriam sedem remeaturos vos sponte nullo prohibente praesumitis; at vero nos istud rerum sine domino fieri neque speramus posse neque ulli hominum tantum potestatis attribui licentiaeque censemus.

author: Arnobius
english: Meanwhile, O you who admire and are stunned by the decrees of the learned and of philosophy, do you not count it most unjust to ride down and mock us as if we say stupid and brutish things, when you yourselves are found saying the same or such things as you laugh to hear said of us? I am not speaking with those scattered through the byways of the sects who have made this and that party by diversity of opinions: I call you who follow Mercury, Plato, and Pythagoras, and you others who are of one mind and walk by the same roads of shared opinions.

Do you dare laugh at us because we venerate and cultivate the Father and Lord of things and because we hand over and entrust our hopes to him? What of your Plato in the Theaetetus — to name him especially — does he not urge the mind to flee from the earth and, as far as can be done, always to dwell in thought and mind around that one? Do you dare laugh at us because we say a resurrection of the dead is to come — which we confess we say, but which is heard by you otherwise than we mean? What in the Politicus of the same Plato — does he not write that when the world has begun to rise from the western parts and to turn toward the hinge of the rising sun, humans will burst again from earth’s bosom as grey decrepit old men, and when the years begin to grow longer they will go down by the same steps by which growth happens today unto the cradles of infancy?

Do you dare laugh at us because we provide for the salvation of our souls — that is, for ourselves? For what are we humans if not souls shut in bodies? Do you yourselves not all take cares for their safety? Is it not fear that holds you — when you abstain from all vices and desires — lest you stick to bodies as if fixed by beam-nails? What do those rites of secret arts mean, by which you address I know not what powers so they may be gentle to you and not set obstacles of hindrance when you return to the ancestral seats?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.13: spes; resurrectio; animarum salus.
latin: 13.1. Interea tamen o isti, qui admiramini, qui stupetis doctorum et philosophiae scita, ita non iniustissimum ducitis inequitare, inludere tamquam stulta nobis et bruta dicentibus, cum vel ea vel talia repperiamini et vos dicere quae nobis dici pronuntiari que ridetis? 2. Nec mihi cum his sermo est qui per varia sectarum deverticula dissipati has atque illas partes opinionum diversitate fecerunt: vos, vos appello qui Mercurium, qui Platonem Pythagoram que sectamini, vosque ceteros, qui estis unius mentis et per easdam vias placitorum inceditis unitate.

3. Audetis ridere nos, quod patrem rerum ac dominum veneramur et colimus quodque illi dedamus et permittamus spes nostras? 4. Quid Plato vester in Theaeteto [Plat. Theaet. 173 e], ut eum potissimum nominem, nonne animo fugere suadet e terris et circa illum semper quantum fieri potis est cogitatione ac mente versari? 5. Audetis ridere nos, quod mortuorum dicamus resurrectionem futuram, quam quidem nos dicere confitemur sed a vobis aliter quam sentiamus audiri? 6. Quid in Politico idem Plato? [Pl. Polit. 270 d] nonne cum mundus occeperit ab occiduis partibus exoriri et in cardinem vergere qui orientis est solis, rursus erupturos homines telluris e gremio scribit senes canos decrepitos et cum anni coeperint accedere longiores per eosdem gradus quibus hodic crescitur ad incunabula infantiae desituros?

7. Audetis ridere nos, quod animarum nostrarum provideamus saluti id est ipsi nobis? quid enim sumus homines nisi animae corporibus clausae? Vos enim non omnes pro illarum geritis incolumitatibus curas? non quod vitiis omnibus et cupiditatibus abstinetis, metus ille vos habet ne velut trabalibus clavis adfici corporibus haereatis? 8. Quid illi sibi volunt secretarum artium ritus, quibus adfamini nescio quas potestates, ut sint vobis placidae neque ad sedes remeantibus patrias obstacula impeditionis opponant?

author: Commodian
english: How long, foolish man, will you refuse to know Christ? You avoid the rich field and cast seed on the barren. You want to stay in the wood where the robber lurks. Enter already now into the hall, so often invited: the harvest is already ripe, the time equally prepared — see, reap now, if you do not then regret it. Now, if you have nothing, gather; the vintage comes; the time of life is at hand for the believer in the time of death.

God’s first law is the foundation of the later law, and it marked you out that you should believe in the second law; and no less did it stun those from that law who were wise for themselves. Now become stunned and speak — believe in Christ — for the old testament proclaims concerning him. Now there is need to believe — only that the dead can rise in him and live for the whole time. Therefore if anyone refuses to believe these things will be, while he is beaten as guilty in the second death, I will sing in a few words in this little book what will come — for it can be known where the hope of life must be set. Still I urge you as soon as possible to believe in Christ.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 24 QUI IMENTET. ? NON CREDENT Quamdiu, stulte homo, Christum cognoscere non uis? Uitas agrum pinguem et stereli semina iactas. In silua manere quaeris, ubi latro moratur. Ingredere iam nunc totiens inuitatus in aula: Matura iam messis, tempus totidemque paratum, Ecce modo mete, quodsi non te paenitet inde. Nunc, si non habes, collige; uindemia uenit;

Tempus adest uitae credenti tempore mortis. Est Dei lex prima fundamentum posterae legis, Teque designabat, crederes in lege secunda; Nec minus et ipsos et ex ipsa sibi prudentes Obstupe iam factus ora tu credere Christo, Nam testamentum uetus de isto proclamat. Credere nun<c> opus est, tantum in isto defunctum Resurgere posse <et> uiuere tempore toto. Ergo si quis ea discredis esse futura Dummodo uincetur reus in morte secunda, Euentura canam paucis in isto libello Nam cognosci potest, ubi sit spes uitae ponenda. Tamen uos adhortor quantocius credere Christo.

author: Commodian
english: Wretched one, you spit out the good of heavenly discipline and rush into death while you want to wander without a bit. Luxuries and the world’s short joys ruin you — from which you will be tormented under hell for the whole time. The joys you foolishly delight in are empty. They do not make you out to have been a human once dead. Can thirty years already not make you taught? If at first you erred unknowing, look back at the grey head. Do you think you now enjoy this life gladly? Injuries, lawsuits are there and daily losses, unspeakable wars, frauds, thefts with blood; the body is vexed with sores and there is groaning and weeping; whether a plague invades or you are held by long disease, or you are robbed of children, or you weep a lost wife; the whole is destroyed, dignities fall from on high; you burn with poverty twice over if you are certainly sick: and you call it life, where you linger in a glass life? Look at last: this time is empty; but in the future there is hope for you of living without deceit.

Little ones snatched away surely wanted to live, and youths robbed of life perhaps to grow old, because the rich man himself was preparing to enjoy delicacies; and yet unwilling we leave all things to the world. I too was a nation, dwelling with a warped mind, and I thought the life of this age was present, and likewise judged as you do that death is there when once the soul has gone out — that the dead has perished. But these things are not so; the founder and author of the world sought the brother slain by the brother: “Impious one,” he says, “tell, where is your brother?” He denied. For the brother’s blood cried to me on high. You are tormented, I see, where you thought nothing is felt — but he will live and hold the right-hand places, and enjoy the delights you lost, wicked one! And when you renew the age, he who went before will already be immortal; for you will wail under Tartarus. God will certainly live, who made the dead live, to give worthy rewards to the innocent and good, but fierce Tartarus to the mad and impious. Begin to feel God’s judgments, you seduced one!
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 25: REPUGNANTIBUS ADVERSUS LEGEM CHRISTI DEI VIVI.

added_allusions.reason: do not refuse him who speaks.

latin: 25 REPUGNANTIBUS ADVERSUS LEGEM CHRISTI DEI VIVI. Respuis, infelix, bonum disciplinae caelestis Et ruis in mortem, dum uis sine freno uagari. Perdunt te luxuriae et breuia gaudia mundi, Unde sub inferno cruciaberis tempore toto. Gaudia sunt uana, quibus oblectaris inepte. Non illa te reddunt hominem fuisse defunctum. Anni te non possunt iam triginta reddere doctum? Nescius si primum errasti, respice canum. Tu putas nunc uitam isti te perfrui laetum? Iniurias, lites ibi sunt et damna diurnum, Bella uel infanda, fraudes, cum sanguine furta, Ulceribus corpus uexatur gemiturque, ploratur, Seu luis inuadit aut longo morbo teneris, Aut natis orbaris, aut perdita coniugula defles; Destruitur totum, ruunt dignitatis ab alto; Ureris pauperie dupliciter certe si languis: Et dicis uitam, ubi uitrea uita moraris? Respice iam tandem hoc tempus inritum esse; Sed in futuro tibi spes est sine dolo uiuendi. Uiuere uoleba<n>t utique paruoli rapti, Sed uita priuati iuuenes senescere forte, Lautities diues perfrui quia ipse parabat; Et tamen inuiti reli<n>quimus omnia mundo. Gens et ego fui peruersa mente moratus Et uitam istius saeculi coram esse putabam Mortemque similiter sicut uos iudicabam adesse, Cum semel exisset animus, perisse defunctum.

Haec autem sic non sunt; sed conditor orbis et auctor Requisiuit enim fratrem a fratre peremptum: Impie, dic, inquit, ubinam frater? Ille negauit. Sanguis enim fratris ad me perclamauit in altum. Torqueris, uideo, ubi nil sentire putabas, Ille autem uiuet et loca dextera tenet, Delicias fruitur, quas tu perdidisti, nefande! Et cum renouasti saeculum, et ille praegressus Iam <in>mortalis erit; nam tu sub tartara planges. Uiuet certe Deus, qui defunctos uiuere fecit Innocuisque bonis ut reddat praemia digna, Uesanis autem et impiis tartara saeua. Incipe sentire iudicia Dei, seducte!

author: Commodian
english: I have spoken of the double wood, from which death proceeded, and again from there life often proceeds. The King of eternity through the cross foreshadows the dread ones, so that they may not believe him. O fools, living in death! Cain killed the younger, found wicked: from there Canaanites are said born of Noah’s stock. So an unjust race grew in the world, which never changes minds to believe the Lord’s cross. It comes into error, and they say they live rightly. The law was first in wood, and from there the second — it came before the terrible first law with peace. In crooked boasting the cruel wicked rushed: they refuse to recognize the Lord pierced with nails, at whose judgment when he comes they then discern. But Abel’s race now believes the kind Christ.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin:
35 DE RUCI STULTITIA. De duplici ligno dixi, mors unde processit, Et iterum inde procedere uita frequenter. Rex aeternitatis per crucem diros adumbrat, Ut sibi non credant. O stulti, morte uiuentes! Cain iuniorem occisit nequam repertus: Inde Noe subolis Cananaei nati feruntur. Sic genus iniquum increuit mundo, qui nunquam Transmutat animos in Domini credere crucem. Uenit in errorem, et dicunt se uiuere recte. Lex in ligno fuit prima, et inde secunda Terribilem legem prima cum pace

raeuenit. In praua iactatione saeua scelerati ruerunt: Traiectum clauis Dominum cognoscere nolunt, In cuius iudicium cum uerit, ibi dignoscunt. Abel genus autem credit modo Christo benigno.

author: Commodian
english: All who believe in Christ, idols left behind, I warn in a few words for your saving goods. In first times if you did anything through error, spent for Christ leave all things, and when you have known God, be a good proven recruit, and let virgin modesty turn with you in the lamb. Let the mind watch among goods: beware lest you offend as before; in baptism only the things of new birth are given you. For if anyone as a catechumen sins, punishments are noted — that mark may live, but you do not linger without losses. The sum for you: always avoid heavy sins.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 45 CATECUMINIS. Credentes in Christo derelictis idolis omnes Admoneo paucis propter salutaria uestra. Temporibus primis per errorem si qua gerebas, Erogatus enim Christo tu cuncta relinque, Cumque Deum nosti, esto bonus tiro, probatus, Uirgineusque pudor tecum uersetur in agno. Mens bonis inuigilet: caue ut non delinquas ut ante; In baptismo tibi genitali sola donantur. Nam si quis peccans catecuminus poena notantur, Insignis illa uiuat, sed non sine damna moraris. Summa tibi: grauia peccata deuita tu semper.

author: Commodian
english: You have become a penitent: pray night and day, yet do not go far from the mother, and the Most High will be able to be merciful to you. Confusion of fault will not happen into a void; in your guilt you ought to weep things openly; if you have a deep wound, seek also a physician, and yet in punishments you will be able to ease your losses. For I will confess I was one of you and long felt the terror of ruin. Therefore I warn the wounded to go more carefully, to foul beard and hair in the dust of the earth and to roll in sackcloth and to ask of the highest King that he help you, lest you happen to perish from the people.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 48 PAENITENTIBUS. Paenitens es factus: noctibus diebusque precare, Attamen a matre noli discedere longe, Et tibi misericors poterit Altissimus esse. Non fiet in uacuum confusio culpae perinde In reatu tuo debes manifesta deflere, Tu si uulnus habes altum, medicumque require, Et tamen in poenis poteris tua damna lenire. Namque fatebor enim unum me ex uobis adesse Terroremque diu quondam sensisse ruinae. Idcirco commoneo uulneratos cautius ire, Barbam <atque> comam foedare in puluere terrae Uolutareque saccis et petere summo de Rege Subuenire tibi, ne pereas forte de plebe.

author: Commodian
english: From heaven the city descends in the first resurrection. And what should we report of so great a heavenly fabric? We rise to it who were devoted to it, and they will already then be incorrupt, living without death, but neither any pain nor groan will be in it. Those also will come who conquer under Antichrist with strong martyrdoms, and they themselves live the whole time and receive goods, because they suffered evils.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 43 DE RESURRECTIONE PRIMA. De caelo descendit ciuitas in anastase prima. Et quod referamus de fabrica tanta caeleste? Resurgimus illi, qui fuimus illi deuoti, Et incorrupti erint iam tunc sine morte uiuentes, Sed nec dolor ullus nec gemitus erit in illa. Uenturi sunt illi quoque, sub Antechristo qui uincunt Robusta mar<tyr>ia, et ipsi toto tempore uiuunt Recipiuntque bona, quoniam mala passi fuere, Et generant ipsi per annos mille nubentes. Conparantur ibi tota uectigalia terrae, Terra quia nimium fundit sine fine nouata. Inibi non pluuiam, non frigus in aurea castra, Obsidiae nullae, sicut nunc, neque rapinae. Nec lucernae lumen desiderat ciuitas illa: Ex auctore suo lucet, nec nox ibi paret. Per duodecim milia stadia lata, longa, sic alta; Radicem in terra, sed caput cum caelo peraequat; In urbem pro foribus autem sol aut luna lucebit. Malus in angore saeptus propter iustos alendos. Ab annis autem mille Deus omnia portat.

author: Commodian
english: Concerning the day of judgment I add for the unbelievers: fire sent again will be ruled by God; the earth then groans at the last end of things, so that then all unbelieving nations are on the earth — and yet it avoids the camp of his saints. In one flame all nature turns; the earth burns from the depths and mountains melt; nothing of the sea remains, conquered by powerful fire; this heaven perishes and this earth is changed.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 44 DE DIE IUDICII. De die iudicii propter incredulos addo: Emissus iterum Dei do<mi>nabitur ignis; Dat gemitum terra rerum tunc in ultima fine In ter<r>a gentes ut tunc incredulae cunctae, Euitat et tamen sanctorum castra suorum. In una flamma conuertit tota natura, Uritur ab imis terra montesque liquescunt, De mare nihil remanet, uincetur ab igne potente, Interit hoc caelum et ista terra mutatur. Conponitur alia nouitas caeli, terrae perennis. Inde qui mereunt mittuntur in morte secunda, Interius autem habitaculis iusti locantur.

author: Commodian
english: When you have given the name of military service, you are held by a bit. Begin then therefore to dismiss former deeds; avoid luxuries, since labor hangs over the arms; the King’s command must be obeyed with every virtue, if you wish to reach the last glad times. Always expect those things to be enjoyed as a good soldier; do not flatter yourself; omit sloth altogether; so that you may be present daily before your purpose, be anxious, revisit the standards early.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 52 MILITIBUS CHRISTI. Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimitte<re> pristina gesta, Luxurias uita, quoniam labor inminet armis; Imperio Regis omni uirtute parendum, Tempora postrema si uis pertingere laeta. Illa bonus milis semper expecta fruenda, Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino omitte; Ut tuo proposito cottidie praesto sis ante, Sollicitus esto, matutinus signa reuise. Cum uideris bellum, agonia sume propinquus; Haec gloria Regis, militem uidere paratum. Rex adest optato; propter spem dimicat uestram; Ille parat dona, ille pro uictoria lectos Suscipit et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in datis parcere noli, Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.

author: Commodian
english: Adam the first-formed, to avoid God’s commands — Belial was the “savior” from envy of the formed creature. Whatever good or evil the leader of our birth did, he brought on us; we die the same through him, himself made an exile from the Word when he withdrew from the divine. When six thousand years are finished we shall be immortal. When the tree’s fruit was tasted, death entered the world: by this wood of death let us seek the fruits of life to come. Life hangs on the wood bearing fruits, the commands: take now, believers, fruits from the living wood. A law to be feared was given the first man from wood, from which death came when the first law was neglected: now stretch out the hand and take from the living wood.

The Lord’s best law that followed proceeded from the wood; the first law was lost; he tastes whence he may who worships forbidden gods, the evil joys of life. Spit out the taste; it will be enough to know what it was. If you want to live, give yourselves back to the second law; avoid the cult of temples, the shrines of demons. Turn yourselves to Christ, and you will be God’s companions. Holy is God’s law, who says the dead live. The Lord commanded hymn to be offered to himself alone; avoid the devil’s law altogether, all of you.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 34 ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUXYZ. Adam protoplaustus ut Dei praecepta uitaret, Belias seruator fuit de inuidia plasmae. Contulisset nobis seu boni seu mali quod egit Dux natiuitatis; morimur idemque per illum, Ex diuino ipse ut recedens exsul factus a uerbo. Finitis sex milibus annis inmortales erimus. Gustato pomo ligni mors intrauit in orbem: Hoc ligno mortis quaeramus uitae futurae. In ligno pendit uita ferens poma, praecepta: Kapite nunc ligno uitali poma credentes. Lex a <ligno> data est homini primitiuo timenda, Mors unde prouenit neglecta lege primordi: Nunc extende manum et sume de ligno uitali.

Optima lex Domini sequens de ligno processit; Perdita lex prima; gustat, unde licet illi, Qui deos adorat uetitos, mala gaudia uitae. Respuite gustum; sufficiet scire quod esset. Si <ui>uere uultis, reddite uos legi secundae, Templorum cultura<m>, daemonum fana uitate. Uertite uos Christo, et eritis Deo sodales. Xancta Dei lex est, qui mortuos uiuere dicit. Ymnum sibi soli Dominus proferre praecepit, Zabolicam legem omnes omnino uitate.

author: Commodian
english: You put it off, rich man, looking too much at all that is yours, still seeking to pile more on it without being filled. You say: “I do not hope to live after these things when I am dead.” Ungrateful to the highest God — you who so judge God to be — who brought you forth when you did not know, then fed you; he himself your meadows, he himself steers the vines, he himself the flocks and whatever you own — and you have not attended to these. Or do you by chance rule all things? He who made this heaven and earth and the salt seas has decreed to restore us ourselves in a golden age; and if you believe now, one lives into God’s secrets. Learn God, fool, who wants you to be present immortal so you may return thanks to him in the everlasting contest. His law teaches — but because you seek to wander, you disbelieve all things and from there you will go into tartarus: soon you give back the soul, you are led where it grieves you to be. But there an eternal spiritual penalty is paid; there are always mourning-songs, nor do you die through in them — already then too late crying out there to almighty God.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 28 DIVITI INCREDULO MALO. Differ<r>is, diues, nimium tua cuncta uidendo, Insatiabiliter quibus adhuc adicere quaeris. Uiuere post ista, dicis, non spero defunctus. Ingrate summo Deo, qui sic Deum iudicas esse, Te qui nesciente protulit, deinde nutriuit; Ipse prata tua, gubernat uineas ipse, Ipse greges pecorum et quicquid possides ipse, Nec istis adtendistis. Aut tu regis omnia forte? Caelum hoc et terram et maria salsa qui fecit, Reddere decreuit nos ipsos in aureo saeclo Et modo si credis, uiuitur in Dei secreta. Disce Deum, stulte, qui uult te inmortalem adesse Ut gratias illi referas in agone perennis. Lex docet ipsius, sed quia uagari tu quaeris, Omnia discredis et inde in tartara ibis: Mox animam reddis, duceris quo te paenitet esse. At luitur ibi poena spiritalis aeterna; Lugia sunt semper, nec permoreris in illa Omnipotentem Deum iam tunc ibi sero proclamans.

author: Commodian
english: Let birds and beasts of the woods be deceived by foods: an incautious nature of mind has been handed to them; they are caught by tricks or following bait, and they do not know how to avoid evil nor are they held by law. Law has been given to the human and a teaching of life to be read, from which he remembers so he can live carefully, and also may refuse his place and the things that are of death. He condemns himself heavily who offends the king: either he is bound with iron or cast down from the dignity of rank, or deprived of life he will lose what he ought to enjoy. Warned by the example do not sin heavily; transferred by the washing rather have charity, and avoid far the bait of the trap where death is. There are many martyrdoms that are without blood poured. Not to desire another’s, to want to have martyrdom, to rein the tongue, to make yourself humble — you ought; not to do violence of yourself nor to return it when done — be a patient mind: understand that you are a martyr.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 47 FIDELES CAVETE MALUM. Fallantur uolucres et siluarum bestei escis: Incauta natura quibus est tradita mentis, Decipiunturque strofia aut esca sequentes, Et uitare malum nesciunt nec lege tenentur. Lex homini data est et doctrina uitae legenda, Ex qua recordatur, ut possit uiuere caute, Sui quoque locum, mortis et deroget ea quae sunt. Condemnat se ipsum grauiter qui regi delinquet: Aut ferro ligatur aut decus gradu deiectus Uel uita priuatus perdet, quod frui deberet. Exemplo moniti grauiter peccare nolite, Translati lauacro magis caritatem habete, Et escam muscipuli, ubi mors est, longe uitate. Multa sunt martyria, quae sunt sine sanguine fuso. Alienum non cupire, uelle martyrii habere, Linguam refrenare, humilem te reddere debes, Uim ultro non facere nec factam reddere contra Mens patiens fueris: intellege martyrem esse.

author: Commodian
english: The trumpet gives a sign from heaven when the lion is taken up, and suddenly there are darknesses with heaven’s crash. The Lord lowers his eyes so the earth may tremble, and he also cries out so that all on the globe may hear: “See, I have long been silent, bearing your things for so much time!” Together they cry, mourning late, groaning; there is wailing, weeping, and no space is given the unjust. What will a mother do for the nursing child when she herself is burned? In the flame of fire the Lord will judge the wicked: but the fire will not touch the just — rather it will lick around. They stay under one [order], but a part will weep in the sentence. So great will the heat be that the stones themselves melt; winds drive in lightning; heaven’s anger will rage so that wherever the impious flees he is caught by fire. There will be no help, not even of ships. Yet the flame is parted in the midst of the nations and keeps, so that for a thousand years they may bear bodies for the saints. For from there after a thousand years they are handed to Gehenna, and the fabric they belonged to is burned with them.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 42 DE SAECULI ISTIUS FINE. Dat tuba caelo signum sublato leone Et fiunt desubito tenebrae cum caeli fragore. Summittit oculos Dominus, ut terra tremescat, Adclamat et<iam>, ut audiant omnes in orbem: 'Ecce diu tacui sufferens tanto tempore uestra!' Conclamant pariter plangentes sero gementes, Ululatur, ploratur, nec spatium datur iniquis. Lactanti quod faciet mater, cum ipsa crematur? In flamma ignis Dominus iudicabit iniquos: Iustos autem non tanget ignis, sed immo delinget. Sub uno morantur, sed pars in sententia flebit. Tantus erit ardor, ut lapides ipsi liquescant, In fulmine cogunt uenti, furet ira caelestis Ut, quacumque fugit, impius occupetur ab igne. Subpetium nullum erit nec nauticae puppes. Flamma tamen gentis media partiturque seruans, In annis mille ut ferant corpora sanctis. Nam inde post annos mille gehennae traduntur, Et fabrica cuius erant cum ipsa cremantur.

author: Commodian
english: Justice and goodness, peace and true patience make one live after death and be examined concerning one’s deed; but a crafty mind — harmless [in show], treacherous, crooked — lifts itself to the side and dwells with a wild mind. Impious one, hear now, you who want to profit by evil deeds: look at earthly judges who now in the body torment the dread with penalties — punishments are prepared by iron for deserts, or weeping in long prison. Do you finally hope to mock the heavenly God and the ruler of the sky through whom all things were made? You rage, you rave, you also pull down God’s name now? From this you will not escape, who will set a penalty after death. Now I want you cautious, lest you come into the heat of fire. Hand yourself already to Christ, so that good deeds may follow you.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 27 IUSTI RES URGUNT. Iustitia et bonitas, pax et patientia uera Uiuere post fata faciunt et quaeri de actu: Subdola mens autem, <in>noxia, perfida, praua Tollit se in parte et fera mente moratur. Impie, nunc audi, qui <uis> malefacta lucrari: Respice terrenos iudices, in corpore qui nunc Excruciant poenis diros: aut ferro parantur Supplicia meritis aut longo carcere flere. Ultime tu speras Deum inridere caelestem Rectoremque poli, per quem sunt omnia facta? Grassaris, insanis, detractas nunc et Dei nomen? Unde non effugies, poenam post fata qui ponet. Nunc uolo sis cautus, ne uenias ignis in aestu. Trade te iam Christo, ut te benefacta sequantur.

author: Commodian
english: Thinking to be free by living doubtfully between both, stripped of the law, worn out, you go ahead in luxury. So many luxuries, vain one, you look toward — why seek unjust things? And whatever you have done remains from here for the dead — look! Fool, you were not, and see, you appear! You do not know whence you came or whence you are fed. You flee the high God, kind to your life, and your Ruler who would rather have you live; you turn your face and send your back to God; you sink yourself in darkness while you think you linger in light. Why do you often run two-faced into the synagogue? You go out from there and again seek the shrines; you want to live between both, but from that you will perish.

Besides you say: “Who is it who has come back from death, that we should believe him that punishments are done there?” Things are not as you think, wicked one! For it also profits him after the funeral who has lived rightly; you nevertheless soon die, you are led into a wicked place; but those who believe in Christ into a kindly place, and that pleasantness sticks to them and flatters them. But you doubtful living ones — a penalty without body raises you to cry late in the torturer’s face.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 23 INTER UTRUMQUE VIVENTIBUS. Inter utrumque putans dubie uiuendo carere Nudatus a lege, decrepitus luxu praecedis. Tot, uane, <luxurias> prospicis; quid quaeris iniqua? Et quidquid egistis, istinc remanere defuncto Respicite! Stulte, non eras, et ecce uideris! Unde processisti nescis nec unde nutriris. Tu Deum excelsum fugis tuae uitae benignum Rectoremque tuum, qui te magis uiuere uelit; Uertis te in faciem et dorsum Deo remittis, Mergis te in tenebris, dum putas te in lucem morari. Quid in sinagoga decurris saepe bifarius? Exis inde foris, iterum tu fana requiris; Uis inter utrumque uiuere, sed inde peribis.

Insuper et dicis: 'Quis est, qui a morte reuenit Ut credamus ei, quoniam ibi poenas aguntur?' Ea non sunt sic, ut tu putas esse, maligne! Nam illique prodest post funera, recte qui uixit, Tu tamen mox moreris, duceris in loco maligno; In Christo credentes autem in loco benigno, Blanditurque quibus haeret amoenitas illa. Uos autem dubios uiuos sine corpore poena Suscitat in faciem tortoris sero clamare.

author: Commodian
english: An untamed hind refuses to bear the yoke for labor; then it likes to fill itself in fat fields with little cabbages. And yet unwilling it is tamed, equally useful, and being tamed it lessens being fierce. Nation, human, you brother — do not be a wild beast; tear yourself free at last and think it over with yourself: you were born not at all a beast nor for beasts, but a human; tame yourself wisely and enter under the caves. You who follow idols — nothing but the vanity of the age. Light hearts lead you into the penal abyss. There you carry gold, clothes, silver in your arms; there is dancing, then love-song is sung for psalms. You think life is where the games are, or you look to those things: you draw lots, ignorant one; you seek extinguished golden things. From there you will not escape the plague, though you yourself divine.

The grace which the Lord has sent to be gathered on earth — you do not seek it, but so wandering as a beast. Golden ages will come to you after fate if you believe rightly, that you may begin again to live immortal forever. This too is given to know what you were before: offer yourself subject to God, who steers all things.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 33 ITEM GENTILIBUS IGNARIS. Indomita ceruia respuit iugum ferre labori, Tunc iuuat in campis crassis satiare cauliclis. Et tamen inuita domatur utilis aeque Minuiturque ferox esse perinde domata; Gens, homo, tu frater, noli pecus esse ferinum, Erue te tandem et tecum ipse retracta: Non utique pecus nec besteis, sed homo natus, Tu te ipse doma sapiens et intra sub antra. Idola qui sequeris, nihil nisi uanitas aeui. Leuia uos corda perducunt poenali barathro. Ibi aurum, uestes, argentum ulnis refertis, Ballatur ibi, dein cantatur pro psalmis amori. Uitam esse putas, ubi ludi, aut prospicis ista: Sortiris, ignare, extincta, aurea quaeris. Inde non effugies pestem, licet ipse diuines.

Gratiam, quam misit Dominus in terra legenda<m>, Non requiris eam, sed sic quasi besteus errans. Aurea post fata ueniet tibi saecla, si credis recte, Rursus ut incipias inmortale uiuere semper. Illud quoque datur scire, quod ante fuisti: Subiectum te praebe Deo, qui cuncta gubernat.

author: Commodian
english: There sits a last hidden holy people, and indeed unknown to us where they dwell. Through nine tribes and a half they act; two tribes and a half were left to us. And Christ commanded the ancients to live through the law. Let us all live now — the handing-over of the new law, as the law itself teaches! I show you more openly. Why were two tribes and a half left behind — half a tribe from those? So there might be martyrs when he would bring war on his elect in the world, or certainly so a choir of holy prophets might rise to that people, who would put a bridle on them whom filthy horses trampled with loosened heel, nor was it their habit ever to hold peace in hand. Those of the tribes were set apart so that all the mysteries of Christ might be completed through them for the whole age. But they were born from the crime of two brothers, at whose omen the deeds that followed were. Were such bloodstained ones not justly scattered? They gather again because of the mysteries in the camps. Then they hurry for the law’s told things to be filled.

Almighty Christ descends to his elect, who were darkened from us for so long a time, made thousands; that is the true heavenly nation. No one born dies there before the father, nor do they feel pains in their bodies like sores born. Resting on their bed they withdraw in due time, fulfilling all things of the law, and therefore they are guarded. They are ordered to pass to the Lord from these parts; the river dries for them as for those who crossed before, and no less the Lord himself leads them out with them. He has passed to our things; they come with the heavenly king. On their way — what shall I say — where God leads them out, mountains sink before them and springs burst: creation rejoices to see the heavenly people. Here nevertheless they hurry to defend a captive mother.

But the unjust king who holds, when he hears him, flees into the north part and gathers all. But when the tyrant dashes himself on God’s army, his soldiers are laid flat by heavenly terror; he himself with the unspeakable false prophet is seized; by the Lord’s decree they are handed living to Gehenna. From then the chiefs and leaders are ordered to serve. Then the holy will enter to the mother’s ancient breasts, so that those too may cool whom that evil one persuaded — he was torturing in various penalties those to be believed to him. It has come to the end, that scandals be taken from the world; the Lord will begin to give judgment through fire.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 41: DE POPULO ABSCONSO SANCTO OMNIPOTENTIS CHRISTI DEI VIVI.
latin: 41 DE POPULO ABSCONSO SANCTO OMNIPOTENTIS CHRISTI DEI VIVI. Desidet <populus> absconsus ultimus sanctus Et quidem ignotus a nobis ubi moretur. Per nouem tribum agant et dimidiam ipsi, Omissae duae tribum haec sunt et dimidia nobis. Praecepitque Christus per legem uiuere priscos. Uiuamus nunc omnes, nouellae traditio legis Lex ut ipsa docet! Apertius indico uobis. Obrelictae duae tribum et dimidia: quare Ab istis dimidia tribum? Ut martyres essent Bellum cum infer<r>et electis suis in orbem, Seu certe sanctorum chorus prophetarum ad illam Consurgeret plebem, qui frenum inponeret illis, Obsceni quos equi trucidarunt calci remissa Nec suerit ad manus pacem aliquando tenere. Semotae sunt isti tribuum, ut mysteria Christi Omnia per istas conpleatur saeculo toto. Sunt autem de scelere duorum fratrum enatae, Auspicio quorum facinus secutae fuere. Non merito tales dispersi sunt ipsi cruenti? Conueniunt iterum propter mysteria castris. Tunc autem properant conpleri legis narrata.

Omnipotens Christus descendit ad suos electos, Obscurati nobis qui fuerunt tempore tanto Milia fot facti; illa est gens uera caelestis. Non natus ante patrem moritur ibi, neque dolores In suis corporibus sentiunt ut ulcera nata. Pausantes in lecto suo mature recedunt Omnia conplentes legis, ideoque tutantur. Transire iubentur ad Dominum partibus istis Exsiccat fluuium quibus sicut ante traiectis, Nec minus et Dominus ipse producit cum illis. Transiit ad nostra, ueniunt cum rege caeleste. In quorum itinere quod dicam, quo Deus educet, Subsidunt montes ante illos et fontes erumpunt: Caelestem populum gaudet creatura uidere. Hic tamen festinant matre<m> defendere capta<m>.

Rex autem iniquus, qui obtinet, illum ut audit, In partem boreae refugit et colligit omnes. Sed cum se inlidet exercitu Dei tyrannus Terrore caelesti prosternuntur milites eius, Ipse cum infando conprehenditur pseudopropheta; Decreto Domini traduntur uiui gehennae. Ex eo primores et duces seruire iubentur. Intrabunt tunc sancti ad antiqua ubera matris, Ut autem et illi refrigerent, quos malus ille suasit, In uariis poenis cruciabat sibi credendos. Uentum est ad finem, quod tollantur scandala mundo; Incipiet Dominus iudicium dare per ignem.

author: Commodian
english: If certain teachers, while they wait for your gifts or fear persons, loosen single things for you — I too do not “teach,” but I am forced to say the truth. With the Evil one’s crowd you go to empty spectacles, where Satan prepares tricks with crashes; you persuade yourself it is allowed, wherever it will please. Mixed, offspring of the Most High, with the sons of the Devil, you do not want to look back at the former things you renounced. You turn again in those very things: what will the One profit? Or if something given for weakness you foolishly profane… Do not love the world nor its ambition: so great is God’s voice, and to you it seems light. You keep a human’s command and slight God’s; you trust a gift, because teachers shut their mouths so they are silent and do not say divine orders to you.

If you were to scorn me saying true things, look to the Highest: whose son you were, assign yourself to him as client. If you seek to live as a gentile, faithful human, the world’s joys remove you from Christ’s grace; what you lightly presume is allowed without discipline, and you seek theater choruses and music songs, nor do you care that offspring is emptied by such madness. While you think to enjoy life, unseeing you err. The Most High lives, and you slight the just precepts.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 56 SAECULARIA IN TOTUM FUGIENDA. Si quidam doctores, dum expectant munera uestra Aut timent personas, laxantes singula uobis, Et ego non doceo, sed cogor dicere uerum. Cum caterua Mali pergis ad expectacula uana, Ubi Satanas fragoribus conparat astus Licere persuadis tibi, quocumque placebit. Altissimi prolis cum filiis Zabuli mixta Respicere non uis, cui renuntiasti, priora. In ipsis uersaris iterum: qui proderit Unus? Aut si pro languore datum quod stulte profanas I........................................ Nolite diligere mundum neque ambitum eius: Tanta Dei uox est, et tibi pro le<ui> uidetur. Obseruas mandatum hominis, et Dei deuitas; Tu fidis muneri, quod doctores ora procludunt Ut taceant neque dicant tibi iussa diuina.

Me uera dicentem si contemneres, prospice Summum: Filius cuius eras, illi te adsigna clientem. Uiuere si quaeris gentiliter homo fidelis, Gaudia te mundi remouent a gratia Christi; Indisciplinate quod leue licere praesumis, Et choros historicos et cantica musica quaeris, Nec tali subolem exuanniri amentia curas. Dum uita frunisci putas, inprouidus erras. Altissimus uiuet, et iusta praecepta deuitas.

author: Commodian
english: You have heard the voice, you who want to remain Christian — how blessed Paul ordered to ask. And heaven-speaking Isaiah, teacher and author (for he detests those who follow the world’s love) says the daughters of Zion were lifted and fell. It is not right in God that a faithful Christian woman be cultivated [in worldly fashion]. Do you seek by gentile custom to go before God’s holy things? These heralds of God condemn, crying in the law, that women who adorn themselves so are unjust. You dye hair, smear eyes with black, bind crescent curls step by step on the brow, treat the cheek with a certain laid-on red, and earrings hang with heaviest weight; you bury the natural neck with gems and gold; you bind palms worthy of God with an evil omen. Why mention clothes or the Devil’s whole pomp? You spit out the law; you prefer to please the world; you dance in houses; for psalms you sing love-songs. Though you be chaste, following the left does not cleanse you: therefore Christ equals such as you with the nations. A holy woman of God shows riches in the heart. Serve Christ with a hymn-made chorus and pleasing [service]; offer zealous fragrance to Christ with favor.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 59 ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUXYZ. Audiuisti uocem, quae uis Christiana manere, Beatus Paulus qualiter rogare praecepit. Caeliloquax autem Esaias doctor et auctor (Detestatur enim caritatem mundi sequentes) Exaltatae, inquit, ceciderunt filiae Sion. Fas in Deo non est Christianam coli fidelem. Gentili more quaeris praecedere Dei sancta? Has Dei praecones damnant in lege clamantes Iniustas esse feminas, quae se taliter ornant. Kapillos inficitis, oculos nigrore linitis, Lunatis comulas gradulatim fronte deuinctas, Mala<m> medicatis quodam superducto rubore, Nec non et inaures grauissimo pondere pendent, Obruitis collum naturale gemmis et auro, Palmas Deo dignas praesagio malo ligatis. Quid memorem uestes aut tota<m> Zabuli pompa<m>? Respuitis legem, mauultis mundo placere, Saltatis in domibus, pro psalmis cantatis amores. Tu licet sis casta, non te purgat sinistra sequendo: Uos ideo tales Christus cum gentibus aequat. Xancta Dei mulier diuitias corde demonstrat. Ymnificato choro placitoque Christo seruire Zelantes fauore Christo offerte odorem.

author: Commodian
english: You want to wage war, fool, as if wars are quiet! From the first-formed day there is fighting for us unto the end. Desire throws headlong: it is war — fight it through with it. Luxury urges: refuse it — you have won the war. Spare abundant wine, lest you wander through it; hold back the tongue of cursing, with which you adore the Lord; check fury, make yourself peaceful to all; beware oppressing with miseries the lesser ones; apply terror only and do not harm; lead yourselves by a straight path sincere through the age; in your riches make yourself common to the little ones; give from your labor, clothe the naked: so you conquer. Lay no snares for anyone, you who serve God: look at the beginning, whence the enemy perished by envies. I am not a teacher, but the law itself teaches by crying out. You carry so many empty words, who in one moment seek to take martyrdom idle for Christ.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 62 BELLUM COTTIDIANUM. Belligerare cupis, stulte, quasi bella quiescunt! Ex protoplausto die pugnatur in fine nobis. Libido praecipitat: bellum est, compugna cum illo. Luxuria suadet: abutere, bellum uicisti. Uino copioso parce, ne per illum aberres; Maledicti retinete linguam, unde dominum adoras; Conpescere furiam, pacificum redde te cunctis; Oppressos miseriis depremere caue minores Terrorem adcommoda tantum et noli nocere; Tramite uos recto ducite sincero per saeclum In tuis diuitiis communem te redde pusillis; De labore tuo dona, nudum uesti: sic uincis. Insidias nullo facias qui Deo deseruis: Aspice principium, unde perit inuidiis hostis. Non sum ego doctor, sed lex docet ipsa clamando. Uerba geris tanta uana, qui sub uno momento Martyrium quaeris otiosus tollere Christo. [ 63 Dum cupis, inde peris, dum ardis proximi zelo; Extinguis te ipsum, quando te incendis abactus. Zelaris alium, inuide, de malo lucrantem, Et te parem concupis fieri pecuniae tantae. Lex sic non aspicit; dum illam incumbere quaeris, Omnia suspensus uiuis in ardore lucrorum; Cumque reus tibi sis ipsum te iudice damnans, Oculorum acies nunquam satiatur auara. Nunc ergo si credeas et cogites: uana cupido est Congere<re> nimium sub fragili uita moranti. Unde Deus clamat: Stulte, hanc noctem uocaris! Postea ruina ruit: cuius erint ista talenta? Suggeret cum Dominus unicuique uicta diurna. Congestet alius: tu bono uiuere quaere, Et Deus cor censens agis super omnia uictor; Nec enim dico, ut in timore te mittas, Cum pro die tuo uigilas sine fraude uiuendo. In esca perit auis aut inhaeret inprouida uisco. Arbitrare tibi simpliciter ualde cauendum. Excedant alii, finem tu prospice semper.]

author: Commodian
english: There is no unbelieving people except yours, unjust ones, so often and in so many places rejected by the law of those who cry out. And the High One scorns your sabbaths and thirtieths; he cut off entirely all yours from the law, so that you would not even make him the commanded sacrifices — he who said he would send a stone for your scandal. If any of you have not believed, by an unjust death — another part of the law cries: “You will see from there Life hung on the wood; and you did not believe him.” God himself is life; he himself hung for us — but you with hardened heart mock the same one.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 39 ITERUM IPSIS. Incredulus populus non est nisi uester, iniqui, Tot locis et totiens reprobatus lege clamantum. Et sabbatas uestras spernit et tricensimas Altus Rescidit omnino uniuersas uestras de lege, Ut nec sacrificia faceret<is> illi praecepta Mittere qui dixit lapidem in scandalo uestro. Iniqua si quis uestrum non crediderint morte Pars alia legis clama<t>: 'Uidebitis inde Suspensam in ligno uitam; nec illi credidistis'. Ipse Deus uita est, pependit ipse pro nobis, Sed uos indurato corde subsannatis eundem.

author: Commodian
english: I warn the faithful that brothers not take up hatreds: impious hatreds are counted to the fire for martyrs; the martyr is destroyed whose confession is such. Law is given the unjust so he can rein himself; thence washed, you likewise ought to be free of it. Twice you sin against God who stretch quarrels to a brother. From which you will not escape sin if you keep pursuing the old way. You are washed once — will you be able to be dipped again?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 46 FIDELIBUS. Fideles admoneo, fratres ne odia tollant: Impia martyribus odia reputantur in ignem; Destruitur martyr, cuius est confessio talis, Lex iniquo datur, ut possit sese frenare; Inde lotus carere debes similiter et tu. Bis Deo peccas, qui lites fratri protendis. Unde non effugies peccatum prisce sectans. Semel es lotus, numquid poteris denuo mergi?

author: Commodian
english: When the Lord says to eat bread in groaning, what are you doing now who want to live glad? You seek to cancel the Highest’s sentence sent — see in the first-formed that the law’s bit goes forth. If almighty God ordered to live with sweat, you who make merry are already outside to him. Scripture says the Lord was indignant at the Jews: refreshed from food the sons rose to play. Why then do we of ourselves chase those who went out? From where they perished we ought to beware. The greatest part of you appears given to luxuries. You transgress the law when you put yourself among musicians. The apostle cries — rather God through him: your license, he says, destroys you in that very thing. Therefore be such as Christ wants you to be: mild and cheerful in him, but sad to the age. Run, labor, sweat, fight with sadness; hope comes with labor and the victory palm is given. If you want to cool the soul, go to the martyrs! Wait for the rest of things to come by the crossing of death.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 57 CHRISTIANUM TALEM ESSE. Cum Dominus dicat, in gemitum edere panem, Hic ut quid nunc agis, qui cupis uiuere laetus? Rescindere quaeris sententiam Summi demissa<m> In protoplausto uide frenum procedere legis. Si Deus omnipotens cum sudore uiuere iussit, Tu qui iocundaris, ergo iam exter es illi. Indignatum ait Dominum scriptura Iudaeis: Ab esca refecti surrexerunt ludere fili. Nunc ergo cur illos persequimur sponte profectos? Unde perierunt illi, nos cauere debemus. Maxima pars uestra luxuriis dedita paret. Transgrederis legem, cum te facis musicis inter. Apostolus clamat, <clamat> immo Deus per illum: Licentia uestra uos, inquit in ipsa, deperdunt. Esto ergo talis, qualem uult esse te Christus: Mitis et in illo hilaris, nam saeculo tristis. Excurre, labora, suda, cum tristitia pugna; Spes cum labore uenit et uictoriae palma donatur. Si refrigerare cupis animam, ad martyres i! Expecta requiem futurorum transitu mortis.

author: Commodian
english: While you desire, from that you perish; while you burn with a neighbor’s envy, you put yourself out when you set yourself on fire, driven. You envy another, envious one, gaining from evil, and you long to become equal to so much money. The law does not look so; while you seek to lean on it, you live suspended in the heat of gains; and while you are guilty to yourself, condemning yourself as judge, the greedy eye’s gaze is never filled. Now therefore if you believe and think: it is vain desire to heap too much under a fragile life that lingers. Whence God cries: “Fool, this night you are called!” Afterward ruin rushes: whose will those talents be? When the Lord supplies each one daily victuals. Let another heap: you seek to live by the good, and God, weighing the heart, you act victor over all things; nor do I say you should cast yourself into fear when you watch for your day living without fraud. A bird perishes in food or sticks unseeing to birdlime. Judge for yourself that you must simply beware hard. Let others go beyond; you always look to the end.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 61 DE ZELO CONCUPISCENCIAE. Dum cupis, inde peris, dum ardis proximi zelo; Extinguis te ipsum, quando te incendis abactus. Zelaris alium, inuide, de malo lucrantem, Et te parem concupis fieri pecuniae tantae. Lex sic non aspicit; dum illam incumbere quaeris, Omnia suspensus uiuis in ardore lucrorum; Cumque reus tibi sis ipsum te iudice damnans, Oculorum acies nunquam satiatur auara. Nunc ergo si credeas et cogites: uana cupido est Congere<re> nimium sub fragili uita moranti. Unde Deus clamat: Stulte, hanc noctem uocaris! Postea ruina ruit: cuius erint ista talenta? In suprema cadis iniusta lucra conando, Suggeret cum Dominus unicuique uicta diurna. Congestet alius: tu bono uiuere quaere, Et Deus cor censens agis super omnia uictor; Nec enim dico, ut in timore te mittas, Cum pro die tuo uigilas sine fraude uiuendo. In esca perit auis aut inhaeret inprouida uisco. Arbitrare tibi simpliciter ualde cauendum. Excedant alii, finem tu prospice semper.

author: Commodian
english: Learn, you who will die, to show good to all. In the people’s midst why make yourself another? You go where you do not know, and unaware you leave from there; you handle wickedly, though you thirst with the body itself. You lift yourself too high over riches and lead feast-days and do not look to the poor willingly — those now subject to you — nor do you even feed your parents. Alas, wretched ones! Let the middling flee farther from you. “The poor lived and went out,” you shout, drunk. Soon you are driven by furies when you yourself perish, Charybdis. Undisciplined, you rich are like cattle: you give law to those, for you spare yourselves. Put off, rich ones, being so evil-twisted toward God, that he may surely help you who now may have worked. Be common to the least while you have time; as the elm loves the vine, so yourselves the little ones. A terrible law to the evil and kind to the good — observe now, barren one; be subject in prosperous things; lift hearts of fraud, rich ones, and take up peace’s. Expiate your evil with good deeds from the Highest.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 29 DIVITES HUMILES ESTOTE. Disce, moriture, bonum ostendere cunctis. In medio populi quid te facis alterum esse? Uadis ubi nescis, et inscius inde recedis; Impie tractas, cum ipso corpore sitis Tu super diuitias, nimium te tollis in altum Et <fe>stiua ducis nec respicis pauperes ultro Subditos nunc uobis, nec parentes pascitis ipsos. Heu miseri! fugiant longius mediocres a uobis. 'Uixit et extinxit pauper' ebriace clames. Mox furiis ageris, cum pereas ipse, Carybdis. Indisciplinati sicut <pecora> diuites estis: Legem datis istis, nam uobis parcitis ipsis. Exuite, diuites, tantis malis Deo peruersos, Subueniat utique tibi, qui nunc operati si forte. Estote communes minimis, dum tempus habetis; Sicut ulmus amat uitem, sic ipsi pusillos. Terribilem legem malis bonis atque benigna<m> Obserua nunc sterelis, subditus in prosperis esto; Tollite corda fraudis, diuites, et sumite pacis. Expiate malum uestrum benefactis a Summo.

author: Commodian
