english: What? Half a Jew, you want to be half profane? From there you will not escape Christ’s judgment when dead. Yourself blind you wander and foolishly go in among the blind; therefore a blind man leads a blind man into the ditch. You go where you do not know, and unaware you leave from there. Learners go to the learned so they may leave learned, but you go to others from whom you can learn nothing. You go out before the doors, and thence also you go to the idols. Ask first what is commanded in the law; let them tell you if it is ordered to adore the gods. For it is ignored because of that for which we chiefly exist; but since they are guilty from the crime itself, they tell nothing of God’s precepts except marvels. Then still, blind, they lead you with them into the ditch. There are funerals; too much to report of them all — or, because I am shut in, I would work cramped among ploughs. The Almighty refused that they understand the King; from so great a crime He Himself fled those bloody men. He handed Himself to us by a superadded new law; thence now they bark with us, deserted by the King. But if you think there is hope in them — ******
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 36: QUI IUDAEI DIANT FANATIC (ANF XXXVII Fanatics Who Judaize; Latin Library numbering).
Source Latin ends in editorial lacuna ******.
latin: 36 QUI IUDAEI DIANT FANATIC. ? Quid? medius Iudaeus, medius uis esse profanus? Unde non effugies iudicium Christi defunctus. Ipse caecus erras et ad caecos intras, inepte; Idcirco caecus caecum in fossa reducit. Uadis ubi nescis, et inscius inde recedis. Discentes ad doctos eunt, ut docti recedant, At tu aliis uadis, unde nihil discere possis. Exis pro foribus, inde et ad idola uadis. Interroga primum, quod sit in lege praeceptum, Dicant illi tibi, si iussum est deos adorare. Ignoratur enim propter quod maxime sumus: At illi quoniam rei sunt ex ipso delicto, Nihil de praeceptis Dei nisi mirabilia narrant. Tunc tamen in fossam secum uos caeci deducunt. Funera sunt; nimium de illis tota deferre, Aut, quia concludor, agerem congustus aratris. Noluit Omnipotens illos intellegere Regem; A scelere a tanto refugit ipse cruentos. Tradidit se nobis <noua> superaddita lege, Inde modo latrant nobiscum re<ge> deserti. Ceterum in illis si spem <in>esse putatis, ********

author: Commodian
english: Isaiah said: This is the man who shook the globe and as many kings, under whom the earth will be made desert. Hear, for the prophet foretold of him; I have composed nothing — I speak by reading the law. Then of course the world is finished when he appears and himself conquers three rulers in the world. But when Nero has been raised from hell, Elias will come first to seal the beloved, before the king rules at the end and the whole constriction. For seven years the earth will tremble everywhere: but half the time Elias, half Nero will hold. Then Babylon the whore will be burned to ash; from there he will go to Jerusalem, and the Latin victor then says: “I am Christ, whom you always pray.” And indeed the first deceived praise him, since his false prophet does many signs. … The Almighty grants that the spiritual one wipe away. Recapitulating the scriptures from him, the Jews cry together to the Highest that they themselves were deceived.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin:
40 DE ANTECHRISTI TEM.

ORE? Dixit Esaias: Hic homo, qui commouit orbem Et reges totidem, sub quo fiet terra deserta. Audite, quoniam propheta de illo praedixit; Nihil ego conposite dixi, sed lege legendo. Tum scilicet mundus finitur, cum ille parebit Et tres imperantes ipse deuicerit orbe. Cum fuerit autem Nero de inferno leuatus, Helias ueniet prius signare dilectos, Rex quam sub fine regit et artatio tota. In septem annis tremebit undique terra: Sed medium tempus Helias, medium Nero tenebit. Tunc Babillon meretrix incinefacta fauilla Inde ad Hierusalem perget, uictorque Latinus Tunc dicit: Ego sum Christus, quem semper oratis. Et quidem conlaudant illum primitiui decepti Multa signa facit quoniam cuius pseudopropheta. ****** Omnipotens tribuit, ut talis eradat. Recapitulantes scripturas ex eo Iudaei Exclamant pariter ad Excelsum sese deceptos.

author: Commodian
english: For deserters are not said of one kind: one is worthless, another withdraws in part, but still true judgments decide on both. See — one soldiers for Christ as for Caesar: obey. Seek the King’s refuge if you were an offender; implore him, confess to him prostrate: he will grant all things, whose also all ours are. Restored to the camp, beware of offending further. Do not wander long, soldier, through the dens of beasts. Let it be for you a vast deed to cease from sinning.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 51 DESERTORES. Desertores enim genere non uno dicunt<ur>: Est alius nequam, alius in parte secedat, Sed tamen utroque iudicia uera decernunt. Ecce militatur Christo sicut Caesari: paret. Refugium Regis pete, si delictor fuisti; Tu illum inplora, prostratus illi fatere: Omnia concedet, cuius sunt et omnia nostra. Repositus castris ulterius caue delinquas. Errare noli diu miles per spelaea ferarum. Sit tibi pro peccare desistere gestum inmensum.

author: Commodian
english: Of the seed of tares, who stand mixed in the church — when times are fulfilled the harvest is separated from the fruit. Tare was born that the Lord did not sow; the farmer gathers every tare and separates it. The law is a field for us: whoever has done good in it, the Dominator himself grants us true rest, where the tare is burned with fire. If therefore you thought, when they linger under one, you err: I mark you sterile Christians. The fig tree without fruit was cursed; at the Lord’s word it at once withered. You do not do works, you do not prepare a gift from the treasury — and so empty do you think to deserve the Lord?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 54 DE LOLII SEMINE. De semine lolii, qui stant in ecclesia mixti Expletis temporibus messis separatur a fructu. Lolium est natum, quod non <in>miserat dominus; Omne lolium agricola collectum separat illud. Lex ager nobis est: qui fecerit bonum in illa, Ipsam uti<que> nobis prestat requiem ueram Ipse Dominator, qua lolium igne crematur. Si ergo putastis, quando sub uno morantur Erratis: sterelis Christianos uos esse designo Maledicta fuit arbor sine fructu ficulna In uerbo Domini et statim exaruit illa. Non operas facitis, non donum gazo paratis: Et sic promereri Dominum putatis inanes?

author: Commodian
english: I am not just, brothers — lifted from a sewer — nor do I lift myself, but I grieve for you, seeing from so great a people none crowned in the agony. If one does not himself fight, at least let him supply them. Rebuke the disaster; serve luxuriously with shouting! A brother labors under arms with the world against him, and you, leaning on wealth, neither fight nor resist for the fighter. … On such the whole church hangs, if he should win. You see a brother abstain and fight with the foe. You wish peace in the camp; outside he fights back. Be merciful, that you may be saved before all things. Do you not see the Lord crying with so great a herald’s call, who orders to offer food even to enemies? Therefore look ahead to daily meals, which he always took on absolutely all days with the poor man. You seek to feed, fool, one who will feed you again. He scarcely appears to me who proposes to be set in order. Well-fed, with stretched belly you declaim; a brother pressed by need is wasting next to you. What do you say of the Lord’s Day? If he did not call before, call out from the crowd a poor man to take to lunch. In such is your hope — in those refreshed from what is yours.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 60: IN ECCLESIA OMNI POPULO DEI.
latin: 60 IN ECCLESIA OMNI POPULO DEI. Iustus ego non sum, fratres, de cloaca leuatus, Nec me supertollo, sed doleo uestri, qui cerno Ex tanto populo nullum in agone coronari. Certe si non ipse pugnat, uel suggerat illis. Cladem obiurgate, ouanter officite luxu! Labora<t> frater aduersante mundo sub armis, Et fretus opibus nec pugnas nec pugnanti resistis. ******** In talem pendit ecclesia tota, si uincat. Abstinere uides fratrem et pugnare cum hoste. Optas tu in castris pacem, foras ille repugnat. Misericors esto, ut sis ante omnia saluus. Nec intuis Dominum praeconio tanto clamante<m>, Inimicis etiam qui iubet alimenta praebere? Prandia ob ea prospice diurna, quae semper Omnibus omnino diebus cum pauperis sumpsit. Pascere tu quaeris, stulte, qui te denuo pascat. Uix ille mihi paret, qui conponi proponit. Laute cibatum distenso uentre declamas, Oppressus inopia frater est iuxta tabescens. De die Dominica quid dicis? Si non ante uocauit, Exuoca de turba pauperem quem ad prandium ducas In talibus spes est uestra de uestro refectis.

author: Commodian
english: Consider Solomon’s sayings, all you judges — how with one word he pulls you down: gifts and presents corrupt all judges! Thence follows: you always love the giver; when a cause is sought, an unjust cause carries the victory. I here am innocent, nor do I, a little one, accuse you — let Solomon take up the open charge. “But your god is the belly, and rewards are laws.” Paul the apostle suggests this, not I a flea. If place or time favors or a person advances, be judge of yourself. Why are you lifted from that? You blaspheme, untaught: from whose bounty you live, in such frailty you never look back. By rank and greedy gain you presume on fortune; you have no law, nor do you count yourself worthy in prosperity — though you may dine in gold with a piping crowd always. If you have not adored the crucified Lord, you have perished. Place and time and person are given you — now if you believe; if not, you will fear for that. Temper yourself to Christ and lay the neck down to him: that honor remains and the whole trust of things. When time flatters you now, be more wary, not foreseeing the last of the fates that must meet you. Without Christ you never even manage to have lived.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 30: IUDICIBUS SIBI PLACENTIBUS (ANF XXXI. To Judges.).
latin: 30 IUDICIBUS SIBI PLACENTIBUS. Intuite dicta Salominis, iudices omnes, Uno uerbo suo qualiter uos ille detractat: Dona quam et xenia corrumpunt iudices omnes! Inde 'nimis', sequit<ur>, 'datorem semper amatis', Cum quaerit<ur>, causa uictoriam tollit iniqua. Innocens hic ego sum, nec uos incuso pusillus, Blasphemium tollat Salomon, qui <clamat> aperte. 'Uobis autem Deus est uenter et praemia iura.' Suggerit hoc Paulus apostolus, non ego pulex. Si locus aut tempus fauet aut persona prouenit, Iudex esto tuus. Quod nunc extolleris inde? Blasphema<s>, indocilis: de cuius praestantia uiuis, In fragilitate tanta non respicis umquam. Per gradu<m> et lucra auidus fortunae praesumis, Lex tibi non ulla est, nec te in prosperitate dignos Auro licet cenes cum turba choraulica semper Cruciarium Dominum si non adorasti, peristi. Et locus et tempus et persona tibi donatur, Nunc si tamen credis; sin autem, pro eo timebis. Tempera te Christo et ceruicem illi depone: Isti honor remanet et tota fiducia rerum. Blanditur quando tibi tempus nunc, cautior esto, Ultima fatorum non prouidens, quae te oportet. Sine Christo nec uixisse te conpotis unquam.

author: Commodian
english: O wild people without a shepherd, wander no longer. I too who warn you was the same, unknowing, astray. Now therefore take your Lord’s figure; lift wild hearts and put roughness aside. Enter the stalls, woodland ones, to the oxen’s mangers, safe from robbers, remaining under the king’s roof. In the wood are wolves — flee under the cave. You make war, you rave, nor look where you linger. Believe in one God, where when dead you can live, and rise in the kingdom, since there is resurrection for the just.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 32: GENTILIBUS (ANF XXXIII. To the Gentiles.).
latin: 32 GENTILIBUS. Gens sine pastore ferox iam noli uagare. Et ego, qui moneo, idem fui nescius errans. Nunc ideo Domini figuram sumite uestri, Tollite corda fera et exasperate seorsum: Intrate stabulis, siluestris, ad praesepia tauri, Latronibus tuti sub regis tecta manentes. In silua lupi sunt, ideo refugite sub antro. Bellaris, insanis nec respicis, ubi moraris. Uno crede Deo, ubi mortuus uiuere possis Surgas et in regno, cum sit resurrectio iustis.

author: Commodian
english: Always wicked and stiff-necked you kick back; you do not want to be conquered: thus you will be disinherited. Isaiah said you are of fattened heart. You look at the law Moses dashed in anger; and the same Lord gave him a second law. In that he placed hope, which you, half-raised, sneer at. Will you therefore not be unworthy of the heavenly kingdom?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 37: IUDAEIS (ANF XXXVIII. To the Jews.).
latin: 37 IUDAEIS. Inprobi semper et dura ceruice recalces, Uinci uos non uultis: sic exheredes eritis. Dixit Esaias incrassato corde uos esse. Aspicis legem, quam Moyses allisit iratus; Et idem Dominus dedit illi lege<m> secunda<m>. In illa spem posuit, quam uos subsannatis erecti. Sic ideo indigni non eritis regno caelesti?

author: Commodian
english: Look on Leah as a type of the synagogue — with eyes so weak — which Jacob received as a sign; and yet he served again for the younger beloved: a true mystery and type of our church. Regard what was fully said of Rebecca from heaven, whence you play the alien, so that you may not believe in Christ. Then go to Tamar’s twin birth; look to Cain, first tiller of the earth, and Abel the shepherd, the early spotless offerer, who in a brother’s savagery was slain by a brother. So then understand the younger ones approved in Christ.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 38: ITEM IUDAEIS (ANF XXXIX. Also to the Jews.).
latin: 38 ITEM IUDAEIS. Inspice Liam typum sinagogae fuisse, Tam infirmis oculis, quam Iacob in signo recepit; Et tamen seruiuit rursum pro minore dilecta, Mysterium uerum et typum ecclesiae nostrae. Intuite plenae dictum Rebeccae de caelo, Unde simulatis aliene, ne Christo credatis. Deinde Thamar partum geminorum adite; Ad Kain intendite, primum terraeque cultorem, Et Abel pastorem, priscus inmaculatus offertor In fratris saeuitie qui fuit mactatus a fratre. Sic ergo percipite iuniores Christo probatos.

author: Commodian
english: But when war is waged or the enemy floods in, whoever can conquer or hide — great trophies; but unhappy will he be who is captured by them. He loses both country and king, which worthily befalls him who would not fight for country or for life. He ought to have died rather than go under a barbarian king, and let slavery lie open — to render it to lawless enemies. If by preaching you die for the land, you have conquered; but if you give hands while unhurt, by law you have perished. Let the enemy cross the river — hide yourself in cover; or if he can enter without slaughter, do not cease. Make yourself safe on every side, and your own: you have conquered; and act watchfully, lest anyone rush into those things. The king will be infamous if anyone exposes himself to the enemy. Who does not know how to conquer and runs to hand himself over, awkward, sent neither himself nor his country any praise; then he refused to live, when life itself will perish. Then if a helpless or profane man flees from the enemy — like sounding brass, or as deaf asps — he ought to pray enough and hide himself as such.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 49: QUI APOSTATAVERUNT DEO (ANF L. Who Have Apostatized from God.).
latin: 49 QUI APOSTATAVERUNT DEO. Quando bellum autem geritur aut inrigat hostis, Uincere qui poterit aut latere, magna tropaea, Infelix autem erit, qui fuerit captus ab illis. Amittit et patriam et regem, cui digne prouenit, Pugnare pro patria qui noluit neque pro uita. Obisse debuerat quam ire sub barbaro rege, Seruitiumque pateat hostibus sine lege deferre. Tu si praedicando moreris pro terra, uicisti, At si manus dederis incolumem, lege peristi. Transfluuiat hostis, tu sub latebra <re>conde, Aut si intrare potest sine c<aede>, ne cessa. Undique te redde tutum tuos quoque: uicisti; Et uigilanter age, ne quis incurrat in illa. Rex infamis erit, si quis se propalat hosti. Uincere qui nescit et occurrit tradere sese, Nec sibi nec patriae laudem remisit ineptus; Tunc uiuere noluit, cum ipsa uita peribit. De<inde> si refugiat inops aut profanus ab hoste, Eramen ut sonans, facti uel ut aspides surdi, Orare satis debet et se condere tali<s>.

author: Commodian
english: The souls of the damned deservedly separate themselves; from him who shelters them they run back again to what is theirs. The Canaanite root, a cursed seed, breaks out and flees into a servile nation under a barbarian king — those the eternal flame will torment on the decreed day. The profane wants to wander without discipline, to rage through the jaws of the roads loosed from law. Such then are these whom no penalty has forced: if they refuse to withdraw from idols, they ought to be spit out.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 53: DE REFUGIS (ANF LIV. Of Fugitives.).
latin: 53 DE REFUGIS. Damnatorum animae merito se ipsae secernunt; Ex hoc protegenti iterum ad sua recurrunt. Radix Cananaea, maledictum semen, erumpit Et in seruili gente sub barbaro rege refugit, Flamma quos aeterna torquebit die decreto. Uult uagus errare sine disciplina profanus Grassari per fauces uiarum lege solutus. Isti ergo tales, quos nulla poena coegit Si <sece>dere nolunt ab idolis, respui debent.

author: Commodian
english: You dissemble the law given with such heralding, while the trumpet is present and the heavenly voice cries. If a prophet had only cried out into a cloud, the Lord’s voice sent through him would surely suffice. In so many volumes of speakers the Lord’s voice proclaims; no one likewise puts malice away from the heart. You want to see good things and seek to live by frauds. Why then did the law itself go forth with such labor? You abuse the Lord’s commands and ask to be a son; if you will be such, you trust in vain, I say. The Omnipotent seeks meek sons for himself — upright, good in heart, devoted to the divine law — but the harsh, you already know where he sank them.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 55: DISSIMULATORI (ANF LVI. To the Dissembler.).
latin: 55 DISSIMULATORI. Dissimulas legem tanto praeconio latam In tuba praesente caeleste uoce clamante. Si propheta tantum declama<ui>sset in nubem, Sufficeret utique Domini uox missa per illum. In tot profatorum uolumina uox Domni proclamat; Malitiam nullus dimittit [ita] aeque de corde. Uis bona uidere et fraudibus uiuere quaeris. Lex ipsa cur ergo processit tanto labore? Abuteris Domini mandata et te filium inquis; Tu si talis eris, sine causa fideris, inquam. Omnipotens mites quaerit sibi filios esse, Rectos, corde bonos, deuotos legi diuinae, Inmites autem iam scitis ubi demersit.

author: Commodian
english: You want to be a Christian matron as one learning the world’s way: you surround yourself with gold or a silk dress, modest one; you send the law’s terror from the ears on the wind; you chase vain things, all from the Devil’s pomp; you adorn at the mirror curls bent back on the brow; and you put false drugs on the cheeks; on pure eyes antimony with twisted beauty; or you dye the hair so it stays black the whole time. God is the inspector who pierces every heart. Besides, for the chaste these things are not needed. With clear and chaste sense pierce the breast; God’s law witnesses that such laws depart. Let the woman who believes from the heart, proven to her husband, be enough — not by adornments but by a good mind. Put on clothes as needed, to show cold or too much sun — only that you be proven chaste and among God’s people show gifts of means. Tabitha, once most bright, gives you a memorial: she lies lifeless, raised by widows’ prayers. By giving she deserved to be lifted — not by hairdressings. You good matrons, flee vanity’s beauty: such culture fits unchaste women, the brothel. Conquer the evil one, chaste women of Christ; in giving show all your riches. [A holy woman of God shows riches in the heart. With a hymning choir and with Christ well pleased to serve, offer a fragrance to Christ, zealous with favor.]
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 58: MATRONIS ECCLESIAE DEI VIVI (ANF LIX. To the Matrons of the Church of the Living God.).
latin: 58 MATRONIS ECCLESIAE DEI VIVI. Matrona uis esse Christiana ut saeculi discens: Auro te circumdas aut sirica ueste, pudica, Terrorem legis ex auribus uento remittis, Res uanas adfectas cuncta de Zabuli pompa, Ornas et ad speclum cincinnos fronte reflexos, Nec non et inducis malis medicamina falsa, In oculis puris stibium peruerso decore, Seu crines tingis, ut sint toto tempore nigri. Est Deus inspector, penetrat qui singula corda. Ceterum pudicis ista necessaria non sunt. Claro ac pudico sensu pertundite pectus; Lex Dei testatur tales abscedere leges, Ex corde quae credit femina marito probata Sufficiat esse non cultibus sed bona mente. Induite uestes quas oportet, frigus ut ostent Aut nimium solis, tantum ut pudico proberis Et in plebe Dei facultatis dona demonstres. Dat tibi memoriam <Tabitha> clarissima quondam; Exanimata iacet precibus uiduarum erecta. In dando promeruit, non comtibus, inde leuari. Uos matronae bonae uanitatis fugite decorem: In<cestas in> feminas congruet cultura lupana. Uincite malignum, pudicae feminae Christi, In dando diuitias uestras ostendite totas. [Xancta Dei mulier diuitias corde demonstrat. Ymnificato choro placitoque Christo seruire Zelantes fauore Christo offerte odorem.]

author: Commodian
english: If the enemy’s war suddenly comes flooding, and before they could flee he seized inert little ones, they are not to be reproached, though they seem captured. Nor do I wholly excuse: perhaps for parents’ faults they earned it, therefore God handed them over. Yet I urge adults to run back into the hall, and be born again as if from their mother’s womb, always fleeing the terrible and bloodstained nation — impious, untaught, living a beast’s life. For when another war must perhaps be waged, whoever can conquer or at least already know how to beware — ******
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.

latin: 50 DE INFANTIBUS. Debellum hostis <si> subito uenit inundans, Et prius quam fugerent, paruulos occupauit inertes, Inproperandum eis non est, licet capti uidentur. Nec quidem excuso: ob delicta forte parentum Fuere promeriti, ideo Deus tradidit illos. Attamen adultos hortor, in aula recurrant, Nascunturque quasi denuo suae matri de uentre, Terribilem gentem fugiens semperque cruentam, Impiam, indocilem, ferina uita uiuentem Bellum enim alium cum fuerit forte gerendum Uincere qui poterit aut certe iam scire cauere, S............................................

author: Commodian
english: Why do you feign yourself good by another’s wound, you worthless one? Whence you give lavishly, another weeps daily. You refuse to believe the Lord sees this — you are taught. “The Highest does not approve gifts of the unjust,” he says. You burst upon the wretched when you have gained places. Another gives gifts to empty another, or if you have lent at a double hundredth of interest, you want to give from that to cleanse yourself as of evil: the Omnipotent utterly refuses such works. You give as a candidate from tears; he, blackened, pressed by usury, weeps made poor. Having gained time besides, the enemy snatches with his mouths; for the moment you, unjust, fill peoples — holy ones — at a price. And if from trade’s profit you want to purify yourself, you strike yourself, not another, I say, unjust one.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.

added_allusions.reason: I hate robbery for burnt offering

latin: 64 QUI DE MALO DONANT. Quid te bonum fingis alieno uulnere, nequor? Unde tu largiris, alter cottidie plorat. Ista tu discredis Dominum uidere: doceris. Dona iniquorum non probat Altissimus, inquit. Erumpis miseris, dum fueris locos adeptus. Munera dat alter, ut alterum reddat inanem, Aut si fenerasti duplicem centesima nummum, Largiri uis inde, ut te quasi malum depurges: Omnipotens tales operas omnino recusat. Donas tu de lacrimis candidatus; ille nigratus Oppressus usuris deplorat factus egenus. Nanctus praeterea tempus captat oribus hostis, Ad praesens populas pretio tu sanctos iniquus. Nec non et de lucro mercis si uis te piare, Te ipsum inlidis, non alium, <inquam> inique.

author: Commodian
english: The arranged time comes — peace for ours in the city — and ruins at once while the age flatters the first. You order the people whom you yourselves cast into schism: either keep the city’s law or leave it. You see the speck sticking in our eyes and will not discern the beam in yours. A deceitful peace comes to you; persecution burns. Wounds do not appear, and so without slaughter you have fallen. ****** Of all of you scarcely one has carried himself carefully. O to be nursed for evil in the predicted slaughter! You praise a deceitful peace, unjust to you. Made soldiers of another’s deed, not of Christ, you have perished.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 65 DE PACE SU. <B>DOLA Dispositum tempus uenit nostris pacem in urbe Et ruinas simul blandiente saeculo primis. Praecipitis populo, quem <ipsi> in schisma misistis: Aut facite legem ciuitatis aut exite de illa. Conspicitis stipulam cohaerentem in oculis nostris, Et uestris in oculis non uultis cernere trabem. Subdola pax uobis uenit, persecutio flagrat. Uulnera non parent, et sic sine caede ruistis, ********** De <omnibus> uobis uix unus caute se gessit. O malo nutriri in occisione praedicti! Laudatis pacem subdolam et uobis iniquam. Alterius facti milites, non Christi, peristis.

author: Commodian
english: I warn certain readers only to know, and to give matter to the rest by an example of living, to flee contest and avoid as many quarrels, to press down terror, and never to be proud. Bring also just obedience of the elders; make yourselves like Christ, little sons, to the teacher; among rustic things be lilies doing good. You have been made blessed when you have done the edicts. You are flowers in the people, you are Christ’s lamps; keep what you are and you can remember.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 66 LECTORIBUS. Lectores moneo quosdam cognoscere tantum, Et dare materiam ceteris exemplo uiuendi, Certamen fugire lites totidemque uitare, Terrorem premere, nec unquam esse superbos. Obsequia iusta maiorum quoque deferte; Reddite uos Christo similes, filioli, magistro; Inter agrestiua benefacitis lilia sitis. Beati facti estis, cum fe<ce>ritis edicta. Uos flores in plebe, uos estis Christi lucernas, Seruate quod estis et memorare potestis.

author: Commodian
english: Exercise Christ’s ministry, chaste deacons; therefore, ministers, do the Master’s precepts. Do not flee the person of a fair judge; keep your place whole, taught in all things. Looking upward, always devoted to the highest God, render to God all the holy things unhurt, ministers. In diverse matters give example, ready; yourselves bow your head to the pastors: so it will be that you can be proven in Christ.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 67 MINISTRIS. Ministerium Christi zacones exercite casti; Idcirco ministri facite praecepta magistri. Nolite fugere personam iudicis aequi, Integrate locum uestrum per omnia docti. Susum intendentes, semper Deo summo deuoti Tota Deo reddite inlaesa sacra, ministri. Rebus in diuersis exemplum date parati; Inclinate caput uestrum pastoribus ipsi: Sic fiet, ut Christo possitis <esse> probati.

author: Commodian
english: If a pastor has confessed, he has doubled the contest. But the apostle orders such to be teachers: let the ruler be patient; let him know where to loosen the reins; let him terrify first and afterward anoint with honey; and let him watch first that he himself do what he says. A pastor keeping worldly things is rendered in fault — against whose face you would dare say anything. Rumor itself of Gehenna boils in hell: woe to the wretched people that perhaps wavers in doubt! If such a pastor is at hand, near-lost ruin threatens; but a devoted one holds her, governing rightly; for she is gladdened in soul by kings fit for her. In such is hope, and the whole church lives.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 68 PASTORIBUS DEI. Pastor si confessus fuerit, geminauit agonem. Apostolus autem tales iubet esse magistros: Sit patiens rector, sciat, ubi frena remittat; Terreat in primis, et postea melle perungat, Obseruetque prius, ut faciat ipse quid dicit; Redditur in culpa pastor saecularia seruans, In faciem cuius sis ausus dicere quicquam. Bullit in inferno rumoribus ipsa gehenna: Uae miserae plebi, dubia quae forte uacillat! Si talis aderit pastor, paene perdita instat; Deuotus autem <eam> continet recte gubernans; Exhilaratur enim ex anima regibus aptis. In talibus spes est et uiuit ecclesia tota.

author: Commodian
english: Time demands that I alone tell you the truth. From one man always is moved what many pull down. In me alone I want to turn your hatreds, that everyone’s hearts may rest from such rumor. Look at the saying — that truth removes hatreds. I already foretold how great the matter of deceitful peace is! By flattering you, Eve’s seducer crept in. Because you do not know, you have fallen like a snare; you utterly drink in that very air of the age. No one for whom you intercede will act for nothing; who flees from the fire drives on in your vortex. Then the wretched man stripped by you seeks help again: the judges themselves already shudder at your greed. On a shorter title I would plow among you. You look at those to whom you show yourselves willingly; with them you also take feasts and you feed them. For that you are already almost preparing the earth’s foundations.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 69 MAIORIBUS NATI DICO. Me solum exposcit tempus uobis dicere uerum. Ab uno semper mouitur, quod multi detractant. In me solo uolo odia conuertere uestra, Omnium ut pausent praecordias tanto rumore. Respicite dictum, quod ueritas odia tollat. Iam praedixi quod est de pace subdola quanta! Blandiendo uobis subrepsit Euae seductor. Uos quia nescitis, laqueo instar ruistis, Sorbitis omnino auram dum saeculi ipsam. Non gratis aget, pro quo interceditis, ullus; Ab igne qui refugit, agit in uoragine uestro. Tunc repetit suppetium miser denudatus a uobis: Ipsi iam horrescunt iudices peculantia uestra. De breuiori titulo nam in uobis inararem. Inspicitis dicentes, quibus uos ostenditis ultro; Cum ipsis et epulas capitis et pascitis ipsos. Ob ea iam terrae paene fundamenta paratis.

author: Commodian
english: When almighty God had adorned the world’s nature, he willed that earth to be visited by angels; sent, they scorned his laws. So great was women’s beauty that it bent them. Contaminated, they cannot return to heaven; rebels from then, they cast words against God. The Highest then sent sentence on them; from their seed giants are said born. By them arts were proven on earth, and they taught dyeing wools and whatever is done, and those mortals were setting the dead in an image. But the Almighty, because they were of a crooked seed, did not decree that they, dead, be received back from death. Whence now wanderers overturn many bodies — especially those you this day worship and pray to as gods.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 2 CULTURA DAEMONUM. Cum Deus omnipotens exornasset mundi naturam Uisitari uoluit terram ab angelis istam; Legitima cuius spreuerunt illi dimissi; Tanta fuit forma feminarum, quae flecteret illos. Ut quoinquinati non possunt caelo redire, Rebelles ex illo contra Deum uerba misere. Altissimus inde sententiam misit in illis; De semine quorum Gigantes nati feruntur. Ab ipsis in terra artis probata fuere, Et tingere lanas docuerunt et quaecumque geruntur, Mortales et illi mortuos simulacro ponebant. Omnipotens autem, quod essent de semine prauo Non censuit illos recipi defunctos e morte. Unde modo uagi subuertunt corpora multa; Maxime quos hodie colitis et deos oratis.

author: Commodian
english: You say there are gods who are plainly bloody, and you say the fates of genesis write things for us? Say now, then, to whom rites should first be borne: between either road untimely death wanders. If the fates of genesis grant, why do you pray to a god? You are deceived, empty one, who seek to pray the Manes, and who name lords fashioned for yourself. Or you also pray I-know-not-what goddesses — Bellona and Nemesis, Furina, Caelestis of the Virgin, and Venus, for whom your wives weaken themselves. There are other demons besides, far from the shrines, which are not yet numbered and are worn on the neck, so that they cannot even render themselves a reason for the plague. They ought rather to be carried out to the earth’s ends.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 15 DE DIS DEABUSQUE. Dicitis esse deos, qui sunt manifeste cruenti, Et dicitis fata genesis adscribere nobis? Dicite nunc ergo, quibus primum sacra ferantur: Inter utrumque uias mors inmatura uagatur. Si tribuunt fata genesis, cur deum oratis? Deciperis, uane, qui Manes quaeris orare, Et qui fabricantur dominos tibi nuncupas esse. Aut feminas quoque nescio quas deas oratis, Bellonam et Nemesim, deas Furinam, Caelestem, Uirginis, et Uenerem, cui coniuges uestrae delumbant. Sunt alia praeterea daemonia <procul a> fanis, Quae nec numerantur adhuc et in collo feruntur, Ut nec ipsi sibi possint rationem reddere pestis. Exportari magis in ultima terra deberent.

author: Commodian
english: A few wicked empty seers delude you while they seek to untangle their own life. They suborn for others from themselves a falsehood under mysteries. Then pretending, shaken by some divinity, they sing majesty and wear themselves under a figure. You have often seen the Bellona-fighters — with what crash they enter luxuries while they seek to feign furies, or when they strike their own backs with a spare two-edged axe, though by their own teaching they discern that they heal by blood. Look: when divinities do not compel them, they themselves first compose themselves with whole mind; but they seek such tricks to take a stipend. From that see that all things are feigned. They shade the suppliant people lest the perishing believe. The matter once proceeded in vain from antiquity, that false things handed over be believed by the soothsayer; but no majesty of theirs has spoken.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 16 DE SIMULACRIS EORUM. Deludunt uos pauci scelerati uates inanes, Extricare suam dum quaerunt ** uitam. Subornant aliis ex se sub mysteria falsum. Inde simulantes concussi numine quodam Maiestatemque canunt et se sub figura fatigant. Uidistis saepe Duellonarios, quali fragore Luxurias ineunt, dum furias fingere quaerunt, Aut cum dorsa sua allidunt parca bipinne, Cum doctrina sua cernant, quod cruore sanent. Respicite, quando non illos numina cogunt, Ipsi qui se primum conponunt integra mente; Sed stipem ut tollant ingenia talia quaerunt. Ex eo uidete, quoniam sunt omnia ficta. Obumbrant populum supplicem, perituri ne credant. Res semel in uano de uetustate processit, Ut uaticinanti credatur prodita falsa; Maiestas autem illorum nulla locutust.

author: Commodian
english: Alas I grieve, citizens, that you are so dulled by the world! One runs to lots, another watches birds; another, wicked, looks when Bellona’s blood is poured and longs to hear good answers — cruel — where so many leaders and kings are consulted about life. Or what did it profit him to have known his own portents? Learn the good, I ask, citizens; beware images: for all of you seek into the Almighty’s law. So it pleased the Lord of lords on high that demons wander in the world for our proving. ****** who leave their altars to become heavenly. Whence I do not care to dispute this in a little book: the law teaches in the midst; I beg, take counsel for yourselves! You have entered into two ways: learn thoroughly the right one.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 21 HEBETUDO SAECULI. Heu doleo, ciues, sic uos hebetari de mundo! Excurrit alius ad sortis, aues aspicit alter Belantum cruore fuso malus inspicit alter Et cupit audire responsa bona crudelis, Tot duces et reges ubi sunt consulti de uita. Uel portenta sua scisse quo profuit illi? Di<s>cite quaeso bonum, ciues, simulacra cauete: Omnipotentis enim in legem quaerite cuncti. Sic ipsi conplacuit domino dominorum in altis Ad probationem nostram daemones in mundo uag<ar>i. **************** Caelestis fieri qui relinquant aras eorum. Unde non hoc curo disputari paruo libello: Lex docet in medio; oror consulete pro uobis! In duas intrastis uias: condiscite rectam.

author: Commodian
english: While you serve the belly you say you are innocent, and as if common you make yourself ready everywhere. Woe to you, foolish man — you yourself look round at death; in barbarian fashion you seek to live without law: you yourself plant an axe in your shin by the word. You who feign the simple — live simply with him. You believe you live while you long to fill the belly. Tiny, you sit back in your house, crooked one, ready for feasts, and you flee the dinner’s precepts. Or because you disbelieve that God judges the dead, do you happen to make yourself Rector of heaven in his place? You look to the belly as if you were provident for it. Now you seem profane, now holy. You come forth against the suppliant under God’s sight, tyrant. You will feel in the fates whose law you now empty.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 22 DE UBIQUE PARATIS. Dum uentri seruis, innocentem esse te dicis, Et quasi communis facis te ubique paratum. Uae tibi, stulte homo, mortem circumspicis ipse, Barbaro de more sine lege uiuere quaeris: Ipse tibi figis asciam in crure de uerbo. Qui simplicem fingis, simpliciter uiue cum isto. Uiuere te credis, dum uentrem cupis implere. Exiguus tua in domo resedes, praue, Paratus ad epulas, et refugis cenae praecepta. Aut quia discredis Deum iudicare defunctos, Rectorem caeli facis te tu forte pro illo? Aspicis ad uentrem, quasi tu sis prouidus illi. Tu modo profanus, modo sanctus esse uideris. In supplicem prodis Dei sub aspectu, tyranne. Senties in fatis, cuias modo legem inanis.

author: Commodian
english: You say, O fools: Jupiter himself thunders and hurls lightning. Even if littleness felt so, why do years still say it? You were infants: will you be so forever? Infancy’s use does not take up mature turning; childish play has yielded — so let hearts also withdraw; your counsels are owed to character. Senseless, then, do you believe Jupiter thunders — born here on earth and nursed on goat’s milk? So if father Saturn had eaten him, in those times who was raining when he was dead? Especially — is a god believed born of a mortal father? Saturn grew old on earth and failed on it. No one prophesied him before he was born. Or, if he himself thunders, law would have been given by him. Histories seduce, when he himself had been made. But he reigned in Crete and failed there. The Omnipotent has been made for you Semele’s lover. Scarcely would he himself likewise love now, if that one lived. You pray to the impure and say they are celestial, born of mortal seed from those Giants. You hear and read he was born on earth: whence did a corrupter well deserve to climb heaven? You also say the Cyclopes made him a thunderbolt. For the immortal had arms from mortals. So guilty of crimes, a parricide of his own too — by your authority you have conferred him on high.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 5: DE FULMINE IPSIUS IOVIS AUDITE.

latin: 5 DE FULMINE IPSIUS IOVIS AUDITE. Dicitis o stulti: Iouis tonat, fulminat ipse. Etsi paruulitas sic sensit, cur anni dicentes? Fuistis infantes: numquid et semper eritis? Uersari inmaturum infantia non capit <usus> Lusus puerilis cessit: sic et corda recedant; Moribus utique consilia uestra debentur. Insipiens ergo Iouem tonitruare tu credis Natum hic in terris et lacte caprino nutritum; Ergo si illum deuorasset <pater> Saturnus, In istis temporibus quis pluebat illo defuncto? Praesertim mortali patre deus nasci credatur? Saturnus in terris senuit et defecit in ipsis. Illum non aliquis prophetauit ante pronasci. Uel, si tonat ipse, lex ab ipso lata fuisset. Seducunt historiae, factus cum fue<rat ipse>. Ille autem in Cretam regnauit et ibi defecit. Omnipotens uobis factus Semelis amator. Uix ipse modo similiter amaret, si uiuere<t> ille. Inpuros oratis et dicitis esse caelestes Semine mortali natos de Gigantibus illis. Auditis et legitis natum in terra fuisse: Unde bene meruit corruptor ascendere caelum? Dicitis et fulmen Ciclopas illi fecissent. Inmortalis enim habuit a mortalibus arma. Tot reum criminibus, parricidam quoque suorum, Ex auctoritate uestra contulistis in altum.

author: Commodian
english: Concerning Sun and Moon: though they are present to us, you err; what I once thought, you think must be prayed to. They are among the stars, but they do not run by their own will. The Omnipotent, when he first founded all things, placed them there with the stars on the fourth of the days. ****** And indeed he ordered into law that no one adore them. You pray to so many gods who promise nothing about life, whose law is not on earth, nor are they themselves foretold. But a few empty priests seduce you, who say divinities somehow profit a man about to die. Approach the law’s book and learn the true.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 7 DE S0LE ET LUNA. De Sole et Luna, licet sint praesentanea nobis, Erratis; quod ego prius, putatis oranda. Sunt quidem in astris, sed non sua sponte currunt Omnipotens illos, cum conderet omnia primum, Locauitque ibidem cum stellis quarta dierum. Errorem antiquus quin cum *** Et quidem in legem iussit, ne quis illos adoret. Tot deos oratis, qui nihil de uita promittunt, Lex quorum in terra non est, nec ipsi praedicti Uos autem seducunt sacerdotes pauci <inanes> Numina qui dicunt aliquid morituro prodesse. Accedite legis <codicem> et di<s>cite uerum.

author: Commodian
english: If Invictus born from a rock is held a god, now therefore I am silent; you give the prior from these! The rock conquered the god — the rock’s creator must be sought. Moreover you still paint him to be a thief, though if he were a god he would certainly not live by theft. He was earthly for sure and of a monstrous nature, and he kept turning others’ oxen in caves, just as that Cacus, Vulcan’s son, also did.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 12 INVICTUS. Inuictus de petra natus si deus habetur, Nunc ergo reticeo; uos de istis date priorem! Uicit petra deum, quaerendus est petrae creator. Insuper et furem adhuc depingitis esse, Cum, si deus esset, utique non furto uiuebat. Terrenus utique fuit et monstruosa natura Uertebatque boues alienos semper in antris Sicut et Cacus Uulcani filius ille.

author: Commodian
english: We have already said much of unspeakable superstition, and still we pursue it lest we be said to have skipped something. Ammudas, whom his worshipers used to cultivate in their fashion — he was great for them when there was gold in the temple. They put their heads under the divinity as if present. It came to the summit that Caesar took the gold: the divinity fails or flees or passes into fire. The author of this crime stands clear — he who was shaping the same. He seduced so many and great men, falsely prophesying, and now he has fallen silent who used to be divine. For a voice used to burst out as if with altered mind, as though a god of wood spoke into his ear. Say now yourselves if the divinities are not false. From that prodigy which he lost, that prophet forgot to prophesy who before used to. Those monsters are feigned for a god by the devourers of wine, whose damnable boldness fashions divinities. For they were carried about, and another such little image: now he himself is silent, nor does anyone prophesy of him. O too much fools — but you want to destroy yourselves.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
Instr. 17: DE AMMUDATE ET DEO MAGNO.
latin: 17 DE AMMUDATE ET DEO MAGNO. Diximus iam multa de superstitione nefanda, Et tamen exsequimur, ne quod praeterisse dicamur. Ammudatem qui suum cultores more colebant, Magnus erat illis, quando fuit aurum in aedem. Mittebant capita sub numine quasi praesenti. Uentum est ad summum, ut Caesar tolleret aurum: Deficit numen aut fugit aut transit in ignem. Auctor huius sceleris constat, qui formabat eundem. Tot uiros et magnos seduxit false prophetans, Et modo retacuit qui solebat esse diuinus. Erumpebat enim uocis quasi mente mutata, Tamquam illi deus ligni loqueretur in aurem. Dicite nunc ipsi, si non sunt numina falsa. Ex eo prodigio, quod perdidit, ille propheta Oblitus est iste prophetare, qui ante solebat. Monstra deo ista fincta sunt per uiniuoraces, Audacia quorum damnabilis numina fingit. Gestabantur enim, et aliut tale sigillum: Nunc et ipse silet, nec ullus de illo prophetat. O nimium <stulti>, sed uos ipsos perdere uultis.

author: Commodian
english: Is it not a disgrace that a prudent man be seduced and worship such a one, or say Diana is wood? In the morning you trust one drunk, raw, about to perish, who speaks by feigned art what seems to him; he truly plays god and demands entrails for himself. One detestable man piles up all the citizens and has joined like men to himself in a made college, with whom he feigns a story to adorn a god. He does not know how to divine for himself; for others he dares. He shoulders him when he likes, and when he likes he sets him down; he turns spinning from himself with the two-pronged wood, as if you would think him breathed on by a wood’s divinity. You do not worship gods that these falsely prophesy: you worship the priests themselves, fearing in vain. But if you thrive in heart, flee now the shrines of death.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 18 NEMESIACIS VANIS. Non ignominium est uirum seduci prudentem Et colere talem aut Dianam dicere lignum? Mane ebrio, crudo, perituro creditis uno, Ex arte qui fincte loquitur, quod illi uidetur; Se uere deum agit, sibi uiscera poscit. Incopriat ciues unus detestabilis omnes Adplicuitque sibi similis collegio facto, Cum quibus historiam fingit, ut deum adornet. Ipse sibi nescit diuinare, ceteris audet. Succollat, quando libet, eum, et quando, deponit; Uertitur a se rotans cum ligno bifurci, Ac si putes illum adflatum numine ligni. Non deos uos colitis, quos isti false prophetant: Ipsos sacerdotes colitis in uano timentes. Sed si corde uiges, fuge iam sacraria mortis.

author: Commodian
english: And old Saturn — if he is a god, when does a god grow old? Or if he was a god, why did he devour his sons driven by terrors? But because he was not a god, he consumed his sons’ bowels in monstrous madness. He was a king on earth, born on mount Olympus; and he was not divine, but called himself a god. He fell into weakness of mind and swallowed a stone for his son. Thus he became a god; of late he is called Jupiter.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 3 SATURNUS. Saturnusque senex si deus, deus quando senescit? Aut si deus erat, cur natos ille uorabat? Terroribus actus, sed quia deus non erat ille, Uiscera natorum rabie monstruosa sumebat. Rex fuit in terris, in monte natus Olympo, Nec erat diuinus; sic deum esse diceba<n>t. Uenit inops animi, lapidem pro filio sorbsit: Sic deus euasit, dicitur modo Iuppiter ille.

author: Commodian
english: This Jupiter was born to Saturn on the island of Crete; and when grown he robbed his father of the kingdom. Then he deluded nobles’ wives and sisters. Moreover Pyracmon the smith had made him a scepter. In the beginning God made the heaven, the earth, and the sea. But that frightful creature, born in mid-time, went out as a youth from a cave and was nourished by stealth. Behold, that God is author of all things — not that Jupiter.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.

latin: 4 IUPPITER. Iuppiter hic natus in insula Creta Saturno Ut fuit adultus, patrem de regno priuauit. Proinde nobilium uxores sororesque delusit. Praeterea sceptra fecerat faber ille Piragmon. Initium caelum, terram Deus et mare fecit; Terribilis autem iste medio tempore natus Ex antro processit iuuenis furtimque nutritus. Respice querellas: Alter est Deus, non Iouis ille.

author: Commodian
english: Concerning the septizonium and the stars: the circle of the zone deceives you by your ignorance, from this that you happen to think Jupiter must be prayed to. ****** The Omnipotent placed the stars when he made all; they do not run that they may give you the fates of genesis. He himself orders their course. Why then do you inquire from them what he did not grant them to tell? Leave the stars’ error; the law teaches what must be followed. ******
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 6 DE SEPTIZONIO ET STELLIS. De circulo zonae fallit uos imperitia uestra, Ex eo quod forte Iouem experitis orandum. Saturnus fertur ibi, sed stella, non ille; exfugit Expulsus a Ioue. Aut Iouis in stella credatur Poli quoque sidera tractauit solisque sator? Troianis qui bellum fecit, auem mortalem amauit. Ipsis sideribus aut Mars qui cum ipsa deprehensus Zelo maritali deus dominetur aduliscens? O nimium stulti, qui putatis moechos ab astris Nascentes regere aut tota<m> mundi natura<m>. In uulnera positi et ipsi sub fata uiuentes, Obsceni, furiosi, bellatores, impii uitae, Et filios totidem mortales illi fecere: Terribilis omnis, stulti, septizonio fortis! Si stellas colitis, colite et bis sena sigilla! Tam arietem, taurum, geminos, toruumque leonem Et dein qui uadunt in piscibus tu quoque probabis. Lex sine lege, fuga uestra, quod uult esse ualebit. Lasciua uult esse, sine freno uiuere quaerit. Ipsi quod uultis erit, et deos et deas oratis. Sic ego colui, dum erraui, quos modo culpo.

author: Commodian
english: Your Mercury is made painted with a purse and with helm and sole, winged and otherwise nearly bare. You say he is a messenger and also a thief. If he were a god, why did he steal? He first invented merchandise and the lyre — earthly arts. From that you paint him a god. A winged thief is no divinity.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 8 MERCURIUS. Mercurius uester fiat cum arabylo depictus Et galea et planta, pinnatus et cetera nudus. Rem uideo miram, deum <cum> saccello uolare: Currite pauperculi, cum gremio quo uolat ille, Ut sacculum effundat: uos extunc estote parati. Respicite pictum: quando uobis hic ab alto Iactabit nummos, uos tunc saltate securi. Uane, non insanis, colere deos pictos in axe? Si uiuere recte nescis, cum besteis perge morari.

author: Commodian
english: You make Neptune a god sprung from Saturn, and he rules a trident so he can spear fish. From that you say he is god of the sea. What divinity is it to chase fish with a fork? He was of watery tale on earth — not to be prayed to as god.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 9 NEPTUNUS. Neptunum facitis deum ex Saturno pronatum, Et tridentem regit, ut pisces suffigere possit. Paret esse deum + cumerale illi parate! Troianis non ipse cum Apolline muros eduxit? Unde deus factus inops cimentarius ille? Non Cyclopem genuit monstrum? non moechus et ipse? Uiuere non poterat de suo, quod structura<m> gerebat. Sic genuit generatus, qui fuit iam mortuus olim.

author: Commodian
english: You make Apollo a lyre-player and also a diviner. First he was born of adultery on the island of Delos. ****** He draws lots and deceives. Why do you seek true things from a false lot-drawer? Leave sortilege; the law of God speaks what is true. ******
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 10 APOLLO SORTILEGUS FALSUS. Apollinem facitis citharoedum atque diuinum. Primum de moechia natus in insula Delo, Oblata mercede postmodum structura<s> secutus Laomedonti regi Troianorum muros eduxit Locauitque sese, quem deum seducti putatis; Ossibus cuius amor Cassandrae flagrauit, Subdole quem lusit uirgo, falliturque diuinus Officio uerbenis <is> potuit scire bicorde<m>, Repudiatus enim discessit inde diuinus. Terruit hunc uirgo specie, quam ille deberet. Illa prior utique debuerat deum amasse. Lasciuientemque Daphnem sic coepit amare. Et tamen insequitur, dum uult uiolare puellam: Gratis amat stultus, nec potuit consequi cursum. Uel, si deus erat, occurreret illi per auras: Sub tectis illa prior uenit remansitque diuinus. Fallit uos genus hominum, nam improbi isti fuerunt. A primitia quoque pecora pauisse refertur. Lusibus in positis dum mitteret discum in altum, Sublapsum non potuit retinere prostrauit amicum: Ultimus ille dies fuit Hyacinthi sodalis. Si diuinus erat, mortem praecessisset amici.

author: Commodian
english: You yourselves say Liber the father was certainly twice-born. Born in India from Jupiter and Proserpina first — ****** You run mad in his rites. What god is celebrated by drunken frenzy? Leave Bacchus’ furies; they are tales, not divinity.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 11 LIBER PATER BACCHUS. Liberum patrem certe bis genitum dicitis ipsi. In India natus ex Ioue Proserpina primum Belligerans contra Titanas profuso cruore Expirauit enim sicut ex mortalibus unus. Rursus flato suo redditus in altero uentre. Percipit hoc Semele iterum Iouis altera moecha, Absciso cuius utero prope partu defunctae Tollitur et datur Niso nutriendus alumnus. Ex eo bis natus Dionisius ille uocatur, Religio cuius in uacuo falsa curatur. Bacchantur et illi, qualis nunc ipsi uidentur, Aut pediculones mineruae omnisque scitoris. Conspirant in malo, proludunt fincto furore, Ceteros ut fallant dicturos numen adesse. Huic manifeste rudes homines suille uiuentes Uino permutati, primo quod expresserat ille, Sub ludicro suo honorem illi dedere.

author: Commodian
english: Whence has Silvanus appeared to be a god again? Perhaps he pleases because the pipe sings well. If a sweet fistula makes gods, every shepherd is divine. Rustic song is not a numen — leave the wood-god tale.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 13 SILVANUS. Siluanus unde deus iterum apparuit esse? Inde forte placet, eo quod bene fistula cantat? Lar igitur quando? lignum nam forte non esset. Uenalem emisti dominum, cum tu ipse sis illi. Aspice, deficit lignum! quid illi debetur? Non te pudet, stulte, tales adorare tabellas? Unum quaere Deum, qui post mortem uiuere dicit! Secede ab istis, qui sunt biothanati facti.

author: Commodian
english: Hercules because he crushed the monster of the Aventine mount — he who used to steal Evander’s herds. A strong cattle-thief is praised as god. Strength and theft do not confer divinity.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.

Hercules quod monstrum Auentini montis elisit Euandri qui solitus erat armenta furare, Rustica mens hominum, indocilis quoque, pro laude Cum gratias agere uellent, absentis Tonantis Laetandas aras in memoriam sibi fecerunt. Ex eo porrexit, de uetusto more colatur. Sed deus hic non est, licet fuit fortis in armis.

author: Commodian
english: You say the Titans are guardians for you; thus you ask the Mute and Silent ones under your roof, ****** Vain is the cult that prays hush-gods in the house.

Adoratis enim stulti malo leto defunctos, Non legem ipsorum legentes; non ipsi loquuntur, Et deos audetis eramine dicere fusos? Solueretis eos magis in uascula uobis.

author: Commodian
english: You say mountain gods — let them rule in the field — darkened by evil, swearing with an alien mind. ****** Leave the countryside’s divinities; the Lord made the hills. Serve him, not the mountain tales.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Commodian Instructiones.
latin: 20 MONTESIANIS. Monteses deos dicitis, dominentur in aruo Obscurati malo aliena mente iurantes. Nam si purus animus et mens serena maneret Tu tibi de illis ipsi disputare deberes. Excordaris homo, si putas, ut isti te saluent Seu regant, seu minuant, nisi quod tu fani decurris. Iustitiam legis quaere magis quam illa, salutis Auxilium portat et fieri dicit aeternum. Nam quicquid in uano sequeris, per tempora gaudes In breui laetaris et postmodum plangis in imis: Subtrahe te illis, si uis resurgere Christo.

author: Commodian
english: The trumpet gives a sign in heaven when the Lion is lifted, and suddenly darkness comes with heaven’s crash. The Lord casts down his eyes that the earth may tremble, and cries out that all in the world may hear: “Behold, I have long been silent, bearing your things so long!” Together they cry out, wailing late, groaning; there is howling, weeping, nor is space given to the unjust: what will a mother do for the nursing child when she herself is burned? In flame of fire the Lord will judge the unjust; but the fire will not touch the just — rather it will leave them. They linger under one, but a part will weep in the sentence. So great will be the heat that the stones themselves melt; in lightning the winds meet, heaven’s wrath rages, so that wherever the impious flees, he is seized by fire; there will be no help, nor ships of the sea. Yet the flame burns the Median and Parthian nations for a thousand years, as bodies burn for the saints. For from there after a thousand years they are handed to Gehenna, and the fabric whose they were is burned with them.

author: Tertullian
english: I. [1] This sort of people — which we ourselves also formerly were, blind without the Lord’s light — know by nature that repentance is a certain passion of mind that comes from offense at a prior judgment. [2] But they are as far from its reason as from the author of reason himself. For reason is a matter of God, because God the maker of all provided, arranged, and ordered nothing without reason, and willed nothing to be handled and understood without reason. [3] Therefore those who are ignorant of God must also be ignorant of his matter, because no one’s treasure at all stands open to outsiders. And so, ferrying the whole conversation of life without the helm of reason, they do not know how to avoid the storm impending on the age. [4] But how unreasonably they turn about in the act of repentance will be enough to show even by this one point: they apply it even to their good deeds. They repent of faith, love, simplicity, liberality, patience, mercy: [5] according as something has fallen into ingratitude, they curse themselves because they did good, and they fix in the heart especially that species of repentance which is imposed on the best works, taking care to remember not to offer any good again. Against the repentance of evils they lean more lightly: in short they more easily offend by the same than do right by the same.
latin: I. [1] Paenitentiam hoc genus homines quod et ipsi retro fuimus, caeci sine domini lumine, natura tenus norunt passionem animi quandam esse quae obveniat de offensa sententiae prioris. [2] Ceterum a ratione eius tantum absunt quantum ab ipso rationis auctore. Quippe res dei ratio quia deus omnium conditor nihil non ratione providit disposuit ordinavit nihilque non ratione tractari intellegique voluit. [3] Igitur ignorantes quique deum rem quoque eius ignorent necesse est quia nullius omnino thesaurus extraneis patet. Itaque universam vitae conversationem sine gubernaculo rationis transfretantes inminentem saeculo procellam evitare non norunt. [4] Quam autem in paenitentiae actu inrationabiliter deversentur, vel uno isto satis erit expedire cum illam etiam in bonis factis suis adhibent. Paenitet fidei amoris implicitatis liberalitatis patientiae misericordiae: [5] prout quid in ingratiam cecidit, semetipsos execrantur quia benefecerint, eamque maxime paenitentiae speciem quae optimis operibus inrogatur in corde figunt meminisse curantes ne quid boni rursus praestent. Contra paenitentiae malorum levius incubant: denique facilius per eandem delinquunt quam per eandem recte faciunt.

author: Tertullian
english: III. [1] For whom, then, repentance seems just and owed — that is, what things are to be counted as sin — the place indeed demands that we mark them, but it can seem idle. [2] For when the Lord is known, the spirit of its own, looking back to its author, rises to the knowledge of truth and, admitted to the Lord’s precepts, is at once taught from them that that is to be counted as sin from which God bars us: since, when God stands as something great of good, assuredly nothing but evil would displease the good, because between contraries there is no friendship. [3] Still it will not irk to note that certain delicts are carnal, that is bodily, and certain truly spiritual — for since man is made from this gathering of a double substance, he does not offend from elsewhere than from what he consists of — [4] but they do not differ among themselves because body and spirit are two; rather they are more equal because the two make one, lest anyone, for the diversity of materials, distinguish their sins so as to think one lighter or heavier than the other. [5] Since both flesh and spirit are God’s things — one shaped by his hand, the other finished by his breath — when therefore they belong equally to the Lord, whichever of them offends equally offends the Lord. [6] Or do you distinguish the acts of flesh and spirit, which both in life and in death and in resurrection have so much communion and partnership that they are raised together then either into life or into judgment, because clearly they either offended together or acted innocently together? [7] We have put this first so that we understand no less necessity of repentance hangs over one part than over both, if either has offended; the guilt of both is common, and the judge is common — God, of course — therefore the medicine of repentance is also common. [8] Thereafter they are named spiritual and bodily, because every delict is either done or thought, so that what is in deed is bodily because a deed, like a body, can be seen and touched, but what is in the mind is spiritual because, like spirit, it is neither seen nor held. [9] By which it is shown that delicts not of deed only but also of will are to be avoided and purged by repentance.
latin: III. [1] Quorum ergo paenitentia iusta et debita videatur, id est quae delicto deputanda sint, locus quidem expostulat denotare, sed otiosum videri potest. [2] Domino enim cognito ultro spiritus a suo auctore respectus emergit ad notitiam veritatis et admissus ad dominica praecepta ex ipsis statim eruditur id peccato deputandum, a quo deus arceat: quoniam, cum deum grande quid boni constet esse, utique bono nisi malum non displiceret, quod inter contraria sibi nulla ami- citia est. [3] Praestringere tamen non pigebit delictorum quaedam esse carnalia, id est corporalia, quaedam vero spiritalia - nam cum ex hac duplicis substantiae eongregatione confectus homo sit, non aliunde delinquit quam unde constat -; [4] sed non eo inter se differunt, quod corpus et spiritus duo sunt, atquin eo magis paria sunt, quia duo unum efficiunt, ne quis pro diversitate materiarum peccata earum discernat ut alterum altero levius aut gravius existimet. [5] Siquidem et caro et spiritus dei res, alia manu eius expressa, alia adflatu [eius] consummata; cum ergo ex pari ad dominum pertineant, quodcumque eorum deliquerit ex pari dominum offendit. [6] An tu discernas actus carnis et spiritus, quorum et in vita et in morte et in resurrectione tantum communionis atque consortii est, ut pariter tunc aut in vitam aut in iudicium suscitentur, quia scilicet pariter aut deliquerint aut innocenter egerint? [7] Hoc eo praemisimus ut non minorem alteri quam utrique parti, si quid deliquerit, paenitentiae necessitatem intellegamus inpendere; communis reatus amborum est, communis et iudex, deus scilicet: communis igitur et paenitentiae medella. [8] Exinde spiritalia et corporalia nominantur, quod delictum omne aut agitur aut cogitatur, ut corporale sit quod in facto est quia factum ut corpus et videri et contingi habet, spiritale vero quod in animo est quia ut spiritus neque videtur neque tenetur. [9] Per quod ostenditur non facti solum, verum et voluntatis delicta vitanda et paenitentia purganda esse. Neque enim, si mediocritas humana facti solummodo iudicat quia voluntatis latebris par non est, idcirco [etiam] crimina eius etiam sub deo neglegamus. [10] Deus in omnia sufficit; nihil a conspectu eius remotum unde omnino delinquitur; quia non ignorat, nec omittit quominus in iudicium decernat: dissimulator et praevaricator perspicaciae suae non est! [11] Quid quod voluntas facti origo est? Viderint enim, si qua casui aut necessitati aut ignorantiae inputantur, quibus exceptis iam non nisi voluntate delinquitur. [12] Cum ergo facti origo sit, non tanto potior ad poenam est quanto principalis ad culpam? Qua ne tunc quidem liberatur cum aliqua difficultas perpetrationem eius intercipit: ipsa enim sibi inputatur nec excusari poterit per illam perficiendi infelicitatem, operata quod suum fuerat. [13] Denique dominus quemadmodum se adiectionem legi superstruere demonstrat nisi et voluntatis interdicendo delicta? Cum adulterum non eum solum definit qui comminus in alienum matrimonium cecidisset, verum etiam illum qui adspectus concupiscentia contaminasset. [14] Adeo quod prohibetur administrare, satis periculose animus sibi repraesentat et temere per voluntatem expungit effectum. Cuius voluntatis cum vis tanta sit ut nos solatio sui saturans pro facto cedat, pro facto ergo plectetur. [15] Vanissimum est dicere: 'volui nec tamen feci'; atquin perficere debes quia vis, aut nec velle quia nec perficis. [16] Sed ipse conscientiae tuae confessionem pronuntias, nam si bonum concupisceres, perficere gestisses; porro si ut malum non perficis, nec concupiscere debueras: quaqua te constitueris, crimini adstringeris qua aut malum volueris aut bonum non adinpleveris!

author: Tertullian
english: IV. [1] Therefore for all delicts committed whether in flesh or spirit, whether by deed or by will, he who destined punishment through judgment also pledged pardon through repentance, saying to the people: “Repent and I will save you.” [2] And again: “As I live,” says the Lord, “I prefer repentance to death.” Therefore repentance is life, which is set before death. You, sinner — my like, rather less than I, for I confess my lead in delicts — invade it, embrace it, as a shipwrecked man the trust of some plank. [3] This will lift you, sunk in the waves of sins, and draw you on into the harbor of divine clemency. Seize the chance of unexpected happiness, that you who were once nothing with the Lord but a drop of a bucket and dust of the threshing-floor and a potter’s vessel may then become a tree — that tree which is planted by the waters and lasts in leaves and in its time yields fruit, which will see neither fire nor axe. [4] Let it repent of errors when truth is found; let it repent of having loved what God does not love, since not even we ourselves allow our servants to know those things by which we are offended: for the reason of obedience is set in likeness of minds. [5] The matter of enumerating the good of repentance is sprawling and for that reason to be committed to great eloquence; but we, for our narrowness, drive one point: that is good and best which God commands. [6] I think it boldness to debate the good of a divine precept; for we ought to listen not because it is good, but because God commanded: for the display of obedience the majesty of divine power is prior, the authority of the one commanding is prior.

latin: IV. [1] Omnibus ergo delictis seu carne seu spiritu, seu facto seu voluntate commissis qui poenam per iudicium destinavit, idem et veniam per paenitentiam spopondit dicens ad populum: paenitere et salvum faciam te. [2] Et rursus: vivo, inquit, dicit dominus et paenitentiam malo quam mortem. Ergo paenitentia vita est, quae praeponitur morti. Eam tu peccator, mei similis - immo me minor: ego enim praestantiam in delictis meam agnosco - ita invade, ita amplexare ut naufragus alicuius tabulae fidem. [3] Haec te peccatorum fluctibus mersum prolevabit et in portum divinae clementiae protelabit. Rape occasionem inopinatae felicitatis, ut ille tu nihil quondam penes dominum nisi stilla situlae et areae pulvis et vasculum figuli arbor exinde fias, illa arbor quae penes aquas seritur et in foliis perennat et tempore suo fructus agit, quae non ignem, non securem videbit. [4] Paeniteat errorum reperta veritate, paeniteat amasse quae deus non amat, quando ne nos quidem ipsi servulis nostris ea, quibus offendimur, nosse permittimus: obsequi enim ratio in similitudine animorum constituta est. [5] De bono paenitentiae enumerando diffusa et per hoc magno eloquio committenda materia est: nos vero pro nostris angustiis unum inculcamus, bonum atque optimum esse quod deus praecipit. [6] Audaciam existimo de bono divini praecepti disputare; neque enim quia bonum est, idcirco auscultare debemus, sed quia deus praecepit: ad exhibitionem obsequi prior est maiestas divinae potestatis, prior est auctoritas imperantis quam utilitas servientis. [7] 'Bonum est paenitere an non?' Quid revolvis? deus praecepit! Atenim ille non praecipit tantum, sed etiam hortatur; invitat praemio: salute; iurans etiam, vivo dicens cupit credi sibi. [8] O beatos nos quorum causa deus iurat; o miserrimos si nec iuranti domino credimus! Quod iterum deus tantopere conmendat, quod etiam humano more sub deieratione testatur, summa utique gravitate et adgredi et custodire debemus, ut in adseveratione divinae gratiae permanentes in fructu quoque eius et emolumento proinde perseverare possimus.

author: Tertullian
english: V. [1] For this I say: repentance, which by God’s grace has been shown and enjoined to us and recalls us into the Lord’s grace, once known and taken ought never afterward to be unsealed by a repetition of delict. [2] Already no pretext of ignorance sponsors you, because when the Lord is recognized and his precepts admitted, and when you have finally performed repentance of delicts, you restore yourself again into delicts. [3] So far as you are parted from ignorance, so far you are glued to contumacy; for if you had repented of having offended because you had begun to fear the Lord, why did you prefer to cancel what you did for fear’s sake unless because you ceased to fear? [4] For nothing else but contumacy overturns fear. But when not even those ignorant of the Lord are screened from punishment by any exception — because God, set in the open and graspable even from the heavenly goods themselves, may not be unknown — how much more dangerous is it to despise him when known? [5] Moreover he despises who, having received from him the understanding of goods and evils, resumes what he understands must be fled and what he has already fled, and so insults his own understanding, that is God’s gift: he spurns the giver when he deserts the gift; he denies the benefit when he does not honor the benefactor. [6] How can he please him whose gift displeases him? So he appears toward the Lord not only contumacious but also ungrateful. [7] Besides, he does not sin lightly against the Lord who, when by his repentance he had renounced the Lord’s rival the devil and under that name had subjected him to the Lord, by his return raises the same again and makes himself the devil’s exultation, so that the evil one recovers him anew.
latin: V. [1] Hoc enim dico, paenitentiam, quae per dei gratiam ostensa et indicta nobis in gratiam nos domino revocat, semel cognitam atque susceptam numquam posthac iteratione delicti resignari oportere. [2] Iam quidem nullum ignorantiae praetextum patrocinatur tibi, quod domino adgnito praeceptisque eius admissis, denique paenitentia delictorum functus, rursus te in delicta restituis. [3] Ita in quantum ab ignorantia segregaris, in tantum contumaciae adglutinaris; nam si idcirco te deliquisse paenituerat quia dominum coeperas timere, cur quod metus gratia gessisti rescindere maluisti nisi quia metuere desisti? [4] Neque enim timorem alia res quam contumacia subvertit. Cum autem etiam ignorantes dominum nulla exceptio tueatur a poena, quia deum in aperto constitutum et vel ex ipsis caelestibus bonis conprehensibilem ignorari non licet, quanto cognitum despici periculosum est? [5] Despicit porro qui, bonorum ac malorum intellectum ab illo consecutus, quod intellegit fugiendum quodque iam fugit resumens intellectui suo id est dei dono contumeliam facit: respuit datorem, cum datum deserit; negat beneficium, cum beneficum non honorat! [6] Quemadmodum ei potest placere cuius munus sibi displicet? Ita in dominum non modo contumax sed etiam ingratus apparet. [7] Ceterum non leviter in dominum peccat qui, cum aemulo eius diabolo paenitentia sua renuntiasset et hoc nomine illum domino subiecisset, rursus eundum regressu suo erigit et exultationem eius semetipsum facit, ut denuo malus recuperata praeda sua adversus dominum gaudeat. [8] Nonne - quod dicere quoque periculosum est, sed ad aedificationem proferendum [est] - diabolum domino praepones? Conparationem enim videtur egisse, qui utrumque cognoverit, et iudicato pronuntiasse eum meliorem, cuius se rursus esse maluerit! [9] Ita qui per delictorum paenitentiam instituerat domino satisfacere, diabolo per aliam paenitentiae paenitentiam satisfaciet eritque tanto magis perosus deo quanto aemulo eius acceptus. [10] Sed aiunt quidam satis dominum habere, si corde et animo suscipiatur, licet actu minus fiat; itaque se salvo metu et fide peccare, hoc est salva oastitate matrimonia violare, salva pietate parenti venenum temperare. [11] Sic ergo et ipsi salva venia in gehennam detrudentur, dum salvo metu peccant. [12] Pro mirum exemplum perversitatis: quia timent delinquunt; opinor non delinquerent, si non timerent! [13] Igitur qui deum nolet offensum, nec revereatur omnino, si timor offendendi patrocinium est! Sed ista ingenia de semine hypocritarum pullulare consuerunt, quorum individua cum diabolo amicitia est, quorum paenitentia numquam fidelis.

author: Minucius Felix
english: XX. I have set out the opinions of almost all the philosophers of brighter fame, who designated one God though under many names, so that anyone may judge either that Christians are now philosophers or that philosophers were already then Christians. But if the world is ruled by providence and directed by the nod of one God, then the ancient fables of the poets and the many gods must yield — truth is older than error, and one God is enough for all. The rest of the chapter presses the same point from the locked Latin: one God and providence against fables.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Minucius Octavius.
latin: 20. "Exposui opiniones omnium ferme philosophorum, quibus inlustrior gloria est, deum unum multis licet designasse nominibus, ut quivis arbitretur, aut nunc Christianos philosophos esse aut philosophos fuisse iam tunc Christianos. "Quod si providentia mundus regitur et unius dei nutu gubernatur, non nos debet antiquitas inperitorum fabellis suis delectata vel capta ad errorem mutui rapere consensus, cum philosophorum suorum sententiis refellatur, quibus et rationis et vetustatis adsistit auctoritas. Maioribus enim nostris tam facilis in mendaciis fides fuit, ut temere crediderint etiam alia monstruosa, mera miracula: Scyllam multiplicem, Chimaeram multiformem et Hydram felicibus vulneribus renascentem et Centauros equos suis hominibus inplexos, et quicquid famae licet fingere, illis erat libenter audire. Quid illas aniles fabulas, de hominibus aves et feras et de hominibus arbores atque flores? Quae si essent facta, fierent: quia fieri non possunt, ideo nec facta sunt. Similiter erraverunt erga deos quoque maiores nostri: inprovidi, creduli rudi simplicitate crediderunt. Dum reges suos colunt religiose, dum defunctos eos desiderant in imaginibus videre, dum gestiunt eorum memorias in statuis detinere, sacra facta sunt quae fuerant adsumpta solacia. Denique et antequam commerciis orbis pateret et antequam gentes ritus suos moresque miscerent, unaquaeque natio conditorem suum aut ducem inclytum aut reginam pudicam sexu suo fortiorem aut alicuius muneris vel artis repertorem venerabatur ut civem bonae memoriae: sic et defunctis praemium et futuris dabatur exemplum.

author: Minucius Felix
english: XXVII. Those impure spirits, then — demons, as shown also by the magi and philosophers — lurk under consecrated statues and images, and by their breath they obtain the authority of a divinity as if present, while at times they inspire seers, linger in shrines, sometimes animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flight of birds, manage lots, and always, mixing falsehood with truth, lead people away from God into error. The rest catalogues demonic frauds in lots, birds, and oracles against the living God.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Minucius Octavius.
latin: 27. "Isti igitur impuri spiritus, daemones, ut ostensum magis ac philosophis, sub statuis et imaginibus consecratis delitiscunt et adflatu suo auctoritatem quasi praesentis numinis consequuntur, dum inspirant interim vatibus, dum fanis inmorantur, dum nonnumquam extorum fibras animant, avium volatus gubernant, sortes regunt, oracula efficiunt, falsis pluribus involuta. Nam et falluntur et fallunt, ut et nescientes sinceram veritatem et quam sciunt, in perditionem sui non confitentes. Sic a caelo deorsum gravant et a deo vero ad materias avocant, vitam turbant, somnos inquietant, inrepentes etiam corporibus occulte, ut spiritus tenues, morbos fingunt, terrent mentes, membra distorquent, ut ad cultum sui cogant, ut nidore altarium vel hostiis pecudum saginati, remissis quae constrinxerant, curasse videantur. Hinc sunt et furentes, quos in publicum videtis excurrere, vates et ipsi absque templo, sic insaniunt, sic bacchantur, sic rotantur: par et in illis instigatio daemonis, sed argumentum dispar furoris. De ipsis etiam illa, quae paulo ante tibi dicta sunt, ut Iuppiter ludos repeteret ex somnio, ut cum equis Castores viderentur, ut cingulum matronae navicula sequeretur. "Haec omnia sciunt pleraque pars vestrum ipsos daemonas de semetipsis confiteri, quotiens a nobis tormentis verborum et orationis incendiis de corporibus exiguntur. Ipse Saturnus et Serapis et Iuppiter et quicquid daemonum colitis, victi dolore quod sunt eloquuntur, nec utique in turpitudinem sui, nonnullis praesertim vestrum adsistentibus, mentiuntur.
