latin: Et quidquid ualuerit, faciet, ut muta loquantur. Balaam caedenti asinam suam colloqui fecit Et canem, ut Simoni diceret: Clamaris a Petro! Paulo praedicanti discerent ut multi de illo Leonem populo fecit loqui uoce diuina. Deinde, quod ipsa non patitur nostra natura, Infantem fecit quinto mense proloqui uulgo. Hic erat uenturus commixto sanguine nostro, Ut uideretur homo, sed Deus in carne latebat. Non senior ueniet nec angelus, dixit Esaias, Sed Dominus ipse ueniet se ostendere nobis. Hunc mare pertimuit, hunc uenti, hunc tartarus ipse; Agnouit Dominum omnis creatura latentem. Solus nequam populus centriam erexit ad illum: 'Absit, ut sic Dominus uenerit in tali figura!' Hic sicut in terra super fluctus maris inibat Et uentis imperat, placidum ut redderet aequor. si Hic lege<m> tartaream derupit uerbo praesenti Et leuat de tumulis Lazarum die quarta fetentem. Nam qui ferebatur, cum fuisset obuius illi: Surge, inquit, iuuenis! Et <re>surrexit ille de ferculo. Archisinagogae filiam deprecatus a patre Iam exanimata<m> plangentibus suscitat illam. Mutum loqui fecit et surdum audire praesertim Et caecum ex utero natum, ut uideret in auras. Post XXXVIII annis paralyticum surgere iussit, Quem admirarentur grabatum in collo ferentem. ......................................... Cuius uestimento tacto profluuio sanata est. Quinque panes fregit hominum in milia quinque Et quattuor milia iterum de septem refecit. Plenius ut sese Dominus demonstraret adesse, In nuptias fuerat inuitatus matre cum ipsa; Quod fuit rogatus, subueniret uino defecto, Tunc iussit implere ydrias uelocius aqua, Quod prius gustauit et sic ministrari praecepit. Nec sic potuerunt Dominum cognoscere factis Sed insanierunt, quasi nequam perdere morti. Quod ipsum concedit, quoniam sic pati decreuit Si tamen crediderint, ueniam tunc demum habebunt. Hic est primogenitus per prophetas ante praedictus, Ut uocitaretur in terris Altissimi proles. Felices, hominum spem suam in isto qui ponunt Nam insipientes tamquam maledictum euitant. Aeternitas illi praeparatur, Christo qui credit, Ut socius Dei sit homo post funera uiuens. Lex et prophetae docent, qui sunt Dei digni caelorum Et quibus absconsa reuelantur aurea saecla. Per tot uates numero de filio Dei clamatur, Et cluserunt oculos fili Dei primi uocati;

author: Commodian
english: But persevering: We are the elect! saying. Still they make the profane foolish to go to baths, whom they make clean to please the most high God themselves. Water washes filths, not the inward wicked things of the heart, nor will sacred things carefully done be able to wash the sacrilegious. The Lord did not so command sacred things to be carried to the malign; and again a place, to be held clean from idols: Let no one make for himself a demon’s image, he says; for he said also to them: Do not serve idols. If God commanded idols to be strongly avoided, why do they deceive the nations that they are pure by washings? Rather when they receive such, they ought to teach to serve no others, except only to please the Highest. While they seek to overshadow the crime of Christ’s death, they open the doors everywhere so it may be entered to them. From here therefore they perish, who think they can become God’s by water, accomplices before with the robber. Now he worships anything in vain, now he seeks holy things; he does not know where first that unknowing one should meet, and he serves idols, again seeks the thirtieth; now he follows unleavened bread, who had sat chaste before. This did not please God — to be partners of demons — who set the law, that a crossing might be made from there. Two ways are set before you: choose which you will, for you will not split yourself so you can go through both; but yet from them you ought to seek the fit one; and do not fall into robbers’ jaws — be more careful. Seek the one Lord, who seeks no sacrificial victim, so that washed you may rise in a renewed age. Why do you attend to the bad and judge the holy unjust, who show you no word from the law? About God’s power it is reported, which he did among them — ****** Baths do not scrub the heart. Two ways — pick one. Seek the one Lord who wants no victim, and rise in the new age.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Carmen (Latin Library HTML).
latin: Sed perseuerantes: Nos sumus electi! dicentes. Adhuc infatuant profanos balneis ire, Quos faciunt mundos ipsi Deo summo placere. Aqua lauat sordes, non intima cordis iniqua, Nec sacra sacrilega poterunt lauare curata. Non ita praecepit Dominus sacra ferre malignis; Et locus iterum, ab idolis mundos haberi: Nemo sibi faciat simulacrum daemonis, inquit; Nam dixit et illis: Idolis seruire nolite. Si Deus praecepit ab idolis ualde caueri, Quid illi decipiunt gentes puros esse lauacris? Immo cum recipiunt tales, docere deberent Seruire non aliis, nisi tantum Summo placere. Dum facinus quaerunt obumbrare Christi de morte, Aperiunt ualuas passim, ut intretur ad illos Hinc ergo depereunt, qui se putant puros ab aqua Posse Dei fieri, conscientes ante latroni. Nunc colit in uano quodlibet, nunc sancta requirit, Nescit ubi primum occurrat inscius ille, Ac idolis seruit, iterum tricesima quaerit; Nunc azima sequitur, qui castum sederat ante. Hoc Deo non placuit participes daemonum esse, Qui legem instituit, fieret quo transitus inde. Sunt tibi praepositas duas uias: elige, quam uis, Nec enim te findes, ut possis ire per ambas; Sed tamen ex ipsis opportunam quaerere debes; Nec cadas in fauces latronum, cautior esto. Unum quaere Dominum, qui quaerit hostia nulla, Ut possis abolitus <re>surgere saeclo nouato. Quid malos attendis et iudicas sanctos iniquos, Qui tibi nullum uerbum de lege demonstra<n>t? De uirtute Dei refertur, quam fecit in illos;

author: Commodian
english: What do these presume, though they were urged, saying: From the whole people we are dearest to the Highest? Can a father’s murderer always, and the proud man in him, be dear or be called heir by right? How much more the Lord, for whom sons to be chosen excel! To the gentle, the humble, pupils full of obedience the goods are divided — not to the impious or to tyrants. The Jews had been openly adopted as sons, but in the testament the impious obtained the name. Let them reckon to themselves: Bloodstained by crime committed, how could they at all be partners of the goods? Why do they hiss at us, why envy us as heirs? They would have done good, and they were in the share bequeathed. Nor today do they keep silent, and they refuse to believe Christ, who had been foretold to them as saving by the law; about whom you already heard how the prophets were singing: That the Lord would come on the lands, whom the nations will adore. This one certainly they themselves warn us to recognize as the Highest, who renews man and grants former sins. For he himself also threatens the worshipers of gods: The one sacrificing to idols will perish in the second death. Whoever therefore follows gods fashioned in gold, silver or stone, wood or cast in bronze — ****** Dearest-to-God is not a murderer’s title. Goods go to the gentle; nations will adore the foretold Lord — refuse him and keep the second death.

latin: Quid isti praesumunt, cum sint adhortati, dicentes: Ex omni populo nos sumus carissimi Summo? Parricida patris semper et superbus in illo Carus esse potest aut heres iure uocari? Quanto magis Dominus, superant cui fili legendi! Mansuetis, humilibus, obsequio plenis alumnis Diuidunturque bona, non impiis neque tyrannis. Adoptati fuerant manifeste fili Iudaei, Sed in testamento consecuti sunt impii nomen. Ipsi sibi reputent: Scelere commisso cruenti Qui poterant utique participes esse bonorum? Quid nobis strident, quid nos aemulantur heredes? Fecissentque bonum, et erant in parte legati. Nam et comminatur deorum cultoribus ipse: Sacrificans periet idolis in morte secunda. Quisque deos ergo sequitur fabricatos in auro, Argento uel lapide, ligno uel aeramine fusos,

author: Commodian
english: Nor does he die away there, but he deals unjust torments. Men are like cattle in this nature, who refuse to take the Most High God’s bridle while they wander; though they themselves cannot bear to endure such things of slaves, into whose blood the fierce often descend. Adding they say: ‘There is nothing after our funerals; while we live, this is it,’ and they lean in like swine; ‘Let no luxury pass us by in the age; while there is time of life, let us enjoy all things of the world.’ The undisciplined flee God’s clemency, chasing new-year gifts as if that alone were life. So they withdraw from God, who promises to live forever: they fight against the good, when the fight should be against the unjust. We all erred openly, persuaded by the age, but by the Lord’s grace we are called to believe the law. For that he came and made trophies hiddenly, and God was man, that he might have us in the future. But very many perish who think to please both — idols and God — when no one can please two. There is one God in heaven, of heaven, earth, and sea, whom Moses taught hung on the wood for us. From which indeed the idle err, that he suffered such things, not intent enough on God’s secret mystery. By the devil’s envy death entered the world, which God secretly destroyed, born of a virgin. By which birth the blind Jews are driven out of mind; bloodstained by crime committed, they make fools foolish. No one can speak any excuse afterward, when now the faculty of believing has been given us. God did not come to earth from heaven in vain, but came to make a people called by his name. If anyone will not have confessed him in this nature, he loses even what he lived, and late cries out into punishments; or certainly while he hopes, waiting to believe when gray, he is shut out a rich man from eternal life when dead. Therefore already we ought to turn back to him faster, who promises after death to give us life back. Besides this he adds, that we will be immortal and enjoy, by seeing, what the eye had not seen before. When six thousand years are filled, these things will come about — ****** Nothing-after-death is swine talk. One God hung on wood; virgin-born he broke death. Confess him now — gray delay can shut the door.

latin: Nec ibi permoritur, sed dat cruciatus iniquos. Sunt homines pecorum similes in ista natura, Qui nolunt accipere frenum Dei summi uagantes; Cum ipsi non durant seruorum talia ferre, In quorum saepe discendunt sanguine diri. Dicentes adiciunt: 'Nihil est post funera nostra; Dum uiuimus. hoc est'. et incumbunt more suillo; 'Nulla sit luxuria, quae nos pertranseat aeuo; Dum tempus est uitae, perfruamur omnia saecli.' Indisciplinati clementiam Dei refugant Strenia<s> sectantes, quasi sola uita sit ipsa. Sic re<ce>dunt a Deo, qui promittit uiuere semper: Contra bonum pugnant, cum sit repugnandum iniquo. Errauimus omnes manifesto, saeculo suasi, Sed gratia Domini prouocamur credere legi. Propterea uenit et fecit trophaea latenter Et fuit homo Deus, ut nos in futuro haberet. Sed plurimi pereunt, qui putant utrisque placere, Idolis atque Deo, placeat cum nemo duobus. Unus est in caelo Deus caeli, terrae marisque, Quem Moyses docuit ligno pependisse pro nobis. Unde quidem errant ignaui talia passum, Non satis intenti mysterio Dei secretum. Inuidia diaboli mors introiuit in orbem, Quam Deus occulte destruxit uirgine natus. Qua natiuitate excordantur caeci Iudaei, Infatuant stulto<s> scelere commisso cruenti. Nemo potest ullum excusamen dicere postquam, Cum modo sit nobis facultas data credendi. Non uenit in uano Deus in terris e caelo, Sed uenit, ut faceret populum suo nomine dictum. Quem si quis confessus non erit in ista natura, Perdit et quod uixit, et in poena<s> sero declamat; Aut certe dum sperat <ex>pectans credere canus, Excluditur diuius ab aeterna uita defunctus. Ergo iam ad illum citius recordari debemus, Qui nobis post obitum pollicetur reddere uitam. Insuper hoc addit, immortales esse futuros Et frui, quod oculus non uiderat ante, uidendo. Sex milibus annis prouenient ista repletis,

author: Commodian
english: At which time I hope we ourselves already at the harbor’s shore. Then man will rise, brought back in the sun’s struggle, and rejoices in God remembering what he was before; who, as he heard while fragile in former flesh, when he is incorrupt, recognizes the things promised before. Marveling that such glory has come to man he says thus: As I heard before, so I see each thing. These things all alike cry, lifted from hell: As we heard before, behold we see! All pain will yield from the body, and the sore will yield, nor will there be any anxiety except joys always. Whoever believes the Three and feels that One is present, this one will be perpetual, reborn into eternal ages. But some say this: When do we think these things will come? Take it in a few words, which things done, those follow. Many signs indeed will happen at the boundary of so great a plague, but the beginning will be our seventh persecution. Behold already it knocks at the door and is forced to be, which will soon cross over with Goths bursting across the river. King Apollyon will be with them, dreadful by name, who would scatter persecution of the saints in arms. He goes to Rome with many thousands of a nation and by God’s decree captures the partly subdued. Many of the senators then will weep captive and blaspheme the God of heaven, conquered by the barbarian. These nonetheless as gentiles feed Christians everywhere, whom rather as brothers they seek, full of joy. For the luxurious and those who worship empty idols they persecute and put the senate under the yoke. These evils they take who have persecuted the beloved: in five months they are slaughtered under that enemy. Meanwhile in that very time a Syrian rises, who would terrify the enemies and free the senate from there. He returns from the underworld, who had been commanded for the kingdom and long kept known with his former body. But we say this is the old Nero, who first punished Peter and Paul in the city. He himself returns again under that end of the age from hidden places, who was reserved for these things. The senate itself wonders that he is hated — ****** Raised bodies see what they only heard. Seventh persecution, Goths, Apollyon — then the reserved Nero at the age’s end.

latin: Quo tempore nos ipsos spero iam in litore portus. Tunc homo resurget solis in agone reductus Et gaudet in Deo reminiscens, quid fuit ante; Qui, sicut audiuit fragilis in pristina carne, Cum sit incorruptus, recognoscit ante promissa. Quam gloria<m> mirans homini prouenisse sic inquit: Qualiter audiui prius, sic singula cerno. Haec pariter omnes clamant ab inferno leuati: Quemadmodu<m> ante audiuimus, ecce uidemus! Cedet dolor omnis a corpore, cedet et ulcus, Nec erit anxietas ulla nisi gaudia semper. Quisque tribus credit et sentit unum adesse, Hic erit perpetuus in aeterna saecla renatus. Sed quidam hoc aiunt: Quando haec uentura putamus? Accipite paucis, quibus actis illa sequantur. Multa quidem signa fient tantae termini pesti, Sed erit initium septima persecutio nostra. Ecce <iam> ianua<m> pulsat et cogitur esse, Quae cito traiciet Gothis irrumpentibus amne. Rex Apollion erit cum ipsis, nomine dirus, Qui persecutionem dissipet sanctorum in armis. Pergit ad Romam cum multa milia gentis Decretoque Dei captiuat ex parte subactos. Multi senatorum tunc enim captiui deflebunt Et Deum caelorum blasphemant a barbaro uicti. Hi tamen gentiles pascunt Christianos ubique, Quos magis ut fratres requirunt gaudio pleni. Nam luxuriosos et idola uana colentes Persecuntur enim et senatum sub iugo mittunt. Haec mala percipiunt, qui sunt persecuti dilectos: Mensibus in quinque trucidantur isto sub hoste. Exsurgit interea sub ipso tempore Syrus, Qui terreat hostes et liberet inde senatum. Ex infero redit, qui fuerat regno praeceptus Et diu seruatus cum pristino corpore notus. Dicimus hunc autem Neronem esse uetustum, Qui Petrum et Paulum prius puniuit in urbem. Ipse redit iterum sub ipso saeculi fine[m] Ex locis apocryphis, qui fuit reseruatus in ista. Hunc ipse <se>natus inuisum esse mirantur;

author: Commodian
english: Who when he has appeared, they will think almost that he is a god. But before that one comes, Elijah will prophesy in a divided time, on the mid-axis of the week. When the span is complete that wicked one succeeds, whom Jews also then adore together with Romans. Although there will be another, whom they await from the east, in our slaughter nonetheless they will rage with king Nero. Therefore when Elijah prophesies in the Judean land and marks the people with a sign in Christ’s name; of whom since very many refuse to believe him, angry he begs the Most High that it not rain there: heaven will be shut from then and will not grow wet with dew; rivers too in anger he turns into blood. ****** Before the quasi-god: Elijah mid-week marks for Christ. Refuse him — shut sky, rivers of blood; Nero still joins the east-king slaughter.

latin: Qui cum apparuerit, quasi deum esse putabunt. Sed priusquam ille ueniat, prophetabit Helias Tempore partito, medio ebdomadis axe[m]. Completo spatio succedit ille nefandus, Quem et Iudaei simul tunc cum Romanis adorant. Quamquam erit alius, quem expectent ab oriente, In nostra caede tamen saeuient cum rege Nerone. Ergo cum Helias in Iudaea terra prophetat Et <signo> signat populum in nomine Christi; De quibus quam multi quoniam illi credere nolunt, Supplicat iratus Altissimum, ne pluat inde: Clausum erit caelum ex eo nec rore madescet, Flumina quoque iratus in sanguine uertit.

author: Commodian
english: That famine may invade, there will then also be plague on the globe. Because he does these things, the tortured Jews of course brew many false charges against him, and first inflame the senate to rise in anger and say Elijah is an enemy to the Romans. Then from there the senate, moved in a mass by them, beg Nero with prayers and unjust gifts: Remove the people’s enemies from human affairs, through whom our gods also are trampled and not worshiped. But he, filled with fury and the senate’s prayers, by public carriage snatches the prophets from the east. Who, that he may do enough for them or at least for the Jews, sacrifices these first and so goes out to the churches. Under their martyrdom a tenth part of the city collapses and seven full thousand people perish there. But the Lord on the fourth day lifts those into the airs, whom they had forbidden to be placed in burial as they lay, and they are raised from the soil made immortal from death, whom their enemies look up to going through the airs. Terrified they are not even so, but more they grow raw inside, cursing the people of Christ with whole hatred. For the Most High hardened the wicked hearts, as formerly he had hardened Pharaoh’s ears. This hard and unjust king then, Nero driven out, orders the Christian people expelled from the city itself, and adds two Caesars as partners to himself, with whom he may persecute this people in dire fury. They also send edicts through all judges everywhere, that they make this race of humans without Christ’s name. They command too that incense be set to images and, lest anyone hide, that all come forth crowned. In that history if a faithful one refused to go, he exits happily: but if not, from the crowd he becomes one. No day of peace will then be, nor offering to Christ, but gore flows everywhere, which I am overcome to describe; for tears win, the hand fails, hearts tremble, although it is fit for martyrs to bear so many funerals; over sea, over lands, over islands and hiding-places he searches long, and they lead the cursed as victims. These things Nero will then do for a whole three-year time ****** Senate buys Elijah’s death; Nero hits the churches; tenth of the city falls; on day four the witnesses rise — then three years without Christ’s name.

latin: Ut famis inuadat, erit tunc et lues in orbe. Ista quia faciat, cruciati nempe Iudaei Multa aduersus eum conflant in crimina falsa, Incenduntque prius senatum consurgere in ira Et dicunt Heliam inimicum esse Romanis. Tunc inde confertim motus senatus ab illis Exorant Neronem precibus et donis iniquis: Tolle inimicos populi de rebus humanis Per quos et dii nostri conculcantur neque coluntur. At ille suppletus furia precibusque senatus Uehiculo publico rapit ab oriente prophetas. Qui satis ut faciat illis uel certe Iudaeis, Immolat hos primum et sic ad ecclesias exit. Sub quorum martyrio decima pars corruit urbis Et pereunt ibi homines septem milia plena. Illos autem Dominus quarto die tollit in auras, Quos illi uetuerant sepulturae condi iacentes Suscita<n>turque solo immortales facti de morte, Quos inimici sui suspiciunt ire per auras. Territi nec sic sunt, sed magis intra crudescunt Ad populum Christi execrantes odio toto. Indurauit enim Altissimus corda nefanda, Sicut Pharaoni prius indurauerat aures. Hic ergo rex durus et iniquus, Nero fugatus, Pelli iubet populum Christianum ipsa de urbe, Participes autem duo<s> sibi Caesares addit, Cum quibus hunc populum persequatur diro furore. Mittunt et edicta per iudices omnes ubique, Ut genus hoc hominum faciant sine nomine Christi. Praecipiunt quoque simulacris tura ponenda Et, ne quis lateat, omnes coronati procedant. In ista historia si fidelis ire negauit, Feliciter exit: sin uero, de turba fit unus. Nulla dies pacis tunc erit nec oblatio Christo, Sed cruor ubique manat, quem describere uincor; Uincunt enim lacrimae, deficit manus, corda tremescunt, Quamquam sit martyribus aptum tot funera ferre; Per mare, per terras, per insolas atque latebras Scrutaturque diu, exsecratos uictima ducunt. Haec Nero tunc faciet, triennii tempore toto

author: Commodian
english: And with a half year he completes the fixed times. For whose crime a deadly vengeance will come, so that the city’s people too with him himself be handed over, the empire be taken away, which was unjustly filled, which by evil tributes long was wasting all. There rises again in this disaster of Nero a king toward the east with four nations from there, and invites to himself how many nations to the city, who would bring help, though he himself is strongest, and he will fill the sea with ships with many thousands, and if anyone meets him, he will be slaughtered by the sword; and he first captures Tyre and Sidon subdued, for from there neighboring nations fail with terror. From here plague, from here wars, from here famine, from here hard tidings are mixed together, whereby confusion of mind may happen. Meanwhile a trumpet gives a roar from heaven suddenly, whose sound in every place disturbs the heart. There will be seen then also a fiery chariot through the stars and a torch running, that it may announce fire to the nations. At last the river Euphrates is dried up wholly, that a road be prepared for the king with those nations. Persians, Medes together, Chaldeans, Babylonians will come, fierce and quick, who would know pain for none. This one therefore rising when he has begun to come from there, Nero is troubled and the senate at the sight near. And those three Caesars will go to resist against; whom that one, slaughtered, gives to the birds for food. Their army must adore the victor, and when returning in the city with changed mind they spoil temples and whatever is inside in the city, they plunder and slaughter men with huge gore; last they drive her made naked to burning, so that not even her trace appear further. At whose exit the hearts of the powerful waste away nor do they find themselves, in what time they are, senseless. These things indeed she was rejoicing, but the whole earth was groaning; yet scarcely has a worthy repayment found her. She mourns forever, who was boasting herself eternal, whose tyrants also then are judged by the Highest. The time stands ripe toward the end with Rome smoking — ****** Half-year seals Nero’s crime-span. East-king dries Euphrates; three Caesars become bird-food; naked Rome burns — the ‘eternal’ city mourns.

latin: Et anno dimidio statuta tempora complet. Pro cuius facinore ueniet uindicta letalis, Ut urbis et populus ille cum ipso tradatur, Tollatur imperium, quod fuit inique repletum, Quod per tributa mala diu macerabat omnes. Exurgit iterum in istius clade Neronis Rex ad oriente<m> cum quattuor gentibus inde, Inuitatque sibi quam multas gentes ad urbem, Qui ferant auxilium, licet sit fortissimus ipse, Implebitque mare nauibus cum milia multa, Et si quis occurrerit illi, mactabitur ense; Captiuatque prius Tyrum et Sidona subactas, Nam inde finitimas gentes terrore fatiscunt. Hinc lues, hinc bella, hinc fames, hinc nuntia dura Miscenturque simul, quo fiat turbatio mentis. Interea fremitum dat tuba de caelo repente, Cuius omni loco sonitus praecordia turbat. Uidebitur et tunc igne quadriga per astra Et facula currens, nuntiet ut gentibus ignem. Siccatur fluuius Euphrates denique totus, Ut uia paretur regi cum gentibus illis. Persae, Medi simul Caldaei, Babyloni uenibunt, Immites et agiles, qui nesciant ulli dolore<m> Hic ergo exoriens cum coeperit inde uenire, Turbaturque Nero et senatus proxime uisum. Cuius in exitio tabescunt corda potentium Nec se adinueniunt, in quo sin<t> tempore, bruti. Haec quidem gaudebat, sed tota terra gemebat; Uix tamen adinuenit illi retributio digna. Luget in aeternum, quae se iactabat aeterna, Cuius et tyranni iam tunc iudicantur a Summo. Stat tempus in finem fumante Roma maturum,

author: Commodian
english: And wages will arrive parted by deserts of places. From there nonetheless the victor proceeds into the Judean land, whom the Jews themselves expect to conquer Rome. He makes many signs, that they may be able to believe him, since the unjust one is sent to seduce them; whom nonetheless a voice returned from heaven of the Highest rebukes. A man from Persia says that he himself is immortal. To us Nero has become Antichrist, that one to the Jews; these two always are prophets at the last end. The city’s ruin is Nero, this one’s the whole earth’s; about whom nonetheless I offer a few things that I have read secret. Meanwhile he displeases the Jews too late even themselves, and they whisper together that they have been deceived by fraud. They cry alike to heaven with weeping voice; then God almighty, that he may end all things I have said, will bring forth a people hidden for a long time. But there are Jews shut beyond Persia by a river, whom God willed to stay there even to the end. Captivity drove them there that they might be; from the twelve tribes nine and a half stay there. There is no lie there, nor is there any hatred; therefore neither does a son die before his parents; nor do they mourn the dead nor grieve in our manner, since they await the resurrection to come; they feed on no soul with added foods, but only herbs, which may be without blood poured. Full of justice they live with unstained body; in them neither does an impious birth exercise forces. Fevers do not approach them, nor savage colds, since they obey all things of the law brightly; which we too ourselves will follow living purely; death only was present and toil, for the rest were mute. This was the people that now is stored away outside. With the river dried he will seek again into the Judean land; with them God also will come to fill promises; who through the whole journey exults with God present. All things grow green before them, all things rejoice; creation itself is glad to receive the holy: in every place springs rise ready to be, where the people of the Highest walks with heavenly awe. ****** Two end-liars: Nero for us, the Persian wonder for the Jews. God then leads out the sealed, bloodless, law-bright people from beyond the river.

latin: Et merces aduenient meritis partita locorum. Inde tamen pergit uictor in terra Iudaea, Quem ipsi Iudaei expectant uincere Roma<m> Multa signa facit, ut illi credere possint, Ad seducendos eos quoniam est missus iniquus; Quem tamen e caelo increpat uox reddita Summi. De Persida homo immortalem esse se dicit. Nobis Nero factus Antichristus, ille Iudaeis; Isti duo semper prophetae sunt in ultima fine. Urbis perditio Nero est, hic terrae totius; De quo pauca tamen suggero, quae legi secreta. Displicet interea iam sero Iudaeis et ipsis, Susurrantque simul, quoniam sint fraude decepti. Exclamant pariter ad caelum uoce deflentes, Tunc Deus omnipotens, terminet ut cuncta, quae dixi, Producet populum celatum tempore multo. Sunt autem Iudaei trans Persida flumine clausi, Quos usque in finem uoluit Deus ibi morari. Captiuitas illos ibidem redegit ut essent; Ex duodena tribu noue<m> semis ibi morantur. Mendacium ibi non est, sed nec est odium ullum; Idcirco nec moritur filius suus ante parentes; Nec mortuos plangunt nec lugunt more de nostro, Expectant quoniam resurrectionemque futuram, Non animam ullam uescuntur additis escis, Sed olera tantum, quod sit sine sanguine fuso. Iustitia pleni illibato corpore uiuunt, In illis nec genesis exercit impia uires. Non febres accedunt in illis, non frigora saeua, Obtemperant quoniam uniuersa candide legis; Quae nos et ipsi sequemur pure uiuentes; Mors tantum aderat et labor, nam cetera surda. Hic erat populus, qui nunc est extra repositus. Siccato fluuio repetet in terra Iudaea; Cum ipsis et Deus ueniet implere promissa; Qui per totum iter exultat Deo praesente. Omnia uirescunt ante illos, omnia gaudent, Excipere sanctos ipsa creatura laetatur: Omni loco fontes exurgunt esse parati, Qua graditur populus Summi cum terrore caelesti.

author: Commodian
english: Clouds make them a shade, lest they be vexed by the sun, and lest they tire, the mountains themselves also lay themselves under; for an angel of the High One will be sent ahead of them, who may offer them a peaceful lead while going. These without toil walk lightly as they go and like lions, where they pass, lay waste all things. Nor will any legion indeed be able to resist against, if it brings war, since God himself is with them. They storm nations, cities too they cast down; by God’s permission they strip all colonies, and are enriched with gold or silver by plundering, and so honored they chant hymns alike. Soon however they hasten to the holy paternal city; for that terrible tyrant grows afraid and flees to the kings of the North with great stir, from where he snatches a people, that he may stand as if fighting back. When however the rebels hasten against God’s army they are strewn on the soil by angels when battle is done, and the caught adulterer of that one and the false prophet are sent into the pool under fiery punishment living. And their chiefs, officers or envoys, in the place of slaves the unjust are reduced to the holy. Meanwhile the holy enter into the holy colony who may take God’s promises rejoicing without end. They beg God for the dead that they may rise, which he himself promised once about the first rising. God will begin already then to be angry at enemies, and the fixed day since it has come for the unjust. When however he has begun to judge the world by fire, he avoids the pious and fire falls over the impious. Scarcely a few remain, who may report such deeds, and who are reserved, that they may serve the just, escape. After the persecution of the saints and so many funerals it hangs that the hateful day may come, burning. Behold it sings from heaven hoarse, but everywhere echoing, which frightens the whole orb falling in ruin. The sun flees carelessly, suddenly an image of night happens, and God cries out: How long did you think to bear me? At whose sign given plague rushes from the whole ether; with the crash of thunder the charge of fire descends. ****** Cloud-led saints take the city; beast and false prophet go living into the fiery pool; first rising; then the world-fire day.

Mox autem properant sanctae ciuitati paternae, Expauescit enim terribilis ille tyrannus Et fugit ad reges Boreae cum concitu magno, Unde rapit populum, ut stet quasi contra <re>pugna<n>s. Cum properant autem exercitu Dei rebelles Sternunturque solo ab angelis proelio facto <Et prensus ad>ulter ipsius et pseudopropheta Mittunt<ur in stagnum sub i>gnea p<o>ena uiuentes. Quorumque pri<m>ores, praeposit<i> siue legati, In loco seruorum rediguntur sancti<s> iniqui. Interea sancti intrant in colonia sancta Qui Dei promissa capiant sine fine laetantes. Exorant Deum pro mortuis uti resurgant, Quod ipse promisit olim de anastasi prima. Incipiet Deus iam tunc inimicis irasci, Statu<tu>sque dies quoniam aduenit iniquis. Cum coeperit autem mundum iudicare per ignem, Deuitatque pios et cadit super impios ignis. Uix remanent pauci, qui referant talia facta, Et qui reseruantur, ut seruiant iustis, euadunt. Post persecutione<m> sanctorum et funera tanta Imminet ut ueniat dies detestabilis, ardens. Ecce canit caelo rauca, sed ubique resultans, Quae pauida<t> totum orbem in ruina cadentem. Sol fugit incaute, subito fit noctis imago, Et Deus exclamat: Quamdiu me ferre putasti? Cuius signo dato pestis ruit aethere toto, Cum strepitu tonitrui discendit impetus ignis.

author: Commodian
english: Then another and another bolt is cast from the stars; a fiery storm flees, reserved so many years; pestilent disaster roars, the stirred earth trembles, nor does every human race foresee where it may turn itself. Stars of heaven fall, the stars are judged with us: the heaven-dwellers are troubled while the age’s ruin is driven. No help then will there be and empty cry; no ship will take a human, nor any hiding-place; nor do those help them whom before they cultivated for a great one: each busies himself for himself, but nothing profits him; for these only will it profit, who have been marked for Christ; dew will be for them, for the rest lethal punishment. A part of the unbelieving is kept softly burned, that their race again at the last may wail. Wherever humans turn, fiery force boils; the air itself of the world, which pleased before, is burned. What shall I say of heaven’s crashes pressing with bolt, when all wrath collected for so many years is poured? From here fire, from here thunders, from here whirlwinds, so many evils, boil, and the pole is snatched by sudden force of death into shade. Partly the trembling earth loosens foundations… partly thunders burst firm walls; and walls are scattered like dust into the airs; rocks fly, roofs of houses tremble with winds. Homelands are laid waste, every city is cast down … that heaven may hand over by a footstep. So many crashes, so many breakings and so many ruins — who will be able to bear or flee such shipwrecks? What will a wretched mother do then for a sweet little one? But if a father pities a son, what profits him? Woe to the Lord’s runaways, woe also to the Christless wicked, whose even glad ones are judged while the pious weep! Meanwhile all nature wails with bellowings until at last the completed heavenly fury ceases. Then for seven months the earth will be cleaned through fire and he who was humble coming from heaven is seen. With him angels of eternal brightness descend; tombs too are burst, just bodies rise; which clouds snatch and carry to meet Christ in the air; the living holy receive the Lord. He raises those also, that they may see his glory, whom they fixed on a cross; but again he will return them in the depths. Woe to those miserable ones! The witness is the one killed by them. … These things we sing not from envy, but we see them fixed. When the just rejoice, those burn in hell; David said to them: Lord, return unjust things to them! And if they will not have believed, they will have in the shadow of death. … From two peoples flees the Highest’s … this greater will make them be changed for him quickly. Amen. ****** Stars fall with us; only the Christ-marked get dew. Seven months’ fire; the humble comes; tombs burst to meet him — cross-fixers see, then sink.

latin: Tunc aliud atque aliud fulmen iactatur ab astris, Ignea tempesta fugit reseruata tot annis, Rugit pestifera clades, tremit excita tellus, Nec, quo se auertat, prouidet gens omnis humana. Stellae cadunt caeli, iudicantur astra nobiscum: Turbantur caelicolae, agitur dum saecli ruina. Suppetium nullum tunc erit et clamor inanis; Non nauis accipiet hominem, non ulla latebra; Nec illi subueniunt, quos ante pro magno colebant: Quisque sibi satagit, sed nihil proficit illi; His tantum proficiet, qui fuerint Christo notati; Ros ad illos erit, nam ceteris poena letalis. Pars incredulorum seruatur molliter usta, Ut genus ipsorum iterum se in ultimo plangat. Quocumque se uertunt homines, uis ignea feruit; Aer ipse mundi, qui placebat ante, crematur. Quod strepitus caeli ingruentes fulmine dicam, Cum ira tot annis collecta funditur omnis? Hinc ignis, hinc tonitrua, hinc turbines, tot mala, feruunt, Raptaturque polus subi<ta> ui mortis in umbram. Partim terra tremens laxat fu<ndamenta...> <Par>tim tonitrua disrumpunt moenia firma; <Atque disturbantur m>uri sicut puluis in auras; Saxa uolant, uen<tis tremescunt> tecta domorum. Uastantur patriae, prosternitur ciuitas omnis .......t ........os caelum uestigio tradat. Tot crepitus, tantos fragores t<otque> ruinas Quis po<te>rit ferre aut na<u>fragia tanta <fugire>? Quid misera mater faciet tunc paruolo dulci? At si pater natum piet, quid proficit illi? Uae refugis Domini, uae et sine Christo n<e>fa<n>dis, Quorum et laeta<n>tes iudicantur pie flentes! Pla<ngit in>terea mugitibus tota natura Donec cesset furia <tandem comp>leta caelestis. Tunc mensibus septem remundabitur terra per ignem Et qui f<uit> humilis ueniens de caelo uidetur. Cum illo descendunt angeli claritatis aeternae, Rumpun<tur> et tumuli, exurgunt corpora iusta; Quae rapiunt nubes et portant <obui>a<m Ch>risto In a<e>ra, Dominum excipiunt sancti uiuentes. Suscitat e<t> illos, ut uideant gloriam eius, Quem cruce fixerunt; sed denuo reddet in imis. Uae miser<is> illis! Testis est necatus ab illis. Quod poenis ipsorum prouidi dolo t..mus istic Haec non de inuidia canimus, sed fixa uidemus. Cum iusti laetantur, <il>li in inferno cremantur; Dau<id> illis dixit: Domine, redde ill<is> iniqua! Et si non crediderint, in umbra mortis habebunt. <H>ic utique poterat plebi suae laeta precari Cur <magis op>tauit: Discendant uiu<i> deorsum Ceteri qui fuera<n>t in aduentum Christi de sanctis? De duobus populis fugit i<..>gia Su<mmi> ... haec maior faciet immutentur ei cito. amen.

author: Novatian
english: IX. 1. The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, also in the Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord God — yet the Son of God, of this God who is both one and alone, namely the founder of all things, as has already been set out above. 2. For this Jesus Christ, I say again the Son of this God, we read promised in the Old Testament and we observe exhibited in the New Testament, filling the shadows and figures of all the sacraments by the presence of embodied truth. 3. For him Abraham’s son, him David’s, him the old predictions and the Gospels alike testify. 4. Him Genesis itself, when it says: To you and to your seed I will give; him, when it shows a man wrestling with Jacob; him, when it says: A prince shall not fail from Judah nor a leader from his thighs until he comes to whom it is promised, and he himself will be the expectation of the nations. 5. Him Moses, when he says: Provide another whom you may send; him the same, when he witnesses: A prophet, he says, God will raise up for you from your brothers; hear him as me; him, when he says: You will see your life hanging night and day and will not believe him. 6. Him Isaiah: A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse and a flower will rise from the root; him the same, when he says: Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son; him, when he places healings to come from him, saying: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame will leap like a deer and the tongue of the mute will be free; him, when he unfolds the virtues of patience, saying: His voice will not be heard in the streets; he will not crush a bruised reed and will not quench smoking flax.

7. Him, when he described his gospels: And I will arrange for you an everlasting covenant, the faithful holy things of David; him, when he prophesies nations that will believe in him: Behold, I have set him as a prince and a commander for the nations. Nations that have not known you will call on you, and peoples that do not know you will flee to you; him the same, when he cries out to his passion, saying: Like a sheep he was led to slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer without voice, so he did not open his mouth in humility. 8. Him, when he described the blows of his scourges and wounds: By his bruise we were healed; or the humility: And we saw him and he had no appearance or honor; a man in plague and knowing how to bear weakness; or that the people would not believe: All day I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people; or that he would rise from the dead: And in that day there will be the root of Jesse and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope and his rest will be honor; or when the time of resurrection: As at dawn we will find him prepared; or that he would sit at the Father’s right hand: The Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand until I put your enemies as a footstool for your feet; or when he is set as owner of all: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession the ends of the earth; or that he is shown judge of all: God, give your judgment to the king and your justice to the King’s Son. 9. Nor will I pursue more in this place, which things announced about Christ are better known to all heretics, but also to those who hold the truth themselves.
translator_notes: De Trinitate IX: regula ueritatis; Filium Dominum Deum; expectatio gentium; liuore sanati.
latin: IX. 1. Eadem regula ueritatis docet nos credere post Patrem etiam in Filium Dei Christum Iesum Dominum Deum nostrum, sed Dei Filium, huius Dei qui et unus et solus est, conditor scilicet rerum omnium, ut iam et superius expressum est. 2. Hunc enim Iesum Christum, iterum dicam huius Dei Filium, et in ueteri testamento legimus esse repromissum et in nouo testamento animaduertimus exhibitum, omnium sacramentorum umbras et figuras de praesentia corporatae ueritatis implentem. 3. Hunc enim Abrahae filium, hunc Dauid, hunc non minus et uetera praedicta et euangelia testantur. 4. Hunc ipsa Genesis, cum dicit: Tibi dabo et semini tuo, hunc, quando luctatum ostendit hominem cum Iacob, hunc, quando dicit: Non deficiet princeps de Iuda neque dux de femoribus eius, donec ueniat is cui repromissum est, et ipse erit expectatio gentium. 5. Hunc Moyses, cum dicit: Prouide alium quem mittas, hunc idem, quando testatur: Propheten uobis, dicendo, suscitabit Deus ex fratribus uestris; eum quasi me audite, hunc, quando dicit: Videbitis uitam uestram pendentem nocte ac die et non credetis ei. 6. Hunc Esaias: Prodiet uirga de radice Iesse et flos de radice ascendet, hunc eundem, quando dicit: Ecce uirgo concipiet et pariet filium, hunc, quando sanitates ab eo futuras collocat dicens: Tunc aperientur oculi caecorum et aures surdorum audient, tunc saliet claudus ut ceruus et diserta erit lingua mutorum, hunc, quando patientiae uirtutes expromit dicens: Non audietur in plateis uox eius; arundinem quassatam non conteret et linum fumigans non exstinguet.

7. Hunc, quando eius euangelia descripsit: Et disponam uobis testamentum aeternum, sancta Dauid fidelia, hunc, quando gentes in ipsum credituras prophetat: Ecce posui eum in principem et praecipientem gentibus. Gentes quae te non nouerunt inuocabunt te et populi qui te nesciunt ad te confugient, hunc eundem, quando ad passionem eius exclamat dicens: Sicut ouis ad occisionem ductus est et sicut agnus coram tondente se sine uoce, sic non aperuit os suum in humilitate. 8. Hunc, quando flagrorum eius ictus plagasque descripsit: Liuore eius nos sanati sumus, aut humilitatem: Et uidimus eum et non erat ei species neque honor; homo in plaga et sciens ferre infirmitatem, aut quod populus non erat crediturus: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem, aut quod resurrecturus a mortuis: Et erit in illa die radix Iesse et qui surget imperare gentibus; in eum gentes sperabunt et erit requies eius honor, aut cum tempus resurrectionis: Quasi diluculo paratum inueniemus eum, aut quod sessurus ad dexteram Patris: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: sede ad dexteram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum, aut cum possessor omnium collocatur: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam et possessionem tuam terminos terrae, aut quod iudex omnium ostenditur: Deus, iudicium tuum regi da et iustitiam tuam Filio Regis. 9. Nec hoc in loco plura persequar, quae annuntiata de Christo omnibus haereticis, sed et ipsis ueritatem tenentibus magis nota sunt.

author: Novatian
english: XIV. 1. And yet the heretic still doubts to call Christ God, whom he notices approved as God by so many deeds and voices. 2. If Christ is man only, how is it that coming into this world he came unto his own, when a man has made no world? 3. If Christ is man only, how is the world reported made through him, when the world is not reported made through a man, but man instituted after the world? 4. If Christ is man only, how is Christ not from David’s seed only, but the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us? For although the first-formed was not from seed, yet the first-formed is not compacted from a joining of Word and flesh. For it is not that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us [in Adam]. 5. If Christ is man only, how does he who comes from heaven testify what he has seen and heard, when it is settled that a man cannot come from heaven, because he cannot be born there? 6. If Christ is man only, how are visibles and invisibles, thrones, powers and dominions reported created through him and in him, when heavenly powers could not have been made through a man, which ought to have existed before man himself? 7. If Christ is man only, how is he present everywhere when invoked, when this is not man’s nature but God’s, that he can be present in every place? 8. If Christ is man only, why is a man invoked as mediator in prayers, when invocation of a man is judged ineffective for granting salvation? 9. If Christ is man only, why is hope placed in him, when hope in man is reported cursed? 10. If Christ is man only, why may Christ not be denied without destruction of the soul, when a fault committed against a man is reported able to be forgiven?

11. If Christ is man only, how does John the Baptist testify and say: he who comes after me has been made before me, because he was prior to me — when if Christ is man only, born after John he cannot be before John, unless because, insofar as he is God, he preceded him beforehand? 12. If Christ is man only, how does whatever the Father does the Son also do likewise, when a man cannot do works like God’s heavenly works? 13. If Christ is man only, how, as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself, when by the Father God’s example a man cannot have life in himself, since he is not glorious in eternity but made in the stuff of mortality? 14. If Christ is man only, how does he report: I am the bread of eternal life who came down from heaven — when a man can neither be the bread of life, being himself mortal, nor have come down from heaven, no stuff of frailty being set in heaven? 15. If Christ is man only, how does he say that no one has ever seen God the Father except he who is from God — this one has seen God? Because if Christ is man only, he could not have seen God, since no one among men has seen God. But if, while he is from God, he has seen God, he wished to be understood as more than man while he saw God. 16. If Christ is man only, why does he say: What if you see the Son of Man ascending there where he was before? But he ascended into heaven. Therefore he was there, while he returns there where he was before. 17. But if he was sent from heaven by the Father, he is not man only; for a man, as we have said, could not come from heaven. Therefore man was not there before, but he ascended there where he was not. But the Word of God descended, which was there — the Word of God, I say, and God through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. Therefore man did not thus come from the heavens from there, but the speech of God, that is God, descended from there.
translator_notes: De Trinitate XIV: non homo tantum; uerbum caro; panis uitae; Dei sermo descendit.
latin: XIV. 1. Et tamen adhuc dubitat haereticus Christum dicere esse Deum, quem Deum tot et rebus animaduertit et uocibus approbatum. 2. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ueniens in hunc mundum in sua uenit, cum homo nullum fecerit mundum? 3. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo mundus per ipsum factus esse refertur, cum non per hominem mundus, sed post mundum homo institutus referatur? 4. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo non ex semine tantum Dauid Christus, sed uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis? Nam etsi protoplastus non ex semine, sed tamen protoplastus non est ex uerbi et carnis coniunctione concretus. Non est enim uerbum caro factum, et habitauit in nobis. 5. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo qui de caelo uenit, quae uidit et audit testificatur, cum constet hominem de caelo, quia ibi nasci non possit, uenire non posse? 6. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo uisibilia et inuisibilia, throni, uirtutes et dominationes per ipsum et in ipso creata esse referuntur, cum uirtutes caelestes per hominem fieri non potuerint, quae ante hominem ipsum esse debuerint? 7. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo adest ubique inuocatus, cum haec hominis natura non sit, sed Dei, ut adesse omni loco possit? 8. Si homo tantummodo Christus, cur homo in orationibus mediator inuocatur, cum inuocatio hominis ad praestandam salutem inefficax iudicetur? 9. Si homo tantummodo Christus, cur spes in illum ponitur, cum spes in homine maledicta referatur? 10. Si homo tantummodo Christus, cur non licet Christum sine exitio animae negari, cum in hominem commissum delictum referatur posse dimitti?

11. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo Ioannes Baptista testatur et dicit: qui post me uenit, ante me factus est, quia prior me fuit, cum si homo tantummodo Christus, post Ioannem natus ante Ioannem esse non possit, nisi quoniam illum, qua Deus est, ante praecessit? 12. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo quae Pater facit, et Filius facit similiter, cum homo caelestibus operibus Dei similia opera facere non possit? 13. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo sicut Pater in se uitam habet, ita dedit Filio uitam habere in semetipso, cum exemplo Patris Dei homo in se uitam habere non possit, cum non in aeternitate sit gloriosus, sed in materia mortalitatis effectus? 14. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo refert: Ego sum panis uitae aeternae qui de caelo descendi, cum neque panis uitae homo esse possit ipse mortalis nec de caelo descenderit nulla in caelo constituta materia fragilitatis? 15. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit quia Patrem Deum nemo uidit umquam, nisi qui est a Deo, hic uidit Deum? Quoniam si homo tantummodo Christus, Deum uidere non potuit, quia Deum nemo hominum uidit. Si autem dum ex Deo est, Deum uidit, plus se quam hominem, dum Deum uidit, intellegi uoluit. 16. Si homo tantummodo Christus, cur dicit: Quid si uideritis Filium hominis ascendentem illuc ubi ante erat? Ascendit autem in caelum. Ibi ergo fuit, dum illuc redit ubi prius fuit. 17. Quodsi de caelo missus a Patre est, non utique homo tantum est; homo enim, ut diximus, de caelo uenire non potuit. Non igitur ibi ante homo fuit, sed illuc ascendit ubi non fuit. Descendit autem Dei uerbum, quod ibi fuit, uerbum, inquam, Dei et Deus per quem facta sunt omnia et sine quo factum est nihil. Non igitur homo inde sic de caelis uenit, sed Dei sermo, id est Deus, inde descendit.

author: Novatian
english: XV. 1. If Christ is man only, how does he say: Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true; because I know where I came from and where I am going; you judge according to the flesh? See, here too he says he will return there whence he testifies he came before, sent namely from heaven. He therefore descended whence he came, just as he goes there whence he descended. From which, if Christ were man only, he would not have come from there; and therefore he would not go there, because he would not have come from there. But by coming from there, whence a man cannot come, he showed that he came as God. 2. But the Jews, ignorant and unskilled about this very descent, made these heretics their heirs, to whom it is said: You do not know where I come from and where I am going; you judge according to the flesh. Both these and the Jews, holding Christ’s birth to be only fleshly, believed Christ to be nothing other than man, not considering that, since a man could not come from heaven so as to be able deservedly to return there, he who descended from there, whence a man could not come, is God. 3. If Christ is man only, how does he say: You are from below, I am from above; you are of this world, I am not of this world? Therefore, if every man is of this world and therefore Christ is in this world, is he man only? Far from it. But consider what he says: I am not of this world. Does he then lie, since he would be of this world if he were man only? Or if he does not lie, he is not of this world. Therefore he is not man only, because he is not of this world. 4. But lest who he was should be hidden, he expressed whence he was: I, he says, am from above, that is from heaven, whence a man cannot come; for he was not made in heaven. He is therefore God who is from above and for that reason is not of this world. Although in a certain way he is also of this world. Whence Christ is not God only, but also man. So that, as he is not of this world according to the Word’s divinity, so he is of this world according to the frailty of the body he took; for man is joined with God and God coupled with man. 5. But for this reason Christ here leaned into the one part of divinity alone, because Jewish blindness looked only at the flesh part in Christ, and so in the present place, with the body’s frailty which is of the world passed over in silence, he spoke only of his divinity, which is not of the world, so that as far as they had leaned to believe him man only, so far Christ could draw them to consider his divinity, that they might believe him God, wanting to overcome their unbelief about his divinity by opposing divinity alone for the time being, with mention of the human lot omitted. 6. If Christ is man only, how does he say: I came forth from God and have come, when it is settled that man was made by God, not that he proceeded from God? But as man did not proceed from God, so God’s Word proceeded, of which it was said: My heart has belched a good word, which, because it is from God, is deservedly also with God, and which, because it was not brought forth idle, deservedly makes all things. For all things were made through him and without him nothing was made. But this Word, through which all things were made, is God. And God, it says, was the Word. God therefore proceeded from God, while the Word that proceeded is God who proceeded from God.

7. If Christ is man only, how does he say: If anyone keeps my word, he will not see death forever? Not to see death forever — what else is that than immortality? But immortality is companion to divinity, because divinity is immortal and immortality is divinity’s fruit. But every man is mortal, and immortality cannot be from what is mortal. Therefore immortality cannot be born from a mortal man Christ. But he who keeps my word, he says, will not see death forever. Therefore Christ’s word grants immortality and through immortality grants divinity. But if he himself mortal cannot bring it about that he make another immortal, yet this word of Christ both brings about and grants immortality, he who grants immortality is not man only — which, if he were man only, he could not grant; but by granting divinity through immortality he proves himself God by extending divinity, which, unless he were God, he could not grant. 8. If Christ is man only, how does he say: Before Abraham I am? For no man can be before him from whom he himself is, nor can it happen that anything was earlier before that from which it itself took origin. But Christ, though from Abraham, says he is before Abraham. Either he lies and deceives, then, if he who was from Abraham was not before Abraham, or he does not deceive if he is also God, while he was before Abraham. Which, unless he had been, he consequently could not, though from Abraham, be before Abraham. 9. If Christ is man only, how does he say: And I know them and my own follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish forever? But since every man is bound by mortality’s laws and therefore cannot preserve even himself forever, much less will he be able to preserve another forever. Yet Christ promises he will give salvation forever. Which if he does not give, he is a liar; if he gives, he is God. But he does not deceive, for he gives what he promises. He is therefore God, who extends perpetual salvation, which a man, who cannot preserve himself, will not be able to grant to another. 10. If Christ is man only, what is it that he says: I and the Father are one? For how are I and the Father one, if he is not both God and Son, who can for that reason be called one, while he is from him and while he is his Son and while he is born from him, while he is found to have proceeded from him, through which he is also God? 11. When the Jews thought this invidious and believed it blasphemous because by these words he had shown Christ to be God and therefore had run to stones and longed to cast rock-blows, he strongly refuted his adversaries by the example and testimony of the Scriptures. If it called them gods, he says, to whom the word was made, and Scripture cannot be dissolved: do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world that you blaspheme, because I said: I am the Son of God? 12. By which words he neither denied himself God; rather he confirmed that he is God. For because without doubt those to whom the word was made are said to be gods, much more is this one God who is found better than all of them. And nonetheless he fittingly refuted the false charge of blasphemy by a lawful arrangement. For he wants himself understood as God in such a way that he wished to be understood as the Son of God and not the Father himself. For he said he had been sent and showed he had displayed many works from the Father, from which he wished to be understood not as the Father but as the Son, and in the last part of the defense he made mention of the Son, not the Father, saying: You say that I blaspheme, because I said: I am the Son of God? 13. So as concerns the charge of blasphemy, he says he is Son, not Father; but as concerns his own divinity, by saying I and the Father are one he proved himself both Son and God. He is therefore God — but God in such a way that he is Son, not Father.
translator_notes: De Trinitate XV: de sursum; uerbum Deus; immortalitas; ante Abraham; ego et Pater unum.
latin: XV. 1. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: Etsi ego de me testificor, uerum est testimonium meum; quia scio unde uenerim et quo eam, uos secundum carnem iudicatis? Ecce et hic illuc se dicit rediturum, unde se testificatur ante uenisse, missum scilicet de caelo. Descendit ergo unde uenit, quomodo illuc uadit unde descendit. Ex quo si homo tantummodo Christus esset, non inde uenisset; atque ideo nec illuc abiret, quoniam non inde uenisset. Veniendo autem inde, unde homo uenire non potest, Deum se ostendit uenisse. 2. Sed enim huius ipsius descensionis ignari et imperiti Iudaei heredes sibi haereticos istos reddiderunt, quibus dicitur: Vos ignoratis unde ueniam et quo eam: uos secundum carnem iudicatis. Tam isti quam Iudaei carnalem solam esse Christi natiuitatem tenentes nihil aliud Christum esse quam hominem crediderunt, non considerantes illud, quoniam [,cum] de caelo homo non potuerit uenire, ut merito illuc posset redire, Deum esse qui inde descenderit, unde homo uenire non potuerit. 3. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: Vos ex inferioribus estis, ego de sursum sum; uos de hoc mundo estis, ego non sum de hoc mundo? Ideo autem si omnis homo ex hoc mundo est et ideo in hoc mundo est Christus, an homo tantummodo est? Absit. Sed considera quod ait: Ego non sum de hoc mundo. Numquid ergo mentitur, cum ex hoc mundo sit, si homo tantummodo sit? Aut si non mentitur, non est ex hoc mundo. Non ergo homo tantummodo est, quia ex hoc mundo non est. 4. Sed ne lateret, quis esset, expressit unde esset: Ego, inquit, de sursum sum, hoc est de caelo, unde homo uenire non potest; non enim in caelo factus est. Deus est ergo qui de sursum est et idcirco de hoc mundo non est. Quamquam etiam quodammodo ex hoc mundo est. Vnde non Deus tantum est Christus, sed et homo. Vt merito quomodo non est ex hoc mundo secundum uerbi diuinitatem, ita ex hoc mundo sit secundum suscepti corporis fragilitatem; homo est enim cum Deo iunctus et Deus cum homine copulatus. 5. Sed idcirco nunc hic Christus in unam partem solius diuinitatis incubuit, quoniam caecitas Iudaica solam in Christo partem carnis aspexit, et inde in praesenti loco silentio praeterita corporis fragilitate, quae de mundo est, de sua sola diuinitate locutus est, quae de mundo non est, ut in quantum illi inclinauerant ut hominem illum tantummodo crederent, in tantum illos Christus posset ad diuinitatem suam considerandam trahere, ut se Deum crederent, uolens illorum incredulitatem circa diuinitatem suam omissa interim commemoratione sortis humanae solius diuinitatis oppositione superare. 6. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: Ego ex Deo prodii et ueni, cum constet hominem a Deo factum esse, non ex Deo processisse? Ex Deo autem homo quomodo non processit, sic Dei uerbum processit, de quo dictum est: Eructauit cor meum uerbum bonum, quod quoniam ex Deo est, merito et apud Deum est, quodque quia non otiose prolatum, merito omnia facit. Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt et sine ipso factum est nihil. Sed enim hoc uerbum, per quod facta sunt omnia, <Deus est>. Et Deus, inquit, erat uerbum. Deus ergo processit ex Deo, dum qui processit sermo Deus est qui processit ex Deo.

7. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: Si quis uerbum meum seruauerit, mortem non uidebit in aeternum? Mortem in aeternum non uidere, quid aliud quam immortalitas est? Immortalitas autem diuinitati socia est, quia et diuinitas immortalis est et immortalitas diuinitatis fructus est. Sed enim omnis homo mortalis est, immortalitas autem ex mortali non potest esse. Ergo ex Christo homine mortali immortalitas non potest nasci. Sed qui uerbum custodierit, inquit, meum, mortem non uidebit in aeternum. Ergo uerbum Christi praestat immortalitatem et per immortalitatem praestat diuinitatem. Quodsi non potest exhibere ut immortalem alterum faciat ipse mortalis, hoc autem Christi uerbum exhibet pariter et praestat immortalitatem, non utique homo tantum est qui praestat immortalitatem, quam, si tantummodo homo esset, praestare non posset; praestando autem diuinitatem per immortalitatem Deum se probat diuinitatem porrigendo, quam, nisi Deus esset, praestare non posset. 8. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo inquit: Ante Abraham ego sum? Nemo enim hominum ante eum potest esse ex quo ipse est nec potest fieri ut quicquam prius fuerit ante illum ex quo ipsum originem sumpsit. Sed enim Christus cum ex Abraham sit, ante Abraham esse se dicit. Aut mentitur igitur et fallit, si ante Abraham non fuit, qui ex Abraham fuit, aut non fallit, si etiam Deus est, dum ante Abraham fuit. Quod nisi fuisset, consequenter cum ex Abraham fuisset, ante Abraham esse non posset. 9. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ait: Et ego agnoscam eas et sequuntur me meae, et ego uitam aeternam do illis, et numquam peribunt in perpetuum? Sed enim cum omnis homo mortalitatis sit legibus alligatus et idcirco in perpetuum se ipse seruare non posset, multo magis in perpetuum alterum seruare non poterit. At in perpetuum se Christus repromittit salutem daturum. Quam si non dat, mendax est; si dat, Deus est. Sed non fallit, dat enim quod repromittit. Deus est ergo, qui salutem perpetuam porrigit, quam homo, qui se ipsum seruare non potest, alteri praestare non poterit. 10. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quid est quod ait: Ego et Pater unum sumus? Quomodo enim ego et Pater unum sumus, si non et Deus est et Filius, qui idcirco unum potest dici, dum ex ipso est et dum Filius eius est et dum ex ipso nascitur, dum ex ipso processisse reperitur, per quod et Deus est? 11. Quod cum inuidiosum Iudaei putassent et blasphemum credidissent eo quod se ostenderat his sermonibus Christum esse Deum ac propterea ad lapides concurrissent et saxorum ictus inicere gestissent, exemplo et testimonio scripturarum aduersarios suos fortiter refutauit. Si illos, inquit, dixit deos, ad quos uerba facta sunt, et non potest solui scriptura: quem Pater sanctificauit et misit in hunc mundum uos dicitis quia blasphemas, quia dixi: Filius Dei sum ego? 12. Quibus uocibus neque se negauit Deum, quinimmo Deum se esse firmauit. Nam quia sine dubitatione dei esse dicuntur ad quos uerba facta sunt, multo magis hic Deus qui melior illis omnibus inuenitur. Et nihilominus calumniosam blasphemiam dispositione legitima congruenter refutauit. Deum enim se sic intellegi uult, ut Filium Dei et non ipsum Patrem uellet intellegi. Missum enim se esse dixit et multa opera se ex Patre ostendisse monstrauit, ex quo non Patrem se, sed Filium esse intellegi uoluit, et in ultima parte defensionis Filii, non Patris fecit mentionem dicendo: Vos dicitis quia blasphemas, quia dixi; Filius Dei sum? 13. Ita quod ad crimen blasphemiae pertinet, Filium se, non Patrem dicit, quod autem ad diuinitatem spectet ipsius, Ego et Pater unum sumus dicendo Filium se esse et Deum probauit. Deus est ergo, Deus autem sic, ut Filius sit, non Pater.

author: Novatian
english: XVII. 1. What if Moses follows this same rule of truth and handed this down to us at the beginning of his writings, that we may learn that all things were created and established through the Son of God, that is through God’s Word? For he says what John says, what the others say; indeed both John and the others are understood to have received from him what they say. 2. For if John says: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, and the prophet reports: I speak my works to the king, and Moses introduces God commanding that light first be made, heaven be firm, waters be gathered, dry land be shown, fruit according to seeds be called forth, animals be produced, lights in heaven and stars be set — he shows no one else then present with God to whom these works were commanded to be done, except him through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. 3. And if this is God’s Word — for my heart has belched a good word — he shows that in the beginning the Word was, and this Word was with the Father, that the Word moreover was God, that all things were made through him. But this Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, Christ namely the Son of God, whom, while afterward we receive as man according to the flesh and before the world’s founding we see as God’s Word and God, we deservedly both believe and hold Christ Jesus both God and man according to the arrangement of the old and new testament. 4. What if the same Moses introduces God saying: Let us make man unto our image and likeness, and below: And God made man, unto God’s image he made him, male and female he made them? If, as we have already taught, it is God’s Son through whom all things were made, then certainly it is God’s Son through whom man also was instituted, for whose sake all things were made.

5. But when God commands that man be made, he who makes man is reported to be God; but God’s Son makes man, namely God’s Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. But this Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Therefore Christ is God. Through Christ, then, man was made, as through God’s Son. But God made man unto God’s image. He who made man unto God’s image is therefore God. Christ is therefore God, so that deservedly neither does the old testament’s authority about Christ’s person waver, while it is propped by the new testament’s manifestation, nor is the new testament’s power cut off, while its truth rests on the same old testament’s roots. 6. From which those who presume Christ, Son of God and of man, to be man only, and not also God, act against both the old and the new testament, while they corrupt both the old and the new testament’s authority and truth. 7. What if the same Moses everywhere introduces God the Father immense and without end, not one enclosed by place, but one who encloses every place, nor one who is in a place, but rather one in whom every place is, containing all things and embracing all, so that deservedly he neither descends nor ascends, since he himself both contains and fills all things, and yet nonetheless introduces God descending to the tower which the sons of men were building, seeking to look and saying: Come and presently let us go down and confuse their tongues there, so that each may not hear his neighbor’s voice? Whom do they want here as God who descended to that tower and sought then to visit those men? God the Father? Then he is already enclosed by place. And how does he himself embrace all things? 8. Or does he mean an angel descending with angels and saying: Come and presently let us go down and confuse their tongues there? But in Deuteronomy we notice that God reported these things and that God said them, where it is set: When he scattered Adam’s sons, he set the nations’ bounds according to the number of God’s angels. Therefore neither did the Father descend, as the matter shows, nor did an angel command those things, as the matter proves. 9. It remains, then, that he descended of whom the apostle Paul says: He who descended is himself who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things — that is, God’s Son, God’s Word. But God’s Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. This will be Christ. Christ will therefore be pronounced God.
translator_notes: De Trinitate XVII: omnia per Filium; uerbum caro; ad imaginem Dei; qui descendit Filius.
latin: XVII. 1. Quid si Moyses hanc eandem regulam ueritatis exsequitur et hoc in principio suarum nobis tradidit literarum, quo discamus omnia creata et condita esse per Dei Filium, hoc est per Dei uerbum? Id enim dicit quod Ioannes, quod ceteri, immo et Ioannes et ceteri ab hoc intelleguntur accepisse quod dicant. 2. Si enim Ioannes dicit: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil, prophetes autem refert: Dico ego opera mea regi, Moyses autem introducit praecipientem Deum ut lux fiat in primis, caelum firmetur, aquae congregentur, arida ostendatur, fructus secundum semina prouocetur, animalia producantur, luminaria in caelo atque astra ponantur, non alium ostendit tunc adfuisse Deo cui praeciperenter haec opera ut fierent, nisi eum per quem facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil. 3. Ac si hic uerbum Dei est — nam eructauit cor meum uerbum bonum —, ostendit in principio uerbum fuisse et uerbum hoc apud Patrem fuisse, Deum praeterea uerbum fuisse, omnia per ipsum facta esse. Sed enim hoc uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis, Christus scilicet Filius Dei, quem dum et postmodum secundum carnem hominem accipimus et ante mundi institutionem Dei uerbum et Deum uidemus, merito secundum institutionem ueteris et noui testamenti et Deum et hominem Christum Iesum et credimus et tenemus. 4. Quid si idem Moyses introducit dicentem Deum: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram, et infra: Et fecit Deus hominem, ad imaginem Dei fecit illum, masculum et feminam fecit eos? Si, ut iam docuimus, Dei Filius est per quem facta sunt omnia, utique Dei Filius est per quem etiam homo institutus est, propter quem facta sunt omnia.

5. Sed enim Deo praecipiente ut homo fiat, Deus refertur esse qui hominem facit; facit autem hominem Dei Filius, uerbum scilicet Dei per quem facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil. Hoc autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis. Ergo Christus est Deus. Per Christum igitur homo factus est, ut per Dei Filium. Sed Deus hominem ad imaginem Dei fecit. Deus est ergo qui fecit hominem ad imaginem Dei. Deus ergo Christus est, ut merito nec ueteris testamenti circa personam Christi uacillet auctoritas, dum noui testamenti manifestatione fulcitur, nec noui testamenti intercepta sit potestas, dum radicibus ueteris testamenti eiusdem nititur ueritas. 6. Ex quo qui Christum, Dei Filium et hominis, tantummodo praesumunt hominem, non et Deum, contra testamentum et uetus et nouum faciunt, dum et ueteris et noui testamenti auctoritatem ueritatemque corrumpunt. 7. Quid si idem Moyses ubique introducit Deum Patrem immensum atque sine fine, non qui loco cludatur, sed qui omnem locum cludat, nec eum qui in loco sit, sed potius in quo omnis locus sit, omnia continentem et cuncta complexum, ut merito nec descendat nec ascendat, quoniam ipse omnia et continet et implet, et tamen nihilominus introducit Deum descendentem ad turrem quam aedificabant filii hominum, considerare quaerentem et dicentem: Venite et mox descendamus et confundamus illic ipsorum linguas, ut non audiat unusquisque uocem proximi sui? Quem uolunt hic Deum descendisse ad turrem illam et homines tunc illos uisitare quaerentem? Deum Patrem? Ergo iam loco clauditur. Et quomodo omnia ipse complectitur? 8. Aut numquid angelum cum angelis dicit descendentem et dicentem: Venite et mox descendamus et confundamus illic ipsorum linguas? Sed enim in Deuteronomio animaduertimus rettulisse Deum haec Deumque dixisse, ubi ponitur: Cum disseminaret filios Adam, statuit fines gentium iuxta numerum angelorum Dei. Neque ergo Pater descendit, ut res indicat, neque angelus ista praecepit, ut res probat. 9. Superest ergo ut ille descenderit, de quo apostolus Paulus: Qui descendit, ipse est qui ascendit super omnes caelos, ut impleret omnia, hoc est Dei Filius, Dei uerbum. Verbum autem Dei caro factum est et habitauit in nobis. Hic erit Christus. Deus ergo pronuntiabitur Christus.

author: Novatian
english: XX. 1. And if some heretic, stubbornly struggling against the truth, should wish in all these examples to understand an angel properly so called, or contend that an angel must be understood, in this too he must necessarily be broken by the force of truth. 2. For if, with all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things subjected to Christ, the angels themselves also, with all the rest that are subject to Christ, are called gods, Christ is rightly God. And if any angel subject to Christ can be called god, and if this is said and brought forward without blasphemy, much more certainly can this belong to God’s Son Christ himself, that he be pronounced God. 3. For if an angel subject to Christ is put forward as god, much more and more firmly will Christ, to whom all angels are subject, be said to be God. Nor does it suit nature that what is granted to lesser ones be denied to greater. So if an angel is less than Christ, yet an angel is called god, it follows more that Christ is said to be God, who is found greater and better than not one but all angels. 4. And if God stood in the assembly of gods, and in the midst God judges gods, and Christ has often stood in the assembly, then Christ stood as God in the assembly, judging those gods to whom he says: How long do you accept persons of men?, accusing the men of the synagogue for not exercising just judgments. 5. Further, if those who are rebuked nonetheless for some cause obtain this name without blasphemy, that they be called gods, much more will this one be held God who is said not only to have stood as God of gods, but also judging and discerning gods. 6. And if they who have fallen by a crime’s desert are nevertheless called gods, much more is this one God who has not fallen into a crime’s desert, but is even found the condemner of others’ crimes. 7. What if he is also found so far God of all that even God the Father applied this name to him? Or does Scripture report: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven? For when the Lord rained fire from the Lord, two are put forward: one who came down and one who rained from heaven — Christ the Lord who was seen, and God the Father who was not seen, who with the Son is Lord as well. 8. And if Abraham also saw God and heard him and spoke with him, yet no one has ever seen God, this one who was seen is proved to be God: God the Son, not the Father. And so that it might be clear that Christ is Lord and God, David says: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.

9. And if Isaiah also reports Egypt laboring and merchants of Ethiopia and Seba crossing to him as slaves who will worship him because God is in him and there is no God besides him — for you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior — who is this who has God in him and who himself is God, except Christ Jesus the Son of God? 10. And if Jeremiah says: This is our God, and no other will be counted with him; he found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved; afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men — who is this who was seen and lived among men, except Christ God the Son? 11. And if Habakkuk too says: God will come from the south, and the Holy One from a shaded dense mountain — who else is this but Christ? 12. And if Daniel reports the Son of man coming in heaven’s clouds and approaching the Ancient of days and receiving power — he who receives power as Son of man is also God. 13. What if John also writes: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; all things were made through him; and later: And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us? Who is this Word made flesh and God, except Christ? 14. And if he also says that Christ washed his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape — the robe and garment are the flesh; he washed the body’s substance with blood, that is wine, washing flesh’s matter by the assumed man’s passion. 15. From which, insofar as it is washed, it is man, because the garment washed is flesh. But he who washes is God’s Word, who, that he might wash the garment, was made the garment’s taker. 16. Deservedly man is expressed from that substance received that it might be washed, just as from the Word’s authority he who washed is shown to be God.
translator_notes: De Trinitate XX: angeli dii / Deus Christus; Dominus a Domino; uerbum lauit amictum carnis.
latin: XX. 1. Ac si aliquis haereticus pertinaciter obluctans aduersus ueritatem uoluerit in his omnibus exemplis proprie angelum aut intellegere aut intellegendum esse contenderit, in hoc quoque uiribus ueritatis frangatur necesse est. 2. Nam si omnibus caelestibus, terrenis et infernis Christo subditis etiam ipsi angeli cum omnibus ceteris quaecumque subiecta sunt Christo dicuntur dii, iure et Deus Christus. Et si quiuis angelus subditus Christo deus potest dici, et hoc si dicitur et sine blasphemia profertur, multo magis utique et hoc ipsi Dei Filio Christo competere potest, ut Deus pronuntietur. 3. Si enim qui subiectus Christo angelus deus promitur, multo magis et constantius Christus, cui sunt omnes angeli subiecti, Deus esse dicetur.
