Denique si acceperis spiritum substantiam Dei, creaturam feceris Deum. Omnis enim spiritus creatura est. Erit ergo iam factus Deus. Quomodo et si secundum Moysen ignem acceperis Deum, creaturam illum esse dicendo institutum expresseris, non institutorem docueris. 5. Sed haec figurantur potius quam ita sunt. Nam et in ueteri testamento ideo Deus ignis dicitur, ut peccatori populo metus incutiatur, dum iudex ostenditur, et in nouo testamento spiritus esse profertur, ut refector et creator in delictis suis mortuorum per hanc bonitatem collatae credentibus indulgentiae comprobetur.

author: Arnobius
english: 2.1. “And has he not held out the light of life to all and removed the danger of ignorance?” 2. - Who, if he were not worthy for you to listen to and believe, still for this very reason ought not to have been scorned by you: that he was showing you saving things, that he was wishing for you ways to heaven and vows of immortality. 3. “But he is worthy of hate, because he drove religions from the world, because he forbade approaching the worship of the gods.”

4. - Is he then accused as the extinguisher of religion and the author of impiety, who brought true religion into the world, who opened the doors of piety to humans blind and truly living in impiety and showed them to whom they should submit themselves? 5. Or is any religion truer, more dutiful, more powerful, more just, than to know the chief God, to know how to entreat the chief God, who alone is head and fountain of all goods, father, founder, and establisher of everlasting things, by whom all earthly and all heavenly things are animated and watered with vital motion, and who, if he were not, there would surely be nothing that would bear any name and substance?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.2: lumen vitae; vias ad caelum; pietatis ianuas.
latin: 2.1. ''Et non in cunctos et lumen praetenderit vitae et periculum ignorationis amoverit?''. 2. - Qui si dignus non esset, cui auscultare deberetis et credere, vel hoc ipso fuerat non aspernandus a vobis, quod salutaria vobis ostenderet, quod vias vobis ad caelum et vota immortalitatis optaret. 3. ''At enim odio dignus est, quod ex orbe religiones expulit, quod ad deorum cultum prohibuit accedi''.

4. - Ergone ille religionis extinctor et impietatis auctor arguitur, qui veram in orbe religionem induxit, qui hominibus caecis et revera in impietate degentibus pietatis aperuit ianuas et cúi se summitterent indicavit? 5. An ulla est religio verior officiosior o potentior iustior, quam deum principem nosse, scire deo principi supplicare, qui bonorum omnium solus caput et fons est, perpetuarum pater fundator et conditor rerum, a quo omnia terrena cuncta que caelestia. animantur motu inriganturque vitali, et qui si non esset, nulla profecto res esset quae aliquod nomen substantiamque portaret.

author: Arnobius
english: 3.1. Unless perhaps you doubt whether that commander of whom we speak exists, and you rather believe Apollo is, Diana, Mercury, Mars. 2. Give a true judgment, and looking around at all these things we see, one will doubt more whether the other gods exist than hesitate about God, whom we all naturally know exists—whether when we cry “O God,” or when we set that God as witness of the wicked and, as if he sees us, lift our face to heaven.

3. “But he forbade humans to entreat the lesser gods.” - Do you even know who the lesser gods are or where they are? Has any suspicion or mention of them ever struck you, that you should deservedly take it ill that cults were taken from them and they were widowed of the bestowal of honor? 4. But if the swelling of mind and that typhus which is called so by the Greeks were not standing against you and blocking you, you could already have known what he forbade to be done and why, within what bounds he willed true religion to stand, how much danger would be born for you from thinking yourselves owed to that obedience, or from what evils you would emerge if you renounced treacherous error.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.3: deus naturaliter; religio vera; error insidiosus.
latin: 3.1. Nisi forte dubitatis, an sit iste de quo loquimur imperator, et magis esse Apollinem creditis, Dianam Mercurium Martem. 2. Da verum iudicium et haec omnia circumspiciens quae videmus magis an sint dii ceteri dubitabit quam in deo cunctabitur, quem esse omnes naturaliter scimus, sive cum exclamamus ''o deus'', sive cum illum testem deum constituimus improborum et quasi nos cernat faciem sublevamus ad caelum.

3. ''Sed minoribus supplicare diis homines vetuit''. - Dii enim minores qui sint aut ubi sint scitis? Perstrinxit vos aliquando suspicio illorum aut mentio, ut merito feratis indigne abrogatos his cultus et honoris inpertitione viduatos? 4. Quod si non mentis elatio et typhus qui appellatur a Graecis obstaret atque officeret vobis, iamdudum scire potuissetis, quid aut quare prohibuerit fieri, intra fines quos stare religionem voluerit veram, quantum vobis periculum nasceretur ex eo quod putaretis obsequio vel ex quibus malis emergeretis, si insidioso renuntiaretis errori.

author: Arnobius
english: 4.1. But all these things will be recalled more brightly and more plainly when we have been carried further still. For we will show that Christ did not teach the nations impiety, but rescued the folly of wretched humans from the worst robbers. 2. “We do not believe,” you say, “that the things he says are true.” - What then? Do the things you deny are true stand clear among you, when things impending and not yet suffered can be refuted by no arguments? 3. “But even he does not prove what he promises.” - So it is: for there can be, as I said, no proving of future things.

4. Since, then, this is the condition of future things, that they cannot be held and grasped by any touch of anticipation, is it not a purer reason, from two uncertain things hanging in ambiguous expectation, rather to believe that which brings some hopes than that which brings none at all? For in the one there is no danger, if what is said to impend should prove empty and void; in the other there is the greatest loss, that is the loss of salvation, if when the time has come it is disclosed that it was not a lie.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.4: non impietatem docuisse; Non credimus; spes / salutis amissio.
latin: 4.1. Verum haec omnia inlustrius commemorabuntur et planius, cum ulterius prorsus fuerimus evecti. Monstrabimus enim Christum non impietatem docuisse nationes, sed ab latronibus pessimis miserorum hominum inprudentiam vindicasse. 2. ''Non credimus, inquitis, vera esse quae dicit''. - Quid enim? quae vos negatis vera esse apud vos liquet, cum imminentia et nondum passa nullis possint rationibus refutari?

3. ''Sed et ipse quae pollicetur non probat''. - Ita est: nulla enim, ut dixi, futurorum potest existere comprobatio. 4. Cum ergo haec sit condicio futurorum, ut teneri et comprehendi nullius possint anticipationis attactu, nonne purior ratio est, [et] ex duobus incertis et in ambigua exspectatione pendentibus id potius credere quod aliquas spes ferat quam omnino quod nullas? In illo enim periculi nihil est, quod dicitur imminere cassum <si> fiat et vacuum; in hoc damnum est maximum id est salutis amissio, si cum tempus advenerit aperiatur non fuisse mendacium.

author: Arnobius
english: 6.1. Unless perhaps those seem to you dull and foolish who already throughout the whole world conspire and gather into the assent of this belief. 2. - What then? Are you alone founded in wisdom and by the sheer force of intelligence seeing I know not what else and deep: do you alone understand all these things to be trifles, alone take as words and childish silliness those things we promise will come from the chief King?

3. From where, I ask, was so much wisdom handed to you, from where so much sharpness and liveliness, or from what disciplines of knowledge were you able to take so much heart, to drink so much of divination? 4. Because you know how to decline words and names through cases and tenses, because you avoid barbarous sounds and solecisms, because you yourselves know how to bring forth numbered and structured and composed speech or know when it has been rough, because you hold sealed in memory Lucilius’s Fornix and Pomponius’s Marsyas, because you know what constitutions there are in lawsuits, how many kinds of causes, how many of speeches, what genus is, what species, by what reasons an opposite is distinguished from a contrary—therefore do you judge that you know what is false, what true, what can happen or cannot, what the nature of lowest and highest things is? 5. Has that common saying never struck your ears, that the wisdom of man is folly with God?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.6: credulitatis adsensus; sapientia hominis stultitia apud Deum.
latin: 6.1. Nisi forte obtunsi et fatui videntur hi vobis, qui per orbem iam totum conspirant et coeunt in istius credulitatis adsensum. 2. - Quid ergo? vos soli sapientiae conditi atque intellegentiae vi mera nescio quid aliud videtis et profundum: soli esse nugas intellegitis haec omnia, soli verba et pueriles ineptias ea quae nobis promittimus principali ab rege ventura. 3. Unde quaeso est vobis tantum sapientiae traditum, unde acuminis et vivacitatis tantum vel ex quibus scientiae disciplinis tantum cordis adsumere, divinationis tantum potuistis hau rire?

4. Quia per casus et tempora declinare verba scitis et nomina, quia voces barbaras soloecismosque vitare, quia numerosum et structum o compositum que sermonem aut ipsi vos nostis ecferre aut incomptus cum fuerit scire, quia Fornicem Lucilianum et Marsyam Pomponi obsignatum memoria continetis, quia quae sint in litibus constitutiones? quot causarum genera, quot dictionum, quid sit lsgenus, quid species, oppositum a contrario quibus rationibus distinguatur, idcirco vos arbitramini scire, quid sit falsum, quid verum, quid fieri possit aut non possit, quae imorum summorumque natura sit? 5. Numquam ne illud vulgatum perstrinxit aures vestras, sapientiam hominis stultitiam esse apud deum primum? (cf 1Cor 3,19).

author: Arnobius
english: 7.1. And you yourselves thoroughly see yourselves, whenever you dispute about obscure matters and proceed to unlock natural secrets, that you do not know even those things which you say, which you assert, which you commonly defend with capital contention, and that each one guards his own suspicions with stubborn wrestling as if they were proved and grasped. 2. For what, if I look at the truth, even if all ages were spent in investigating things, can we know through ourselves—we whom I know not what thing has brought forth so blind and proud, and envy has put together, so that, though we know nothing at all, we still deceive ourselves and are lifted into an opinion of knowledge under the swelling of an inflated breast? 3. For to pass over divine things and things sunk in natural obscurity, can any of mortals explain—that which Socrates in the Phaedrus cannot grasp—what a human is or whence he is, two-sided, varying, movable, deceitful, manifold, many-formed, 4. for what uses he was brought forth, by whose ingenuity he was devised, what he does in the world, why he experiences such swarms of evils, 5. whether the earth, turned by the rottenness of some moisture, animated him like worms, like mice, or whether he received these outlines of body and the form of the face by the hand of some potter and craftsman?

6. Can he know, I say, these things placed in the midst and set in common senses: by what causes we sink into sleeps, by what we wake, by what means dreams happen, by what visions: 7. indeed what Plato doubts in the Theaetetus—whether we ever wake or that which is called waking is a portion of perpetual sleep, and what we seem to do is a dream; 8. when we say we see, whether we see by an aiming of rays and light or whether images of things fly and settle in our pupils; whether taste is in things or happens by contacts of the palate; by what causes hairs lay aside inborn blackness and not all equally but by gradual adding grow white; 9. what it is that makes all liquids one body by mixture, while oil alone refuses to suffer immersion into itself, but is always clearly gathered into its own nature impenetrable; 10. finally the mind itself, which is said by you to be immortal and a god, why in the sick it is sick, in infants dull, in old age worn out it pours out delirious and insane things? 11. Whose weakness and pitiable ignorance is this the more, that although it can happen that we sometimes say something true, even this itself is uncertain for us—whether we have said something true.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.7: nescire; suspiciones; opinio scientiae; Phaedrus/Theaetetus.
latin: 7.1. Atque ipsi penitus perspicitis vos ipsos, si quando de rebus disceptatis obscuris et naturalia pergitis reserare secreta, et ipsa quae dicitis, quae adseveratis, quae capitali plerumque contentione defenditis, nescire vos et unumquemque suspiciones suas < pro > probatis et comprehensis pertinaci obluctatione tutari. 2. Quid enim, si verum perspiciam, etiamsi omnia saecula in rerum investigatione ponantur, scire per nos possumus, quos ita caecos et superbos nescio quae res protulit et concinnavit invidia, ut, cum nihil sciamus omnino, fallamus nos tamen et in opinionem scientiae sub inflati pectoris tumore tollamur? 3. Ut enim divina praeteream et naturali obscuritate res mersas, potest quisquam explicare mortalium, id quod Socrates ille conprehendere nequit in Phaedro [Pl. Phaedr. 230], homo quid sit aut unde sit, anceps varius mobilis pellax multiplex multiformis, 4. in quos usus prolatus sit, cuius sit excogitatus ingenio, quid in mundo faciat, cur malorum tanta experiatur examina,

5. utrum ne illum tellus uliginis alicuius conversa putore tamquam vermes animaverit, tamquam mures, an fietoris alicuius et fabricatoris manu liniamenta haec eorporis atque oris acceperit formam? 6. Potest, inquam, scire in medio haec posita atque in sensibus constituta communibus, quibus causis mergamur in somnos, quibus evigilemus, quibus modis fiant insomnia, quibus visa: 7. immo quod ambigit in Theaeteto Plato [Plat. Theaet. 158 b], vigilemus aliquando an ipsum vigilare quod dicitur somni sit perpetui portio, et quod agere videamur, insomnium; 8. cum videre nos dicimus, radiorum et luminis intentione videamus an rerum imagines advolent et nostris in pupulis sidant; utrum sapor in rebus sit an palati contagionibus fiat quibus ex causis pili nigrorem ingenitum ponant neque omnes pariter sed paulatim adiciendo canescant; 9. quid sit quod humores universi unum corpus efficiant mixtione, solum oleum respuat immersionem in se pati, sed in suam naturam impenetrabile semper perspicue colligatur; 10. ipse denique animus, qui inmortalis a vobis et deus esse narratur, cur in aegris aeger sit, in infantibus stolidus, in senectute defessus delira effutiat et insana? 11. Quorum infirmitas et inscientia miserabilis hoc magis est, ut cum fieri possit ut veri aliquid aliquando dicamus, et hoc ipsum nobis incertum sit, an veri aliquid dixerimus.

author: Arnobius
english: 9.1. What? Those things about matters set apart from human knowing which you yourselves write, which you read—have you seen them by eyed inspection and held them handled with hands? Does not each of you believe this or that set of authors? Does not each protect that he is persuaded truth is spoken by another as if by a kind of assent of faith?

2. Who says the origin of all things is fire or water—does he not believe Thales or Heraclitus? Who sets the cause in numbers—not Pythagoras of Samos, not Archytas? 3. Who divides the soul and sets up incorporeal forms—not Plato the Socratic? Who applies a fifth element to principal causes—not Aristotle, father of the Peripatetics? Who threatens fire to the world, and that it will burn when the time has come—not Panaetius, Chrysippus, Zeno? 4. Who is always fashioning and destroying worlds with indivisible bodies—not Epicurus, Democritus, Metrodorus? Who affirms that nothing is grasped by a human and that all things are wrapped in blind obscurities—not Arcesilaus, Carneades, not finally some devotee of the old or newer Academy?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.9: fidei astipulatione; credit auctoribus.
latin: 9.1. Quid? illa de rebus ab humana cognitione sepositis, quae conscribitis ipsi, quae lectitatis, oculata vidistis inspectione et manibus tractata tenuistis? nonne vestrum quicumque est huic vel illi credit auctoribus? non quod sibi persuaserit quis verum dici ab altero velut quadam fidei astipulatione tutatur?

2. Qui cunctarum <rerum> originem <ignem> esse dicit aut aquam, non Thaleti aut Heraclito credit? qui causam in numeris ponit, non Pythagorae Samio, non Archytae? 3. qui animam dividit et incorporales constituit formas, non Platoni Socratico? qui quintum elementum principalibus adplicat causis, non Aristoteli Peripateticorum patri? qui ignem minatur mundo, et venerit cum tempus arsurum, non Panaetio Chrysippo Zenoni? 4. qui individuis corporibus mundos semper fabricatur et destruit, non Epicuro Democrito Metrodoro? qui nihil ab homine comprehendi <autumat> atque omnia caecis obscuritatibus involuta, non Arcesilae, Carneadi, non alicui denique Academiae veteris recentiorisque cultori?

author: Arnobius
english: 15.1. Therefore there is nothing that should deceive us, nothing that should promise us empty hopes—that which is said by certain new men and ones lifted up by an immoderate opinion of themselves—that souls are immortal, nearest to the Lord and Prince of things in grade of dignity, brought forth from that Begetter and Father, divine, wise, learned, and no longer touchable by any handling of the body.

2. Because this is true and certain, and we have been brought forth from a perfect, unamendable perfection, we live blameless and therefore unreproveable, good, just, and upright, of no vicious matter; no desire conquers us, no lust dishonors us; we keep and make whole the course of all virtues. 3. And because the souls of us all flow down from one fountain, for that reason we feel one agreeing thing; we do not differ in manners or opinions; we all know the same things, and there are not as many opinions as there are humans on earth, nor ones split by infinite variety.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.15: spes cassas; animas immortales; gradu proximas; ironic perfection.
latin: 15.1. Quare nihil est quod nos fallat, nihil quod nobis polliceatur spes cassas, id quod a novis quibusdam dicitur viris et inmoderata sui opinione sublatis, animas immortales esse, domino rerum ac principi gradu proximas dignitatis, genitore illo ac patre prolatas, divinas sapientes doctas neque ulla iam corporis attrectatione contiguas.

2. Quod quia verum et certum est, et a perfecto sumus inemendabili perfectione prolati, inculpabiles et ideo inreprehensibiles vivimus, boni iusti et recti, vitiositatis nullius rei, nulla cupiditas nos vincit, nulla libido dehonestat, virtutum omnium servamus atque integramus tenorem. 3. Et quia uno ex fonte omnium nostrum defluunt animae, idcirco unum conveniensque sentimus, non moribus, non opinionibus discrepamus, idem omnes novimus nec, quot in orbe sunt homines, non sunt sententiae totidem neque infinita varietate discretae.

author: Arnobius
english: 30.1. “But the punishments mentioned among the dead and the many kinds of torments?” - And who will be so stupid and ignorant of consequences of things as to believe that Tartarean darknesses can harm incorruptible souls, or fiery rivers, or marshes with muddy gulfs, or the turnings of whirling wheels? 2. For what is not touchable and is removed from the laws of dissolution, though it be surrounded by all the flames of torrential rivers, rolled in mire, covered by falls of looming rocks and ruins of huge mountains, must remain unharmed and untouched and take on no sense of death-bearing suffering.

3. What of this—that that persuasion is not only a goad to vices by the very freedom of sinning, but even takes away philosophy’s own reason and declares it to be taken up emptily by the difficulty of superfluous work? For if it is true that souls share in no end and proceed with all ages in the perpetuity of times, what danger is there, when virtues—by which life is narrower and harsher—have been scorned and passed over, in giving oneself to pleasures and in pouring out through all kinds of lusts the unbridled heat of immense desire? 4. Lest it wilt in delights and be corrupted by softness of vices? - And by what reason can that be corrupted which is immortal, which always is and is liable to no suffering? Lest it grow filthy and be polluted by the foulness of base acts? - And how can that be polluted which does not have bodily substance, or where can contamination set a seat where there is no space in which a mark of contamination itself can fasten? Again, if souls approach the gates of death, as Epicurus’s judgment defines, neither then is there a fitting cause why philosophy ought to be sought, even if it is true that by it souls are purged and rendered clean from all viciousness. 5. For if they commonly die and in the bodies themselves their sense perishes and vital sense is extinguished, it is not only of greatest error but of stupid blindness to rein in inborn appetites, to keep life in narrows, to indulge nature nothing, not to do what desires have ordered and spurred, when no rewards of such great toil await you when the day of death has come and you have been loosed from bodily bonds.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.30: poenae inferorum; animae incorruptibiles; philosophiae causa.
latin: 30.1. ''Sed memoratae apud inferos poenae et suppliciorum generibus multiformes?''. - Et quis erit tam brutus et rerum consequentias nesciens, qui animis incorruptibilibus credat aut tenebras Tartareas posse aliquid nocere aut igneos fluvios aut caenosis gurgitibus paludes aut rotarum volubilium circumactus? 2. Quod enim contiguum non est et ab legibus dissolutionis amotum est, licet omnibus ambiatur flammis torrentium fluminum, volvatur in caeno [non], saxorum imminentinm casibus et immanium montium operiatur ruinis, inlibatum necesse est permaneat et intactum neque ullum sensum mortiferae passionis adsumere. 3. Quid quod ista persuasio non tantum est incitatrix ad vitia libertate ex ipsa peccandi, verum etiam philosophiae ipsius causam tollit et inaniter eam suscipi supervacanei operis difficultate declarat. Nam si verum est, animas nullius esse participes finis et cum omnibus saeculis aevorum perpetuitate procedere, quid periculi res habet contemptis praetermissisque virtutibus, quibus est contractior atque horridior vita, voluptatibus se dare ac per omnia libidinum genera eflrenatum spargere inmensae cupiditatis ardorem?

4. Ne deliciis marceat et corrumpatur mollitudine vitiorum? - Et qua poterit ratione corrumpi id quod immortale, quod semper est et nulli obnoxium passioni? Ne sordescat et polluatur actionum turpium foeditate? - Et qui poterit pollui corporalem quod substantiam non habet, aut ubi sedem contaminatio ponere, ubi spatium nullum est in quo nota se possit ipsius contaminationis adfigere? Rursus vero si animae leti adeunt ianuas, Epicuri ut sententia definitur, nec sic causa est conpetens, cur expeti philosophia debeat, etiamsi verum est purgari hac animas atque ab omni puras vitiositate praestari. 5. Nam si communiter obeunt et in ipsis corporibus sensus eis deperit extinguiturque vitalis, non lantum est erroris maximi verum stolidae caecitatis, frenare ingenitos adpetitus, cohibere in angustiis vitam, nihil indulgere naturae, non quod cupidines iusserint atque instigaverint facere, cum nulla te praemia tanti laboris expectent cum dies mortis advenerit et corporalibus fueris vinculis exsolutus.

author: Arnobius
english: 31.1. A certain mid-state, then, and the doubtful and ambiguous nature of souls, gave birth to a place for philosophy and found a cause why it should be sought, while of course that one fears danger from evils admitted, the other conceives good hopes if he does nothing of crime and leads life with duty and justice.

2. From this it is that among learned men and those gifted with excellence of talents there is a contest about the quality of souls, and some say they are of mortal nature and cannot sustain a divine substance, but others that they are perpetual and cannot degenerate into mortal nature, because that this happens is effected by the law of mid-state: for both those have arguments ready by which they are found passible and perishable, and these in turn do not lack arguments by which they are shown to be divine and immortal.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.31: medietas animarum; periculum ex malis; spes bonas; iustitia.
latin: 31.1. Medietas ergo quaedam et animarum anceps ambigua que natura locum philosophiae peperit et causam cur appeteretur invenit, dum periculum scilicet ex malis iste formidat admissis, alter concipit spes bonas, si nihil sceleris faciat et cum officio vitam iustitiaque traducat.

2. Inde est quod inter doctos viros et ingeniorum excellentia praeditos de animarum qualitate certamen est et eas alii dicunt mortali esse natura nec divinam posse substantiam sustinere, alii vero perpetuas nec in naturam posse degenerare mortalem, quod istud ut fiat, medietatis efficitur lege: quod et illis argumenta sunt praesto, quibus eas passivas atque interibiles invenitur, et his contra non desunt quibus esse divinas immortalesque monstratur.

author: Arnobius
english: 37.1. But if souls were, as rumor has it, of the Lord’s offspring and a principal generation of power, nothing would have been lacking to them for perfection when they were begotten by most perfect virtue; all would have had one understanding and one consent; they would always inhabit the royal hall and, not neglecting the seats of blessedness in which they had known and retained most august teachings, they would not foolishly seek these earthly places, to live wrapped in dark bodies among phlegms and blood, among these bags of dung and most filthy sacks. 2. “But even these parts had to be inhabited, and therefore the almighty God sent souls here as if into some colonies.” - And how do humans benefit the world, or for the sake of what necessary thing are they needed, so that they should not be thought to have had to act in this part in vain and be tenants of an earthly body?

Do they contribute some part toward completing this mass’s integrity, and unless they have been added is this sum of the universe imperfect and lame? 3. What then? If humans should not be, will the world cease from its offices, will the stars not carry out their turns, will there be no summers and winters, will the blasts of winds fall silent, and will rains not fall from gathered hanging clouds to bring temperings to droughts? 4. And yet all things must go through their courses and not depart from the continuation of born order, even if no name of a human is heard in the world and this orb of lands falls silent in the silence of empty solitude. How then is it boasted that a dweller had to be added to these regions, when it is clear that nothing returns from the human to the world’s perfection and that all his pursuits always look to private convenience and do not leave the bounds of his own usefulness?
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.37: dominicae prolis; aulam regiam; mundus sine homine.
latin: 37.1. Quodsi essent ut fama est dominicae prolis et potestatis animae generatio principalis, nihil eis ad perfectionem defuisset virtute perfectissima procreatis, unum omnes intellectum habuissent unumque consensum, aulam semper incolerent regiam nec praetermissis beatitudinis sedibus, in quibus augustissimas noverant retinebantque doctrinas, imprudenter adpeterent terrena haec loca, tenebrosis ut corporibus involutae inter pituitas et sanguinem degerent, inter stercoris hos utres et saccati obscenissimas serias. 2. ''Sed habitari oportuit et has partis, et idcirco huc animas tamquam in colonias aliquas deus omnipotens misit''. - Et quid homines prosunt mundo aut ob rei cuius sunt necessarii causam, ut non frustra debuisse credantur parte in hac agere et terreni esse corporis inquilini? Ad consummandam molis huius integritatem partem aliquam conferunt, et nisi fuerint additi, inperfecta et clauda est universitatis haec summa?

3. Quid ergo, si homines non sint, ab officiis suis cessabit mundus, vicissitudines suas non peragent sidera, aestates atque hiemes non erunt, ventorum flamina conticescent nec ex coactis et pendentibus nubilis ad terram decident imbres ariditatibus temperamenta laturi? 4. Atquin necesse est cuncta suos ire per cursus nec ab ordinis nati continuatione discedere, etiamsi nomen in mundo nullum hominis audiatur orbisque iste terrarum solitudinis vacuae silentio conticiscat. Quemadmodum ergo iactatur, habitatorem debuisse regionibus his addi, cum ab homine liqueat nihil ad mundi perfectionem redire omniaque eius studia commoditatem semper spectare privatam nec a finibus propriae utilitatis abscedere?

author: Arnobius
english: 61.1. “What is it to you,” he says, “to investigate and inquire who made the human being, what the origin of souls is, who devised the causes of evils, whether the sun is larger than the world or is measured by the breadth of one foot, whether the moon shines from another’s light or by her own flashes? Things it is no advantage to know and no loss to be ignorant of.

2. Leave these things to God and grant that He Himself know why or whence a thing is, whether it ought to have been or not, whether something is supernaturally produced or has first origins, whether it is fitting that it be abolished or reserved, burned, dissolved, or renewed with recovered integrity. Is it not free for your reasonings to entangle yourselves in such matters and to care for what is so remote from usefulness?

3. Your affair is set in uncertainty—I mean the salvation of your souls—and unless you apply yourselves to the knowledge of God the Prince, a savage death awaits you when you are loosed from bodily bonds, not bringing a sudden extinction but consuming you through a stretch of time by the bitterness of torturing punishment.”
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.61: salus animarum; dei principis notio; mors saeva.

added_allusions.why: fear destruction of soul; death beyond body.

latin: 61.1. '' Quid est , inquit, vobis investigare, conquirere, quisnam hominem fecerit, animarum origo quae sit, quis malorum excogitaverit causas, orbe sit sol amplior an pedis unius latitudine metiatur, alieno ex lumine an propriis luceat fulgoribus luna? Quae neque scire compendium neque ignorare detrimentum est ullum.

2. Remittite haec deo atque ipsum scire concedite, quid quare aut unde sit, debuerit esse aut non esse, supernatum sit aliquid an ortus primigenios habeat, aboleri conveniat an reservari, exuri, dissolvi an repetita integritate renovari. Vestris non est rationibus liberum inplicare vos talibus et tam remota in utilitate curare?

3. Res vestra in ancipiti sita est, salus dico animarum vestrarum, et nisi vos adplicatis dei principis notioni, a corporalibus vinculis exsolutos expectat mors saeva, non repentinam adferens extinctionem sed per tractum temporis cruciabilis poenae acerbitate consumens''.

author: Arnobius
english: 74.1. “And why,” he says, “did it seem good to God the King and Prince that before a few little hours, as the saying goes, Christ the Savior should be sent to you from the citadels of heaven?” — We ask in turn: what cause, what reason is there that the seasons are not sometimes restored to their own months, but winters come later, summer and autumn later?

2. Why after harvests dried up and grain extinguished do rains sometimes fall that ought to have slid upon things still safe and been supplied at the season’s opportunities? Rather we ask this: why, if Hercules had to be born, if Aesculapius, Mercury, Liber, and some others who would be joined to the councils of the gods and bring mortals some usefulness, were they produced by Jupiter so late that only posterity would know them, while the antiquity of earlier people would be ignorant?

3. You will say there was some reason. Therefore there was also a reason here why not recently but today the Savior of our race arrived. “What then is the reason?” — We do not deny that we do not know. For it is not ready for anyone to see God’s mind, nor can a human—a blind animal and not knowing even himself—attain by any reasonings the ways He ordered His affairs: what ought to be done, when or in what kind, the Father of all things Himself, the Governor and Lord, alone knows.

4. And if I cannot set out for you the causes why something happens in that way or this, it does not at once follow that what has been done becomes undone, and that the matter loses the credit which has been shown indubitable by such great kinds of virtues and powers.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.74: sospitator Christus; nostri generis; potestates.
latin: 74.1. ''Et quid, inquit, est visum deo regi ac principi, ut ante horas, quemadmodum dicitur, pauculas sospitator ad vos Christus caeli ex arcibus mitteretur?''. - Interrogamus et nos contra: quae causa, quae ratio est, ut non suis aliquando reddantur mensibus tempora, sed serius hiemes, serius aestas atque autumnitas fiant?

2. Cur post messes arefactas atque extincta frumenta nonnumquam decidant pluviae, quas rebus oportuit incolumibus labi et temporis opportunitatibus ministrari? Immo illud exquirimus potius, cur, si Herculem oportuit nasci, si Aesculapium Mercurium Liberum aliosque nonnullos, qui et conciliis adiungerentur deorum et mortalibus aliquid utilitatis adferrent, tam sero a Iove sint proditi, ut sola illos posteritas sciret, superiorum vero ignoraret antiquitas?

3. Rationem aliquam fuisse dicetis. Ratio ergo et hic fuit, cur non nuper sed hodie sospitator nostri generis adveniret. ''Quaenam igitur ratio est?''. - Non imus infitias nescire nos. Neque enim promptum est cuiquam dei mentem videre, aut quibus modis ordinaverit res suas homo animal caecum et ipsum se nesciens ullis potest rationibus consequi: quid oporteat fieri, quando vel quo genere, ipse rerum cunctarum pater, moderator et dominus scit solus.

4. Nec si ego nequivero causas vobis expromere, cur aliquid fiat illo vel hoc modo, continuo sequitur ut infecta fiant quae facta sunt et amittat res fidem quae generibus virtutum tantis et [potestatibus] potestatum indubitabilis esse monstrata est.

author: Arnobius
english: 55.1. When we have agreed, defeated, that these things are, and have not emptily nodded that all human affairs teem with them, it will follow that they ask: “Why then does almighty God not take away these evils but suffer them to be and to go on through all ages in stubborn continuation?”

2. — If understanding of God the King and Prince is with us and we do not wish to wander through impious insanities of suspicions, we must answer that we do not know those things and never sought or studied to learn what could be grasped by no faculties; and you will judge it better—indeed rather more—to remain within the bounds of not-knowing and ignorance than to say that nothing happens except by God’s will, so that He would at once be understood both to give causes to evils and to be the founder of countless miseries.

3. “Whence then,” you will say, “are all these evils?” “From the elements,” the wise say, “and from their unevenness”—which how it can happen that things without sense and judgment are alleged malicious and harmful, or rather that he is not the more malicious and harmful who took into the making of some work things that would be worst and most injurious—belongs to those who claim to see through it.

4. “What then of us? whence?” — There is no necessity of an answer. Whether we can say or are less able and cannot, either is small with us; nor do we count it among great weights either to be ignorant of this or to know it, content to have set down one thing alone: that nothing harmful and deadly proceeds from God the Prince. This we hold, this we know, in this one truth of knowledge and science we stand: that nothing is done by Him except what is saving for all, what is sweet, what is fullest of love and joy and gladness, what has infinite and incorruptible pleasures, what each by all vows seeks to obtain for himself, and counts outside these things what is deadly and death-bearing.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.55: non aufert mala; conditorem; salutare.

added_allusions.why: God tempts no one with evil.

latin: 55.1. Quae cum esse consenserimus victi et universa his scatere non inaniter adnuerimus humana, consequetur ut rogitent: ''Cur ergo haec mala deus omnipotens non aufert sed esse perpetitur et cum omnibus saeculis pertinaci continuatione procedere?''.

2. - Si intellectus nobis adfuerit dei regis ac principis nec per impias vagari suspicionum voluerimus insanias, respondeamus necesse est, nescire nos ista nec quae nullis possent facultatibus comprehendi expetisse aliquando aut studuisse cognoscere: meliusque ducetis, quinimmo potius magis <in> inscientiae finibus atque ignorantiae permanere quam nisi dei dicere nihil fieri per voluntatem, ut simul intellegatur et malis eum causas dare et miseriarum esse innumerabilium conditorem.

3. ''Mala ergo, dicetis, unde sunt haec omnia?''. ''Ex elementis'' inquiunt, ''et ex eorum inaequabilitate,'' sapientes: quod fieri qui possit ut quae sensum et iudicium non habent malitiosa esse perhibeantur et noxia aut non ille sit potius malitiosus et noxius, qui res pessimas et nocentissimas futuras in alicuius operis adsumpsit effectum, eorum est qui adserunt pervidere.

4. ''Quid ergo nos? unde?''. - Responsionis necessitas nulla est. Sive enim possumus dicere, sive minus valemus nec possumus, utrumque apud nos parvum est; nec in magnis ponderibus ducimus vel ignorare istud vel scire, unum solum posuisse contenti, nihil a deo principe quod sit nocens atque exitiabile proficisci. Hoc tenemus, hoc novimus, in hac una consistimus cognitionis et scientiae veritate, nihil ab eo fieri nisi quod sit omnibus salutare, quod dulce, quod amoris et gaudii laetitiaeque plenissimum, quod infinitas habeat atque incorruptibiles voluptates, quod sibi quisque contingere votis omnibus expetat, forisque ab his esse exitiabile ac mortiferum ducat.

author: Arnobius
english: 45.1. But far be this monstrosity of a wicked opinion—that almighty God, sower and founder, begetter of great and invisible things, should be believed to have begotten souls so mobile, of no gravity or weight or constancy, liable to vices, sloping down into every kind of sins, and though He knew them such and of this sort, to have ordered them to go into bodies, whose prisons they would wear under the storms and tempests of fortune daily,

2. and now do shameful things, now suffer obscenities, perish by shipwrecks, ruins, burnings of fires, that poverty press some and beggary others, that some suffer the mangling of beasts, others die by the poison of little flies, that some walk lame, that others lose the light, that others sit with joints bound, that they be cast before all diseases which unhappy and pitiable mortality sustains by the tearing of diverse punishments; then at last, forgetful that they are of one fountain, one begetter and head, they would tear and break the rights of kinship, overturn their cities, plunder lands as enemies, make slaves of free persons, insult virgins and others’ marriages, hate one another, envy others’ joys and felicities, then at last all curse one another, carp, and mangle with the bite of savage teeth.
translator_notes: Source-locked to Latin Library Adversus Nationes II.
Adv. Nat. 2.45: mobiles animas; vitia labiles; carceribus.

added_allusions.why: true image not vice-labile divinity myth.
Father of lights; no shadow of turning—contra mobile souls from God.

latin: 45.1. Sed procul haec abeat sceleratae opinionis immanitas, ut deus credatur omnipotens, magnarum et invisibilium rerum sator et conditor, procreator, tam mobiles animas genuisse, gravitatis ac ponderis constantiaeque nullius, in vitia labiles, in peccatorum genera universa dcclives, cumque eas tales atque huiusmodi sciret, in corpora ire iussisse, quorum indutae carceribus sub procellis agerent tempestatibusque cotidie fortunae,

2. et modo turpia facerent modo paterentur obscena, naufragiis ruinis incendiorum conflagrationibus ut perirent, pauperies alias, alias ut mendicitas premeret, ut ferarum paterentur aliae laniatus, muscularum aliae ut interirent veneno, claudae ut incederent aliae, ut aliae lumen amitterent, ut articulis sederent aliae colligatis, morbis denique obiectarentur ut cunctis, quos infelix et miseranda mortalitas diversarum sustinet dilaceratione poenarum; tunc deinde oblitae unius esse se fontis, unius genitoris et capitis, germanitatis convellerent atque abrumperent iura, urbes suas everterent, popularentur hostiliter terras, servos de liberis facerent, insultarent virginibus et matrimoniis alienis, odissent invicem sese, aliorum gaudiis et felicitatibus inviderent, tum deinde se omnes maledicercnt, carperent et saevorum dentium mordacitate laniarent.

author: Arnobius
english: 70.1. But why do I speak of small things? The immortal gods themselves, whose temples you now approach and whose powers you adore as suppliants, according to your own letters and opinions, began not to be and not to be known from certain times, and to be named by imposed appellations of names?

2. For if it is true that Jupiter with his brothers was begotten from Saturn and his wife, before the marriages and births of Ops Jupiter had been nowhere—Jupiter as well the supreme as the Stygian—nowhere the lord of the salt dance, nowhere Juno; nay, no other at all besides the two parents inhabited the seats of heaven, but from their concubinage they were conceived and born and drank in the living breath.

3. Therefore from a fixed time Jupiter began to be a god, from a fixed time to earn cult and sacrifices, from a fixed time to be set before his brothers in powers. Again, if Liber, Venus, Diana, Mercury, Apollo, Hercules, the Muses, the Tyndarid Castors, and fire-potent Vulcan were brought forth with Jupiter as father and begotten from the Saturnian begetter, before Memory, before Alcmena, Maia, Juno, Latona, Leda, Dione, and then Semele were made pregnant by Diespiter’s embraces, these too were nowhere among the nations nor in any part of the nature of things, but from Jupiter’s congress they were seeded and born and began to have some sense of themselves.

4. Therefore these also began to be at a fixed time and to be invoked in the number of sacred powers for ceremonies—which the same may likewise be said, transferred, of Minerva. For if, as you assert, she flashed from Jupiter’s brain without the cast of any seed, before Diespiter was begotten and received in his mother’s womb the form of bodily outline, it is certain that Minerva did not exist nor was reckoned in the number of things or in any substance, but she was born from Jupiter’s head and began to be some thing constituted in essence. She therefore has first origins, and from a fixed time she began to be called a goddess, to be set in sacred buildings, and to be sanctioned by inviolable religion.

5. Since this is so, when you speak of the newness of our religions, your own do not come to your mind, nor do you care to inspect when your gods arose, what origins they have, what causes, or from what roots they burst and flashed forth. And of what shame is it—nay, of what shamelessness—to reprove another in that which you see yourself doing, to give as insult and crime things that can be hurled back upon you by reciprocal exchange?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 70.1. Sed quid ego haec parva? Ipsi dii immortales, quorum modo aditis templa et numina suppliciter adoratis, sicut vestris litteris atque opinionibus traditur, non esse, non sciri ab temporibus coeperunt certis et impositis nominum appellationibus nuncupari?

2. Nam si verum est ex Saturno atque eius uxore Iovem suis cum fratribus procreatum, ante nuptias et partus Opis nusquam fuerat Iuppiter, Iuppiter tam supremus quam Stygius, nusquam sali dominus, nusquam Iuno, quinimmo alius nullus genitoribus duobus exceptis caeli habitabat in sedibus, sed ex eorum concubitu concepti et nati sunt et spiritum hausere vitalem.

3. Certo ergo a tempore deus esse Iuppiter coepit, certo cultus et sacrificia commereri, certo fratribus in potestatibus anteponi. Rursus vero si Liber Venus Diana Mercurius Apollo Hercules Musae, Tyndaridae Castores ignipotensque Vulcanus Iove patre sunt proditi et genitore Saturnio procreati, ante quam Memoria, quam Alcmena Maia Iuno Latona Leda Dione, tum et Semela Diespitri factae sunt compressionibus fetae, nusquam et hi gentium nec in aliqua parte rerum fuere naturae, sed ex conventu Iovis inseminati et nati sunt et aliquem sensum sui habere coeperunt.

4. Ergo et hi quoque tempore esse coeperunt certo et in numero numinum sacrorum ad caerimonias invocari, quod ipsum similiter dicere translatum in Minervam licebit. Si enim Iovis, ut adseveratis, ex cerebro sine ullius seminis emicuit iactu, antequam est Diespiter genitus et in utero matris corporeae formam circumscriptionis accepit, certum est utique Minervam non fuisse neque rerum in numero aut ulla esse in substantia computatam, sed ex capite Iovis enata est et esse res coepit nonnulla in essentia constituta. Habet ergo primigenios ortus, et a certo coepta est tempore dea dici, sacris in aedibus statui et inviolabili religione sanciri.

5. Quod cum ita se habeat, cum de novitate loquimini religionum nostrarum, vestrae vobis in mentem non veniunt, nec curatis inspicere, quando sint exorti dii vestri, quas origines habeant, quas causas, vel ex: quibus proruperint emicuerint que radicibus? Cuius est autem pudoris, quinimmo inverecundiae cuius, quod agere te videas, in eo alterum reprehendere, maledicti et criminis loco dare ea quae in te possint reciprocata vicissitudine retorqueri?

author: Arnobius
english: 60.1. Since therefore the origins, causes, and reasons of so many and such great things flee even you yourselves, and you can neither say nor explain what was done or why, or why it ought not to have been, you tear and rend our modesty—we who confess that we do not know what cannot be known and do not care to seek or investigate what it is most clear cannot be grasped, though human suspicion stretch itself through a thousand hearts.

2. And therefore Christ—God, though against your will, God, I say, Christ (for this must often be said, that the hearing of unbelievers may split and burst)—speaking by the command of God the Prince under the form of a human, since He knew mortals’ nature to be blind and unable to grasp any truth of things set even before the eyes, commanded that they hold as ascertained and known whatever they had persuaded themselves of, and not, hesitating for their suspicions, sow and stretch litigious questions;

3. He ordered us to leave and postpone all those things and not to cast fruitless thoughts upon matters far removed from our knowledge, but, as far as can be done, to set out toward the Lord of things with whole mind and soul, to be raised from these places and transfer into Him the suspended turnings of the breast, to keep perpetual memory of Him, and though He can be formed by no imagination, still to fashion for oneself some I-know-not-what breezes of His contemplation:

4. for from all the things that the obscurity of august divinity contains, He alone is undoubted, alone true, and about whom no one can hesitate unless mad and of insane despair—whom it is enough to know so that you know nothing else, and you have obtained true and greatest knowledge, fixed in the cognition of God the head of things.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 60.1. Cum igitur et vos ipsos tantarum ac tot rerum fugiant origines, fugiant causae, fugiant rationes, neque dicere neque explanare possitis, quid sit factum aut quare, aut cur oportuerit non esse, verecundiam convellitis et dilaceratis nostram, qui quae nequeunt sciri nescire nos confitemur neque ea conquirere aut investigare curamus quae comprehendi liquidissimum est non posse, quamvis mille per corda suspicio se porrigat atque intendat humana.

2. Et ideo Christus licet [in] vobis invitis deus, deus, inquam, Christus - hoc enim saepe dicendum est, ut infidelium dissiliat et dirumpatur auditus - dei principis iussione loquens sub hominis forma, cum mortalium sciret caecam esse naturam neque ullam posse comprehendere veritatem positarum nec ante oculos rerum, pro comperto habere et cognito quidquid sibi esse suasisset nec pro suis suspicionibus haesitare litigiosas serere atque intendere quaestiones,

3. omnia ista nos linquere et posthabere praecepit neque in res eas quae sint a nostra procul cognitione dimotae infructuosas inmittere cogitationes, sed, quantum fieri potis est, ad dominum rerum tota mente atque animo proficisci, sustolli ab his locis atque in eum traducere suspensas pectoris conversiones, memoriam eius habere perpetuam et licet nulla possit imaginatione formari, auras tamen nescio quas eius sibi contemplationis adfingere:

4. rebus enim ex omnibus, quas augustae continet divinitatis obscuritas, solum esse indubitabilem, solum verum et de quo nullus ambigere nisi amens possit et desperationis insanae, quem satis sit scire ut nihil aliud noveris, sisque veram et maximam scientiam consecutus in dei rerum capitis et cognitione defixus.

author: Arnobius
english: 16.1–2. And while we slip and hurry toward human bodies, from the worldly circles causes follow us by which we are evil and worst, burn with desires and anger, spend life in outrages, and are condemned to public lust by prostitution of bodies for sale. And how can bodies join themselves to incorporeals, or things made by God the Prince be led by weaker causes into the dishonors of vices?

16.3–6. Will you humans put down the inborn puff and eyebrow—you who claim God as father for yourselves and contend with Him that you have one immortality? Will you seek, track, and probe what you yourselves are, whose you are, by what father you are rated, what you do in the world, by what reason you are born, by what pact you spring forth to life? Will you, favor laid aside, perceive with silent thoughts that we are animals either like the rest or not distant by very much difference? For what is it that shows us differing from their likeness? Or what eminence so great is in us that we disdain to be enrolled in the number of animals?

16.7–12. From bones those bodies were founded and bound with sinews: and for us by like reason from bones bodies were founded and bound with sinews. They take breaths with nostrils and return them by panting: and we likewise draw spirit and breathe with frequent passages. They are distinguished into feminine and masculine kinds: into as many sexes we too were formed by our author. They bring forth offspring through wombs and procreate by bodily unions; and we are born by joinings of bodies and are poured out from mothers’ bellies. They are sustained by food and drink and drive out superfluous foulnesses below: and we are sustained by food and drink and pour out what nature rejects through the same paths. They all have care to forbid death-bearing hunger and watch for food: what else do we do in such occupations of life except seek things by which hunger’s danger is avoided and unhappy anxiety set down? They feel diseases and starvations and at last are loosed by old age: what then? are we immune from these evils and not by the same reason broken by diseases and destroyed by old age’s wasting?

16.13. But if that also is true which is said in more secret mysteries—that the souls of the wicked go into cattle and other beasts after they are severed from human bodies—it is more plainly proven that we are neighbors and not parted by longer intervals, since the same one thing is for us and for them through which we are said to be animals and to drive vital motion.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 16.1. Ac dum ad corpora labimur et properamus humana, ex mundanis circulis secuntur nos causae, quibus mali simus et pessimi, cupiditatibus atque iracundia ferveamus, exerceamus in flagitiis vitam et in libidinem publicam venalium corporum prostitutione damnemur. 2. Et quemadmodum se possunt incorporalibus corpora coniungere aut a deo principe res factae ab infirmioribus causis ad vitiorum dehonestamenta traduci?

3. Vultis homines insitum typhum superciliumque deponere, qui deum vobis adsciscitis patrem et cum eo contenditis immortalitatem habere vos unam? 4. Vultis quaerere pervestigare rimari, quid sitis vos ipsi, cuius sitis, censeamini quo patre, quid in mundo faciatis, quanam ratione nascamini, quo pacto prosiliatis ad vitam? 5. Vultis favore deposito cogitationibus tacitis pervidere animantia nos esse aut consimilia ceteris aut non plurima differitate distantia? 6. Quid est enim, quod nos ab eorum indicet similitudine discrepare? Vel quae in nobis eminentia tanta est, ut animantium numero dedignemur adscribi?

7. Ex ossibus illis fundata sunt corpora et nervorum conligatione devincta: et nobis comparili ratione ex ossibus fundata sunt corpora et nervorum conligatione devincta. 8. Auras accipiunt naribus et per anhelitum reciprocatas reddunt: et nos spiritum consimiliter ducimus et respiramus commeatibus crebris. 9. Femininis generibus masculinisque distincta sunt: in totidem et nos sexus nostro sumus ab auctore formati. Edunt per uteros fetus et corporalibus conciliis procreant; et nos corporum coniugationibus nascimur et ex alveis fundimur atque emittimur matrum. 10. Cibo sustentantur et potu et superfluas foeditates inferioribus egerunt abiciuntque posticis: et nos cibo sustentamur et potu et quod natura iam respuit per eosdem effundimus tramites. 11. Cura illis est omnibus famem prohibere mortiferam et necessario invigilare pro victu: quid aliud nos tantis agimus in occupationibus vitae, nisi ut ea quaeramus quibus famis periculum devitetur et infelix sollicitudo ponatur? 12. Morbos illa et inedias sentiunt et ad ultimum senectute solvuntur: quid enim? nos immunes malis ab his sumus et non eadem ratione morborum incommoditatibus frangimur et senectutis destruimur tabe?

13. Quod si et illud est verum, quod in mysteriis secretioribus dicitur, in pecudes atque alias beluas ireanimas improborum, postquam sunt humanis corporibus seiunctae, manifestius comprobatur vicinos nos esse neque intervallis longioribus disparatos. Siquidem res eadem nobis et illis est una, per quam esse animantia dicimur et motum agitare vitalem.

author: Arnobius
english: 26.1. But when I hear the soul called I-know-not-what outstanding thing, near and next to God, knowing all things as it arrives here from superior ages, I refuse that it learn and instead want it to teach, and not become from learned an elementary pupil, as they say, but, keeping its own things, bind itself round with earthly bodies. For unless the matter stands so, how can it be discerned whether what it hears it remembers or learns, when it is much easier to believe that it learns what it does not know than that it has forgotten what it knew a little before?

2. “By the opposition of the body it loses the recollection of prior things.” — And where is that which is said, that souls have an incorporeal substance? For what is of no body is not hindered by another’s opposition, nor can that lose anything from its own stock which cannot sustain the touch of an opposed thing. For as number, constituted without bodies, though buried by a thousand bodies, stands intact and inviolable, so souls, if they are incorporeal as alleged, must suffer no oblivion of prior things, though the solidest bindings of bodies have wrapped them.

3. What of this—that the same reasoning not only shows they are not incorporeal, but also strips them all of immortality and applies them to limits by which accustomed life is wont to be ended? For whatever, when some cause comes on, is so changed and turned that it cannot keep its integrity must be judged passive in nature. And what is ready and exposed to passion declares by that very passibility intervening that it is corruptible.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 26.1. Sed ego cum audio nescio quid praestans animam dici, deo vicinum et proximum, scientem huc omnia superioribus adventare de saeculis, nolo illam discere set docere nec ex docta ut dicitur elementariam fieri sed retinentem res suas corporibus semet circumligare terrenis. Nisi enim sese habuerit res ita, discerni qui poterit, utrumne illud quod audit reminiscatur an discat, cum multo facilius <sit> credere, discere illam quod nesciat quam oblitam quod paulo ante sciebat.

2. ''Ex oppositu corporis amittit repetentiam priorum'' [Plat., Phaedr. 248 a-c]. - Et ubi est illud quod dicitur, incorporalis animas substantiam non habere? Quod enim nullius est corporis, oppositione alterius non inpeditur nec potest aliquid sua de re perdere id quod non potest tactum rei oppositae sustinere. Ut enim numerus sine corporibus constitutus, quamvis mille corporibus obruatur, intactus et inviolabilis constat, ita necesse est animas, si sunt ut perhibetur incorporeae, oblivionem priorum nullam pati, quamvis eas solidissimae corporum circumligaverint vinctiones.

3. Quid quod eadem ratio non tantum incorporeas indicat eas non esse, verum etiam privat immortalitate has omnis et ad fines adplicat quibus vita consueta est terminari? Quicquid enim causa ingruente nonnulla ita mutatur et vertitur ut integritatem suam retinere non possit, id necesse est iudicari natura esse passivum. Quod autem est promptum atque expositum passioni, corruptibile esse ipsa passibilitate interveniente denuntiat.

author: Arnobius
english: 56.1. All the other matters that are usually tossed in questions and controversies—from what parents they arise or by what authors they are made—we neither strive to know nor care to inquire or investigate: we leave all things to their own causes and do not judge them joined and applied to that which we seek.

2. For what is there that human wits do not dare to shake and dissolve in the zeal of contradiction, even if what they try to weaken is pure and clear and fortified by the seal of truth? Or what again can they not assert with plausible arguments, though it be most openly false, though an evident and plain lie? For when someone has persuaded himself that a thing is or is not, he loves to assert what he opines and to outstrip others in acumen, especially if the matter is remote and hidden and wrapped in nature’s fog.

3. Some of the wise judge the world neither to have been born nor to be about to perish in any time; some call it immortal though they write that it was born and begotten; to a third it is pleasing to say that it was both born and begotten and will perish by ordinary necessity. And though of these three opinions one must be true, still all have arguments by which they confirm their own decrees and snatch away and weaken others’ opinions.

4. This same world some hand down as standing from four elements, others from two, a third from single ones; there are who say that from none of these, but that indivisible bodies are its matter and first origin. And though of these one sentence is true, yet none of them is certain; here too arguments are ready for all, by which they establish what they say as true and refute falsities set in others’ opinions.

5. So also some deny gods altogether; others say they doubt whether they are anywhere; others that they exist and do not care for human things; still others allege that they both take part in mortal affairs and administer earthly reckonings.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 56.1. Caetera quaecumque sunt alia, quae in quaestionibus adsolent controversiisque versari, quibus genitoribus orta sint vel quibus auctoribus fiant, neque nosse contendimus neque inquirere aut vestigare curamus: suis omnia relinquimus causis nec ad id quod expetimus esse nobis adiuncta atque adplicata iudicamus.

2. Quid est enim, quod humana ingenia labefactare, dissolvere studio contradictionis non audeant, quamvis illud quod infirmare moliuntur sit purum et liquidum et veritatis obsignatione munitum? Aut quid rursus adserere verisimilibus argumentis non queunt, quamvis sit apertissime falsum, quamvis evidens manifestumque mendacium? Cum enim sibi persuaserit quis, esse aliquid aut non esse, amat quod opinatur adserere et acumine alios anteire, maxime si agatur res submota et abdita et caligine involuta naturae.

3. Mundum quidam ex sapientibus aestimant neque esse natum neque ullo esse in tempore periturum; immortalem nonnulli, quamvis eum conscribant esse gnatum et genitum; tertiis vero conlibitum dicere est, et esse natum et genitum et ordinaria necessitate periturum. Et cum ex istis opinionibus trinis unam esse necesse sit veram, cunctis tamen argumenta non desunt quibus et sua decreta confirment et aliorum subripiant et labefaciant scita.

4. Eundem hunc alii elementis ex quatuor tradunt et pronuntiant stare, ex geminis alii, ex singulis tertii, sunt qui ex his nullo set individua corpora eius esse materiem et primam originem dicant. Cumque ex his vera sit una sententia, at nulla ex his certa, similiter hic quoque argumenta omnibus praesto sunt, quibus et ea quaedicunt vera esse constituant et redarguant positas in aliorum sententiis falsitates.

5. Sic et deos nonnulli esse abnegant prorsus dubitare se alii an sint uspiam dicunt; alii vero existere neque humana curare: immo alii perhibent et rebus interesse mortalium et terrenas administrare rationes.

author: Arnobius
english: 75.1. You oppose and retort: “Why was the Savior sent so late?” — In infinite, perpetual ages nothing at all should be called late. For where there is no end and no beginning, nothing is premature, nothing tardy. Time is known from limits and extremities, which the series and boundless continuation of ages cannot have.

2. What if the very things to which help had to be brought demanded that opportunity of time? What if things of old were of one condition, later things of another? What if the ancients had to be aided one way, and later people had to be provided for another way?

3. Do you not hear your own letters recalling that there were once demigod men, heroes, with huge and vast bodies? Do you not read that infants under their mothers’ breasts uttered a hundred-year wail, whose bones dug up in various regions made their finders believe they were remains of human limbs?

4. It can therefore be that almighty God, God alone, then at last sent Christ after the race of humans began to be of a more broken and weaker nature—ours. If what was done today could have been done before thousands of years, the highest King would have done it; or if after as many thousands what was done today ought to have been fulfilled, nothing compelled God not to wait for the necessary measures of times. His affairs are carried through by fixed reasons, and what has once been decreed to happen can be changed by no novelty.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.

added_allusions.reason: Christ died at the right time

latin: 75.1. Tu opponas et referas: ''Cur tam sero emissus est sospitator?''. - In infinitis, perpetuis saeculiis nihil omnino dicendum est serum. Ubi enim finis et initium nullum est, nihil praematurum est, nihil tardum. Tempus enim a finibus et extremitatibus noscitur, quae habere non potest series et immoderata continuatio saeculorum.

2. Quid enim si res ipsae, quibus opem conveniebat ferri, oportunitatem istam temporis exigebant? quid si alterius condicionis antiqua, alterius fuere sequentia? quid si priscis aliter subveniri, aliter debuit posterioribus consuli?

3. Nonne litteras auditis commemorantes vestras fuisse homines olim semideos, heroas, cum immanibus corporibus atque vastis? non infantes sub uberibus matrum centenarios legitis edidisse vagitum, quorum ossa variis in regionibus eruta vi? repertoribus fecerunt fidem humanorum reliquias esse membrorum?

4. Potest ergo fieri, ut tum demum emiserit Christum deus omnipotens, deus solus, postquam gens hominum fractior et infirmior coepit nostra esse natura. Si quod hodie factum est, ante milia fieri potuisset annorum, fecisset istud rex summus, aut si post totidem milia id quod hodie factum est debuisset inpleri, nihil deum cogebat necessarias temporum non expectare mensuras. Rationibus fixis peraguntur res eius et quod semel decretum est fieri nulla potest novitate mutari.

author: Arnobius
english: 72.1. “But your religions precede ours by many years, and for that reason are truer because they are fortified by the authority of antiquity.” — And what does it profit them to go before by as many years as you like, when they began from a fixed time—or what space are two thousand years of ages compared with so many thousands?

2. And yet, lest we seem to betray the cause by such long concealment, tell us, if it is not troublesome: does almighty and first God seem to you a novel thing, and do those who honor and cultivate Him stir up and introduce unheard-of, unknown, sudden religions?

3. Is there anything older than He, or can anything be found that precedes Him in thing, time, or name? Is He not alone unbegotten, alone immortal and perpetual? Who is the head and fountain of things if not He Himself? To whom does eternity owe this very thing that it is called eternity if not to Him? That infinite ages go forth—is it not accomplished from His perpetuity? That is undoubted and true.

4. Therefore what we follow is not new, but we learned late what ought to be followed and cultivated, or where it was fitting to fix the hope of salvation and place saving helps. For He had not yet shone who would show the way to wanderers and to those set in deepest fog, send in the light of knowledge, and scatter the blindness of ignorance.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
2.72 antiquity vs first God / spes salutis.
latin: 72.1. ''At religiones vestrae multis annis praecedunt nostram, et eo sunt veriores quod vetustatis auctoritate munitae sunt''. | f. 61? / - Et quid eas prodest annis quam plurimis anteire, cum a certo coeperint tempore, autspatii cuius sunt milia annorum duo saeculorum tantis comparata cum milibus?

2. Ac tamen ne causam tam longa prodere dissimulatione videamur, nisi molestum est, dicite, omnipotens et primus deus novella vobis videtur res esse, et qui eum venerantes colunt, inauditas incognitas repentinas agitare atque inducere religiones?

3. Estne illo antiquius quicquam, aut quod eum praecedat re tempore nomine potest aliquid inveniri? Nonne solus ingenitus, immortalis et perpetuus solus est? quis caput ac fons rerum ests non ipse? cui debet aeternitas hoc ipsum quod nuncupatur aeternitas? non ipsi? infinita ut prodeant saecula, non ex eius perpetuitate perficitur? Indubitabile istud et verum.

4. Non ergo quod sequimur novum est, sed nos sero addidicimus quidnam sequi oporteat <ac>colere aut ubinam conveniret spem salutis adfigere et salutaria subsidia conlocare. Nondum enim adfulserat qui viam monstraret errantibus et caligine in altissima constitutis cognitionis lumen inmitteret et ignorationis discuteret caecitatem.

author: Arnobius
english: 29.1. Since things are so, cease, I ask, cease valuing small things and of slight name at huge prices; cease enrolling the proletarian man among the first classic and head-counted orders when he is needy, poor of household and of a poor hut, and never deserved to be named of patrician brightness. For when you ought, as true authors of right and integrity, to break the puff and arrogance on whose wings we all are lifted and swollen with emptiness of vanities, you not only think those evils happen, but—what is far heavier—you have added causes by which vices would grow and incorrigible wickedness would remain.

2. For who of humans, though he be of a character always fleeing by infamy and ignominy, when he hears it said especially by wise men that souls are immortal and not subject to the laws of the fates, will not rush headlong into all outrages, not meet and attempt illicit things secure and unshaken, and finally not lavish on his desires all that powerless lust has ordered, fortified besides by the freedom of impunity?

3. For what will forbid him from doing these things? Fear of a higher power and divine judgment? And how will he be terrified by the horror of any dread, who has been persuaded that he is as immortal as the first God Himself and that nothing about him can be judged by Him, since there is one immortality in both and the one cannot be vexed by equality of the other’s condition?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.

added_allusions.reason: fear of falling into God’s hands

latin: 29.1. Quae cum ita se habeant, desinite, quaeso, desinite res parvas atque exigui nominis immanibus pretiis aestimare, desinite hominem proletari<us> cum sit classicis et capite < cum > censeatur adscribere ordinibus primis, cum sit inops, pauper lare et tugurii pauperis nec patriciae claritatis unquam meritus nuncupari. Cum enim vos oporteret veros recti atque integritatis auctores typhum et adrogantiam frangere, quorum alis cuncti extollimur et inanium distendimur vanitate, non tantum ** accidere mala ista censetis, verum, quod gravius multo est, addidistis causas quibus et vitia crescerent et inemendabilis nequitia permaneret.

2. Quis est enim hominum, quamvis ille sit indolis infamia semper atque ignominiosa fugientis, qui cum dici exaudiat viris ab sapientibus maxime, immortalis animas esse nec fatorum esse obnoxias legibus, non in omnia flagitia praeceps se ruat, non securus, intrepidus res obeat atque adgrediatur inlicitas, non denique omnia suis cupiditatibus largiatur quae libido inpotens iusserit, inpunitatis praeterea etiam libertate munita?

3. Quid enim prohibebit quominus haec faciat? metus supernae potestatis iudiciumque divinum? et qui poterit territari formidinis alicuius horrore, cui fuerit persuasum tam se esse immortalem quam ipsum deum primum nec ab eo iudicari quicquam de se posse, cum sit una immortalitas in utroque nec in alterius altera condicionis possit aequalitate vexari?

author: Arnobius
english: Does Christ not free all with equal munificence? Does he not free equally when he calls all equally? He opens the fountain of life to all; no one is forbidden to drink.

If you scorn the gift, why does the one who invites wait? His only part is to set the fruit of his kindness under the decision of your own right (sub tui iuris arbitrio). Plato said the lot of choosing a life is not God’s doing as a cause forced on another; free decision (voluntatis libertas) sits in the power of the one who willed.
God lays necessity on no one; he terrifies no one with bullying fear. Our salvation is not so necessary to him that he gains or loses something if he makes us gods or lets us dissolve into nothing.
translator_notes: Obscure to most Logos users; sharp pagan-world apologetic.
notes: Locus remapped from ANF-style 2.29 to Latin Library 2.64 where voluntatis libertas / non necessitas sits.

author: Arnobius
english: 24.1. Why in the Meno, O Plato, do you ask a little boy things fitted to the reasonings of number and try from his answers to prove that we do not learn but return into the memory of what we knew of old? If he answers you truly—for it is not fitting for us to refuse faith to the things you say—he is led not by knowledge of things but by intelligence, and from the fact that he has some numbers known from daily uses it comes about that he follows when asked and the very addition of multiplication always leads him on.

2. But if you truly trust that immortal souls fly hither full of knowledge, stop asking that adolescent whom you see acquainted with affairs and set within the bounds of humanity: call to yourself that forty-year-old and ask from him not something abstruse, not wrapped up, not about triangles or squares, what a cube or a power is, a sesquioctave or a final sesquitertian, but what sits in the middle—ask what sum twice two, twice three make.

3. We wish to see, we wish to know, what he answers when asked, whether he resolves the sought question. Will he then feel, though his ears lie open, whether you are saying something, asking something, or demanding that something be answered you from him? And will he not stand speechless and mute like some log or, as it is said, a Marpesian cliff, ignorant and not knowing this very thing—whether you are conversing with yourself or with another, whether that is speech which you put forth or a sound of voice signifying nothing of things but drawn out in empty continuation?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 24.1. Quid in Menone, o Plato [Plato, Men. 82], quaedam rationibus numeri admota ex puerculo sciscitaris et ex eius niteris responsionibus comprobare, quae discamus non discere sed in eorum memoriam quae antiquitus noveramus redire? Qui si tibi vere respondet - non enim nos convenit fidem rebus abiudicare quas dicis - non rerum scientia sed intellegentia ducitur, et ex eo quod aliquos numeros cottidianis habet ex usibus notos fit ut sequatur rogatus et ipsa illum semper multipilicationis adducat accessio.

2. Quodsi vere confidis immortales huc animas et plenas scientiae pervolare, adulescentulum istum rogare desinito, quem esse conspicis gnarum rerum et humanitatis esse in finibus constitutum: quadragenarium istum ad te voca et ex eo percontare non abstrusum aliquid, non involutum, non de triangulis, non de quadratis, quid sit cubus aut dynamis, sesqueoctavus aut sesquetertius ultimus , sed quod in medio situm est, bis bina, bis terna quam efficiant summulam quaerito.

3. Volumus videre, volumus scire, quid rogatus respondeat, an inquisitam expediat quaestionem. Ita ille sensurus est, quamvis ei pateant aures, an aliquid dicas, an aliquid quaeras, an tibi ab sese responderi aliquid postules? Et non stipes ut aliquis aut Marpesia ut dictum est [Verg. Aen. 6, 471] rupes stabit elinguis et mutus, hoc ipsum ignorans et nesciens, secum potius an cum altero conloquaris, cum altero sermocineris an secum, oratio sit ista quam promis an sonitus vocis nihil rerum significans sed inani continuatione pertractus?

author: Arnobius
english: 47.1. "But if God is not the parent and begetter of souls," you say, "by what author were they begotten and by what reason brought forth?" — If you wish to hear it unpainted and not drawn from any show of voice, we likewise confess that we are ignorant of that, do not know it, and judge that knowledge of so great a matter surpasses not only our weakness and fragility but even that of all the powers that are in the world and that have seized for themselves by mortals' opinions the name of divinities.

2. But because we deny they are of God, must we show whose they are? That does not follow of necessity. For if we deny that flies, beetles and bugs, dormice, weevils and moths are the work of the almighty King, it is not to be demanded of us in consequence that we say who made and instituted them: we can without any blame not know who gave them origin too, and still maintain that things so superfluous, so empty, so pertaining to no reasons—nay sometimes even harmful and bringing injuries upon necessities—were not brought forth by God from on high.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 47.1. ''Sed si parens et genitor animarum, inquitis, deus non est, quo auctore progenitae et qua sunt ratione prolatae?''. - Si infucata vultis audire nec ab aliqua vocis ostentatione deducta, item confitemur nos istud ignorare, nescire scientiamque tantae rei non tantum nostram ducimus infirmitatem fragilitatemque transire, verum etiam potestatum quae in mundo sunt omnium et quae numina se esse opinionibus usurpavere mortalium.

2. Sed quas dei negamus, cuius sint debemus ostendere? Minime istud necessario sequitur. Non enim si negemus muscas scarabeos et cimices, nitedulas curculiones et tineas omnipotentis esse opus regig, sequaciter postulandum a nobis est, ut quis ea fecerit institueritque dicamus: possumus enim nulla cum reprehensione nescire, quis et illis originem dederit, et optinere non esse deo ab superiore prolata tam supervacua, tam vana, tam ad nullas pertinentia rationes, quinimmo aliquando et noxia et necessariis inportantia laesiones.

author: Arnobius
english: 39.1. Unless perhaps the king of the world—whom it is utmost rashness to utter from a human mouth—sent hither souls begotten from himself so that those who had been goddesses with him, free of bodily touch and temporary bound, should be plunged into human seeds, spring from women's births, utter and continue most silly wailings, suck milk-filled breasts, smear and soak themselves in their own filth, then be led frightened to silence by a nurse's motions and rattles when heard.

2. Did he send souls so that those who had been simple and of recently harmless goodness should learn among humans to pretend, dissemble, lie, circumvent, deceive, catch by flattering humility, roll one thing in the mind and promise another on the face, ensnare, trick the unknowing with wiles and ambushes, seek poisons through countless arts of malice and be shaped for the moment by mobility of deceit?

3. Did he send souls so that those living in peaceful placid tranquillity should take from bodies causes to become savage and monstrous, carry grudges and enmities, join wars, storm and overturn cities, oppress and enslave themselves under servitude's yoke and at last become another's power with birth-condition changed?

4. Did he send souls so that, made forgetful of truth and having forgotten what God is, they should entreat inert images, address wood, bronze and stones as divine powers, demand help from slain animals' gore, make no mention of themselves—nay, that some from these should doubt they exist or deny utterly that any exists?

5. Did he send souls so that those who in their own seats had been of one mind, equal in understanding and knowledge, after putting on mortal forms should disagree by splits of opinions, one thing seem just to some and another useful and right to others, contend about things to seek and flee, set for others limits of evils and goods, and that obscurity of things should face those wanting to know the truth and, as if bereft of eyes' lights, they should see nothing certain and be led into error through doubtful paths of suspicions?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 39.1.
