Nisi forte rex mundi, is quem temeritatis est maximae humano ex ore depromere, idcirco ex se genitas huc animas misit, ut quae fuerant apud se deae, corporei tactus et temporariae circumscriptionis expertes, humana inmergerentur in semina, feminarum ex genitalibus prosilirent, ineptissimos ederent continuarentque vagitus, exsugerent fellitantes mammas, proluvie linerent et madidarent se sua, tunc ad silentium pavidae nutricis motibus et crepitaculis adducerentur auditis.

2. Idcirco animas misit, ut quae fuerant simplices et bonitatis nuper innoxiae, simulare in hominibus discerent, dissimulare mentiri circumscribere fallere, adulatoria humilitate captare, mente aliud volvere aliud in facie polliceri, inlaqueare, decipere dolis atque insidiis nescios, per innumeras artes malitiarum venena conquirere et ad usum temporis pellaciae mobilitate formari?

3. Idcirco animas misit, ut in pacata et placida tranquillitate degentes adsumerent ex corporibus causas quibus ferae fierent et immanes, simultates atque inimicitias gererent, consererent inter se bella, expugnarent atque everterent civitates, servitutis opprimerent et manciparent se iugo et ad ultimum fierent alterius altera potestatis natalium condicione mutata?

4. Idcirco animas misit, ut inmemores veritatis effectae et quidnam esset deus oblitae simulacris inertibus supplicarent, ligna aera et lapides divina adloquerentur ut numina, auxilia poscerent ex caesorum animantium cruore, nullam sui facerent mentionem, quinimmo ex: his aliae ut dubitarent se esse aut ullum esse penitus abnegarent?

5. Idcirco animas misit, ut quae in sedibus propriis mente fuerant una, intellectu et scientia paribus, postquam formas induere mortales, opinionum discriminibus dissiderent, aliud aliis iustum, aliud utile videretur et rectum, de appetendis rebus fugiendisque certarent, malorum ac bonorum alios aliae constituerent fines, veritatem cupientibus noscere rerum opponeretur obscuritas et velut oculorum luminibus viduae nihil certum viderent et per ancipites semitas suspicionum inducerentur errore?

author: Arnobius
english: 68.1. On the Alban mount of old it was allowed to sacrifice no bulls but of snowy whiteness: did you not change that custom and religion and, that reddish ones might be given, settle it by senate decree? When Romulus and Pompilius reigned, entrails were burned for the gods thoroughly cooked and moist: under king Tullus did you not begin, despising the ancient observance, to offer them half-raw and lightly inspired?

2. Before Hercules' coming into Italy, when by Apollo's warning human heads were sacrificed to father Dis and Saturn, did you not likewise change this custom also by shrewd deceit and ambiguity of names?

3. Since therefore you yourselves have followed now those customs, now other laws, and many things have been repudiated and despised by you either when errors were recognized or by attention to better things, what have we done against common sense and judgment if we have chosen greater and more certain things and have not suffered ourselves to be held by the religions of false things?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 68.1. In Albano antiquitus monte nullos alios licebat quam nivei tauros immolare candoris: nonne istum morem religionemque mutastis atque, ut rufulos liceret dari, senatus constitutum sanctione? Cum Romulo Pompilioque regnantibus percocta plane ac madida concremarentur diis exta, nonne rege sub Tullo semicruda coepistis et leviter animata porrigere prisca observatione contempta?
2. Ante adventum in Italiam Herculis cum ex Apollinis monitu patri Diti ac Saturno humanis capitibus supplicaretur, et hunc similiter morem non fraude callidula et nominum ambiguitate mutastis?

3. Cum igitur et vos ipsi modo illos mores modo alias leges fueritis secuti, multaque vel erroribus cognitis vel animadversione meliorum sint a vobis repudiata, contempta, quid est a nobis factum contra sensum iudiciumque commune, si maiora et certiora delegimus nec sumus nos passi falsorum religionibus attineri?

author: Arnobius
english: 27.1. Therefore if souls also lose all they had known when occupied by bodily bonds, they must necessarily suffer something that makes them put on the blindness of forgetfulness. For neither, having suffered nothing at all or preserving their own integrity, can they lay aside knowledge of things or pass into other habits without changeability of themselves.

2. But we judge that what is one, what is immortal, what is simple, in whatever matter it is, must necessarily always keep its own nature and ought not and cannot suffer anything, if only it thinks to be perpetual and to cling within the bounds of its own immortality. For every passion is a door of death and destruction, a way leading to death and bringing to things an inevitable discharge: which if souls feel and yield to its touch and onsets, life is for them by use, not handed over by ownership—though some infer otherwise and place the faith of so great a matter in their own argumentations.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 27.1. Ergo si et animae perdunt omne quod noverant, corporalibus vinculis occupatae, patiantur necesse est aliquid quod eas efficiat oblivionis induere caecitatem. Neque enim nihil omnino perpessae aut integritatem conservantes suam possunt rerum scientiam ponere aut in alios habitus sine sui mutabilitate transire.

2. Atquin nos arbitramur, quod est unum, quod immortale, quod simplex, quacumque in re fuerit, necessario semper suam retinere naturam nec debere aut posse aliquid perpeti, si modo e sse perpetuum cogitat et in finibus propriae immortalitatis haerere. Omnis enim passio leti atque interitus ianua est, ad mortem ducens via et inevitabilem rebus adferens functionem: quam si sentiunt animae et tactui eius atque incursionibus cedunt, usu et illis est vita, non mancipio tradita, quamvis aliter quidam inferant et rei tantae fidem suis in argumentationibus ponant.

author: Arnobius
english: 51.1. But our answer is a laugh to you, because when we deny that souls are royal offspring we do not bring against you from what causes and origins they were procreated. — For what kind of crime is it either to be ignorant of some matter or to profess without dissembling that you do not know what you do not know: or who seems more worthy of mockery, he who assumes for himself no knowledge of some dark matter, or he who thinks that from himself he most openly knows that which leaps over human notion and which is wrapped in blind obscurities?

2. If the nature of each thing is thoroughly looked at, you also are in a similar cause to that which you rebuke in us. For because you say that souls descend from the king himself and succeed into human forms, you do not say something explored and set in the light of most manifest truth. For you conjecture, you do not know; you suspect, you do not hold: for if to know is to contain in the mind that which you yourself have seen or learned, you can say you have never seen any of the things you assert—that is, souls descending from the upper seat and region.

3. You therefore use suspicion, not the faith of expressed cognition. And what is suspicion except an uncertain opinion of things and a casting of the mind brought in upon nothing set forth? Therefore he who suspects does not hold and does not walk set in the light of cognition. And if that is true and fixed, before right and most wise judges that suspicion of yours also in which you trust is to be held for ignorance.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.

added_allusions.reason: thinks he knows; knows not as he ought

latin: 51.1. Sed risui vobis est nostra responsio, quod cum regias suboles esse animas abnegemus, non referamus contra, ex quibus sint causis atque originibus procreatae. - Quod est enim criminis genus, aut rei esse alicuius ignarum aut ipsum quod nescias sine aliqua profiteri dissimulatione nescire: aut uter magis videtur inrisione esse dignissimus vobis, qui sibi scientiam nullam tenebrosae rei alicuius adsumit, an ille qui retur se ex se apertissime scire id quod humanam transiliat notionem et quod sit caecis obscuritatibus involutum?

2. Si penitus spectetur rei cuiusque natura, in simili et vos estis quam in nobis reprehenditis causa. Non enim quia dicitis ab ipso animas rege descendere ac succedere in hominum formas, exploratum aliquid dicitis et in luce positum manifestissimae veritatis. Conicitis enim, non scitis; suspicamini, non tenetis: nam si scire est illud quod ipse tu videris aut cognoveris animo continere, nihil eorum quae adseritis potestis vos dicere aliquando vidisse, id est, animas sede ab supera et regione descendere.

3. Suspicione ergo utimini, non cognitionis expressae fide. Quid est autem suspicio, nisi opinatio rerum incerta et <in>nihil expositum iaculatio mentis inlata? Ergo qui suspicatur, non tenet nec in lumine positus cognitionis incedit. Quodsi verum et fixum est, apud rectos et sapientissimos iudices et ista vestra qua fiditis pro ignoratione est habenda suspicio.

author: Arnobius
english: 54.1. "Can anything then," someone will say, "happen apart from God's will?" — We must examine carefully and look with no small care lest, while we think we honor God by such a question, we slide into the opposite impiety, destroying the eminence of his majesty.

2. "By what reason, for what cause?" — Because if all things are accomplished by his will and nothing can arise or fall among things without his nod, it necessarily follows that all evils also are understood to spring by his will.

3. But if we should wish to say the contrary, rejecting from him the causes of the worst things, that he is conscious of no evil and generator of none, then either the worst things will begin to appear to happen against his will or—what is monstrous to say—with him not knowing, unaware, and I-know-not. Again, if we should wish to say that there are no evils, as we have found it thought and pleasing to some, all peoples and entire nations will cry out, showing us their tortures and many forms of dangers by which at every point the human race is burned and torn.

4. Then they will ask us: "Why, if there are no evils, do you abstain from certain works and crimes? why do you not do all that impatient lust has ordered and commanded? why finally do you set penalties by terrible laws against the guilty? For what more monstrous stupidity can be found than to contend that there are no evils and yet to destroy and condemn sinners as if they were evil?"
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 54.1. ''Ergone, inquiet aliquis, sine dei voluntate quicquam potis est fieri?''. - Considerandum est nobis sollicite et cura inspiciendum non parva, ne dum honorare nos deum tali interrogatione censemus, in contrarium labamur nefas maiestatis eius eminentiam destruentes.

2. ''Qua ratione, qua causa?''. - Quoniam si cuncta eius voluntate confiunt nec citra eius nutum quicquam potest in rebus vel provenire vel cadere, necessario sequitur, <ut> mala etiam cuncta voluntate eius intellegantur enasci.

3. Sin autem dicere voluerimus contra, pessimorum ab eo reicientes causas, mali esse conscium generatoremque nullius, incipient evideri aut eo invito res pessimae fieri aut, quod sit immane dixisse, nesciente, ignaro ac nescio. Rursus autem si dicere nulla esse voluerimus mala, sicut esse nonnullis opinatum et placitum repperimus, reclamabunt cunctae gentes universaeque nationes, cruciatus nobis ostentantes suos et discriminum species multiformes, quibus puncta per singula genus uritur et laceratur humanum.

4. Tum deinde a nobis exquirent: ''Cur, mala si nulla sunt, ab operibus vos certis et facinoribus abstinetis? cur non omnia facitis quae inpatiens iusserit atque inperaverit libido? cur in noxios denique terribilibus poenas constituitis legibus? Nam stoliditas inveniri quae inmanior potest, quam mala esse nulla contendere et tamquam malos perdere et condemnare peccantis?''.

author: Arnobius
english: 76.1. "Why then," he says, "if you serve an almighty God and trust that he has care of your salvation and safety, why does he suffer you to endure such great persecutions and undergo all kinds of penalties and tortures?"

2. — Let us ask in turn also why you, when you worship so many and so countless gods and build them sacred temples, fashion images of gold, slaughter flocks of living things, and cast all incense-boxes on altars full of frankincense, why you do not live immune from so many dangers and storms by which deadly and manifold fortunes drive you daily?

3. Why, I say, do your gods cease to turn away from you so many kinds of diseases and illnesses, shipwrecks, ruins, fires, pestilences, barrenness, loss of children and confiscation of goods, discords, wars, grudges, captivities of cities and servitudes with free births taken away?

4. But God also does not at all help us in cases of this kind. The cause is ready and plain. For nothing has been promised us for this life, nor has any help been pledged or aid decreed for those set in this little sack of flesh; rather we have been taught to count all threats of fortune, whatever they are, as small and to value them lightly, and if ever some heavier force should fall which must end in death, to ascribe the pleasure to misfortune and neither to fear nor to flee, so that we may more easily be stripped of bodily bonds and escape dark blindness.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.

added_allusions.reason: all who live godly suffer persecution

latin: 76.1. ''Cur ergo, inquit, si omnipotenti servitis deo et eum habere confiditis salutis atque incolumitatis vestrae curam, cur persecutiones patitur perpeti vos tantas atque omnia genera poenarum et suppliciorum subire?''.

2. - Perquiramus et nos contra, cur et vos, cum tantos et tam innumeros colatis deos cumque illis aedes constituatis sacras, simulacra effingatis ex auro, animantium mactetis greges, acerras omnes thuris plenis coniciatis altaribus, cur non immunes agitis tot discriminibus et procellis, quibus cotidie vos agunt exitiabiles multiplices que fortunae?

3. Cur, inquam, dii vestri cessant a vobis avertere tot morborum et valetudinum genera, naufragia ruinas incendia pestilentias sterilitatem, amissionem pignorum et proscriptionem bonorum, discordias bella simultates, captivitates urbium et sublatis ingenuitatibus servitutes?

4. Sed et nobis in huiusmodi casibus minime auxiliatur deus. Prompta et manifesta causa est. Nihil est enim nobis promissum ad hanc vitam nec in carunculae huius folliculo constitutis opis aliquid sponsum est auxiliique decretum; quinimmo edocti sumus minas omnes quaecunque sunt parvi ducere atque aestimare fortunae, ac si quando ingruerit vis quaepiam gravior, quam finem necesse sit consequi, adscribere infortunio voluptatem nec timere nec fugere quo facilius exui corporalibus possimus ex vinculis et tenebrosam evadere caecitatem.

author: Arnobius
english: 22.1. Where then do these things look? So that, since it has been believed that souls are divine, immortal from God, and fly to human bodies with all disciplines, we may test from that one whom we have wished to be raised in this manner whether the matter takes faith or has been lightly believed and presumed by a frustrable expectation.

2. Let there come forth for us one nourished in a covered solitude for as many years as you wish—twenty, thirty, nay when he has measured forty years—let him be brought into assemblies of mortals, and if it is true that he is a portion of principal substance, already living here derived glad from fountains of life, before he takes acquaintance of any thing or is imbued with human speech, let him give answer when asked who he himself is or by what father, in what regions he was brought forth, how or by what reason nourished, what work or business he celebrated as he ran through the age of prior time:

3. will he not then stand duller and blunter than every beast, log, rock—sent into new things never known to him before—about to be ignorant first of all of himself? Will he be able, if you ask, to show what the sun is, earth, seas, stars, clouds, mist, rains, thunders, snow, hail? will he be able to know what trees are, herbs or grasses, bull, horse or ram, camel, elephant or kite?
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 22.1. Quorsum igitur haec spectant? Ut, quoniam creditum est animas divinas a deo immortales esse et ad hominum corpora disciplinis cum omnibus advolare, experiamur ex isto quem hoc genere voluimus educari, capiatne res fidem an sit leviter credita et frustrabili expectatione praesumpta.

2. Procedat igitur nobis solitudine in operta nutritus quot vultis annos agens, vultis vicenarius, vultis tricenarius, immo cum annos fuerit quadraginta permensus, mortalium conciliis inferatur, et si verum est illum principalis esse substantiae portionem, iam laetae ex fontibus vitae derivatum hic agere, antequam notitiam rei sumat alicuius aut sermone imbuatur humano, det responsum rogatus, quisnam sit ipse aut quo patre, quibus sit in regionibus editus, quo pacto aut quanam ratione nutritus, quid operis aut negotii celebrans ante acti temporis decurrerit aevitatem:

3. ita ille non omni pecore ligno saxo obtunsior atque hebetior stabit, non missus in res novas et numquam sibi ante eognitas ipsum sese est ante omnia nesciturus? Poteritne, si quaeras, sol quid sit ostendere, terra maria sidera nubes nebula pluviae tonitrua nix grando? poterit arbores scire quid sint, herbae aut gramina, taurus equus aut aries, eamellus elephantus aut milvus?

author: Arnobius
english: 25.1. What do you say, O men attributing to yourselves more than enough from another's nobility? Is this that learned soul which you say, immortal, perfect, divine, holding the fourth place after God the prince of things and after the twin minds, and flowing from living bowls?

2. Is this that precious human endowed with most august reasonings, the so-called lesser world fashioned and formed into the likeness of the whole: better than no beast, as it appeared, blunter than wood, than rock, who does not know humans and always lives in mute solitudes, remains idle, thrives emptily, though he live countless years and never be loosed from bodily knots. But when he has reached schools and been trained by teachers' institutions, he is made prudent, learned, and puts off the ignorance he had lately had.

3. And the ass and the ox likewise by use and continual compelling learn to plow and to grind; the horse to undergo the yoke and recognize turns in the course; the camel to lower itself whether when it takes burdens or when it lays them down; the dove released to fly back to the master's seats; the dog when it has found prey to restrain and hold its bark; the parrot to restore words and the raven to bring forth names.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 25.1. Quid dicitis, o viri plus quam satis est vobis ex aliena generositate tribuentes? Haecine est anima docta illa quam dicitis, immortalis perfecta divina, post deum principem rerum et post mentes geminas locum optinens quartum et afluens ex crateribus vivis?

2. Hic est ille pretiosus et rationibus homo augustissimis praeditus, mundus minor qui dicitur et totius in speciem similitudinis fabricatus atque formatus: nullo melior ut apparuit pecore, obtunsior ligno, saxo, qui nesciat homines et in mutis semper solitudinibus degat, demoretur iners, valeat inaniter , quamvis annis vivat innumeris et numquam nodis corporeis eximatur. Sed cum scholas attigerit et magistrorum fuerit institutionibus eruditus, efficitur prudens, doctus et quam nuper habuerat imperitiam ponit.

3. Et asellus et bos aeque usu atque adsiduitate cogendi discit arare ac molere, equus iugum subire et agnoscere in curriculo flexiones, camellus sese summittere sive cum sumit onera sive cum ponit, columba manumissa revolare ad dominicas sedes, canis cum invenerit praedam cohibere et continere latratum, verba psittacus et integrare et nomina corvus expromere.

author: Arnobius
english: 18.1. "They do not know clothing, to join chairs, ships and plows, nor finally the other furniture that household use demands." — Those are not gifts of knowledge but inventions of poorest necessity. Nor did the arts fall from heaven's inner chambers with the souls, but all were sought out and born here on earth and little by little by practice fused together as times advanced.

2. But if souls had the sciences which it is fitting for a divine and immortal kind to have, from the beginning all humans would know all things and there would be no age ignorant of any art or unprepared by experience of things. — Now indeed needy life, lacking many things, seeing that some things come about usefully by chance, while it imitates, tries and tests, while it slips, reshapes and changes, from continual correction has assembled the small tidy little sciences of the arts and by many times has brought them amended to one outcome.
translator_notes: Latin Library Adv. Nat. II lock.
latin: 18.1. ''Vestem illa non norunt, sellas naves atque aratra conpingere nec denique superlectilem ceteram quam familiaris usus exposcit''. - Non sunt ista scientiae munera sed pauperrimae necessitatis inventa. Neque cum animis artes caeli ex penetralibus ceciderunt, sed exquisitae et natae sunt in terris hic omnes et cum processu temporum paulatim meditatione conflatae.

2. Quodsi haberent scientias animae, quas genus et habere divinum atque immortale condignum est, ab initio homines cuncti omnia scirent nec saeculum essct ullum, quod artis esset ignarum alicuius aut rerum experientia non paratum. - Nunc vero inops vita et multarum indigens rerum fortuita conspiciens quaedam commodule provenire, dum imitatur experitur et temptat, dum labitur reformat immutat, ex adsidua reprehensione parvas et concinnavit scientiolas artium et ad unum exitum temporibus plurimis coemendata perduxit.
